**Why the values are "JavaScript".** A message about a value speaks
of the language the value is written in. `ZENO_NODE` names the Node
to use, as `ZENO_PYTHON` does (26.10). Only `node` is looked for: it
has no second name.

### 28.2 `node.global` and `node.new`, because JavaScript has both

Python has everything in a module, `builtins` included, and makes an
object by calling its class. JavaScript has neither: `JSON`, `Math`,
`Date` and `process` are in no module, and a class has to be given to
`new`.

`node.global(name)` gives what JavaScript has under that name
everywhere. `node.new(Class, a, b)` is `new Class(a, b)`.

**Why not make `Class(a, b)` do `new`.** Calling and `new` are two
things in JavaScript, and one value can take both with different
answers: `Date()` gives a str and `new Date()` a date. Guessing which
was meant would be right most of the time, and wrong with nothing to
say so.

**Alternatives rejected.** A module of pretend, `node.module("global")`:
it reads like a package that might not be installed. A `new` word in
the language: one module's need is not the language's.

### 28.3 A number that is whole is an int

JavaScript has one kind of number. One that is whole arrives as an
int, and any other as a float.

**Why.** Nearly every whole number a library returns is a count, a
size, an index or a year, and in Zeno those are ints: `items[n]` needs
one. Had every number arrived as a float, each of them would need
`int(...)` around it. The other way round costs less: an int goes
where a float is wanted.

**The cost.** `Math.sqrt(16.0)` is `4` and prints so, where Zeno's own
would print `4.0`. JavaScript does not keep which was written, so
there is nothing to go by.

**Past what is exact.** A whole number above 9007199254740991 arrives
as a float: by then JavaScript's number is not exact, and an int would
say that it is. An int of Zeno above that goes as a `BigInt`, since a
number would silently round it, and a `BigInt` that fits 64 bits comes
back as an int.

**`null` and `undefined` are both `none`.** Zeno has one nothing. A
field that an object does not have is therefore `none`, with no error.
That is JavaScript's rule and it is kept, because a library's own
documentation is written to it.

### 28.4 Named arguments are the object of options

`thing(1, key=3)` is `thing(1, {key: 3})`.

**Why.** JavaScript has no named arguments, and its libraries agree
on what stands in for them: one object, last. So the Zeno call reads
as the same call does with Python (26.4), and a program does not have
to build an object first for the common case.

**Why refuse nothing.** Whether a function takes options is not known
before it is called. Giving named arguments to one that does not is
one argument more than it reads, which JavaScript ignores.

`node.global("Object")(a=1, b="x")` makes such an object by itself,
which is `python.module("builtins").dict(a=1, b="x")` for JavaScript.
`node.new` takes no named arguments: no function that comes with Zeno
takes any, and one exception would be a second rule.

### 28.5 A promise is waited for

A call or a field that gives a promise gives what the promise
resolves to. One that is rejected is an error at that line.

**Why.** A Zeno program is one line after another. There is nothing
it could do with a promise but wait for it, and writing that wait on
every call would be a word that never changes. Because of it the
whole promise side of Node works today: `fs/promises`,
`timers/promises`, `fetch`.

**The cost.** A program cannot start two things and wait for both.
That waits for the day a function of Zeno can be given to JavaScript
(28.10).

### 28.6 What a method is called on

`thing.name` in JavaScript gives a function that no longer knows
`thing`. The helper keeps, with each value, the object it was read
from, and calls it on that. So `start.getFullYear()` works, and so
does keeping `start.getFullYear` in a name and calling it later, which
in JavaScript itself fails.

**Why go further than JavaScript does.** In Zeno a method taken from
an object stays that object's: `let get = box.get` and then `get()`
is `box.get()`. A Zeno program that reads a method and calls it later
is written to that rule.

### 28.7 `==` is the same object; `print` is what the console shows

`a == b` on two values of JavaScript is `a === b`.

**Why not compare what is in them.** JavaScript has no such
comparison, and each library that needs one writes its own. Inventing
one here would give answers no JavaScript program gets.
`node.copy(a) == node.copy(b)` compares what is in them, by Zeno's
rule, and says so.

`print(thing)` shows what `console.log(thing)` shows, because that is
what a person who uses the library has seen. A value that writes
itself, a date or an error or a URL, is shown as it writes itself:
`str(thing)` should be the text the value means.

### 28.8 An error of JavaScript is `Error`, or `FileError`

What JavaScript throws is an `Error` of Zeno, and its message begins
with JavaScript's name for it (`TypeError: ...`). An error that the
system gave, which is one with an `errno` and a `syscall`, is a
`FileError`. No Node, and no such module, are a `FileError` too
(26.8).

**Why no `ValueError` or `IndexError`.** JavaScript's `RangeError`
and `TypeError` do not mean what Zeno's kinds mean: `RangeError` is
thrown for a bad length and for a stack that is too deep. Matching
names that only look alike would make `except ValueError` catch
things it was not written for. Reading past the end of an array is
not an error in JavaScript at all.

### 28.9 A module is looked for from the folder of the program

`node.module("dayjs")` looks in `node_modules` beside the `.zeno`
file, then in each folder above. `node.module("./helper.js")` is a
file beside the program. For Python the folder of the program is the
first place looked in, before the installed packages, so a
`helper.py` beside the program is `python.module("helper")`.

**Why.** It is where each language looks for a program of its own,
and it is where Zeno's own `import` looks (7.1). A program then finds
its modules wherever it is run from. Looking from the folder Zeno was
started in, which is what a helper started with `-e` or `-c` does by
itself, would make `zeno run project/main.zeno` fail for a program
that runs when started inside `project`.

This changed Python as chapter 26 first had it. It was in no release.

### 28.10 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to JavaScript. More of JavaScript needs it
  than of Python: `map`, `on("data", f)`, a server.
- Node ends when the program does. A server or a timer started there
  does not keep the program alive.
- Starting two things and waiting for both (28.5).
- `node` in a built program, and in `--target js`, as 26.9 has it for
  Python.

## 29. The libraries of Java

The third language of the first version (26.1): `import java`, for the
classes that come with Java and for libraries that are jars.
[`java.md`](java.md) is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it
does for JavaScript (28): Java runs beside the program, they talk over
a socket, numbers and text cross and everything else stays, what Zeno
gives is a copy, a value from there is not a condition, the types are
known when the program runs, and nothing changes for a program that
does not ask. What follows is what Java made different.

### 29.1 `java.type(name)` gives a class, by its whole name

```zeno
let ArrayList = java.type("java.util.ArrayList")
```

**Why `type` and not `class`.** `class` is a word of Zeno and cannot
follow a dot (5.19c). `type` is also what the bridges from JavaScript
to Java call it (`Java.type` in Nashorn and GraalVM), so it is the
word a person who has done this before looks for.

**Why the whole name.** Java's own short names come from an `import`
at the top of each file, which this program does not have. One rule,
the name the documentation gives, is less to know than a list of
packages that are looked in without being asked.

### 29.2 Calling a class is `new`

`ArrayList()` is `new ArrayList()`.

**Why here and not for JavaScript (28.2).** In JavaScript a class can
also be called without `new`, with another answer, so the two had to
be told apart. A class of Java cannot be called at all, so the call
has one meaning. It is also how an object is made in Zeno itself, and
in Python.

### 29.3 A dot after a class is what is `static`; a method is kept until it is called

`Math.PI`, `Math.max(3, 9)`, `Thread.State.NEW`. On an object,
`thing.name` is its public field, or its method.

**What `java.type` gives is not Java's `Class` object.** That object
has methods of its own (`getName`, `getMethods`), and `Math.max` would
have to be looked for among them. So the helper has a value of its
own for "the class as its name is written" (`Type`), and gives Java
the `Class` object when a method asks for one.
`thing.getClass()` still gives Java's.

**A method not yet called is a value too** (`Bound`), because Zeno
reads `names.add` before it calls it, and because a method can be
kept in a name and called later, as in Zeno.

**Only what is public.** A program of Java outside the class could
use nothing else, and a library's private parts are not its promise.

### 29.4 Of several methods with one name, the arguments choose

Java can have `valueOf(int)`, `valueOf(double)` and `valueOf(Object)`
side by side. Each is given a number for how well the arguments of
this call fit what it takes, and the lowest is called.

**The order is Java's own** as far as it has one: an int of Zeno is an
`int` before a `long`, a `long` before a `double`, and a plain type
before its boxed one; a method that takes its arguments one by one
comes before one that gathers them (`Object...`).

**Two that fit equally are an error**, which lists what there is, and
so is none that fits. A guess would call something, and the program
would go on with the wrong answer.

**Alternatives rejected.** Saying the types in the call, as
`thing.method["int", "Object"](1, x)`: it is exact, and it is a
second language to learn for the few calls that need it. It can be
added for those if they turn up. Taking the first method that fits:
which is first is not something Java promises.

### 29.5 An int that goes as an `Object` is an `Integer` if it fits

A collection of Java takes anything (`Object`), so the method does not
say which whole number it wants. An int of Zeno goes as an `Integer`
when it fits 32 bits and as a `Long` when it does not.

**Why.** It is what the number is when written in a Java program: `5`
is an `int` there and `5000000000L` a `long`. A library compares what
it is given with numbers of its own, and `Integer` 5 does not equal
`Long` 5 in Java. Always `Long` would be simpler to say and would fail
quietly inside `contains` and `get`.

**Every whole number that comes back is an int**, whatever its size
in Java, and `float` and `double` are a float. A `float` is written
the short way it prints, `0.1`, and not with the digits it gains as a
`double`.

### 29.6 `==` is `equals`

**Why not the same object, as for JavaScript (28.7).** Java has both,
and its own `==` on objects is the one programs are told not to use
for values: two `String`s or two `Integer`s with one value can be two
objects. `equals` is what a class of Java says its equality is.

`print` shows `toString()`. An array has none worth reading
(`[I@1b6d3586`), so its items are shown.

### 29.7 An exception of Java is an error of Zeno

`IndexOutOfBoundsException` is `IndexError`,
`IllegalArgumentException` is `ValueError`, `IOException` is
`FileError`, each with the kinds built on it, and every other is
`Error`. The message begins with Java's name for it.

**Why these and no more.** Each of the three means in Java what the
kind means in Zeno, by Java's own description of it. That is not so
for `ArithmeticException`, which is both a division by zero and an
overflow, two kinds in Zeno; it stays an `Error` (28.8 has the same
reasoning for JavaScript).

### 29.8 A library is a jar, and the program says where it is

`java.jar("lib/gson.jar")`, or a folder: every jar in it.

**Why the program says it.** Python and Node each have one place
where `install` puts packages, and each finds them there by itself.
Java has none: a jar is found only if the class path names it. So
the program names it, at a line that can be read, with a path from
its own folder (28.9).

`CLASSPATH` is read as Java reads it, and with none the folder of the
program is looked in for classes, which is what `java Main` does in
that folder.

**Alternatives rejected.** Every jar beside the program, without
being asked: which jars are used would depend on what happens to lie
in the folder. A name as Maven writes it
(`com.google.code.gson:gson:2.11.0`), found in Maven's own folder: a
library there usually needs others, and which ones is worked out by
Maven from files Zeno would have to read as Maven does. A folder
filled by Maven or by hand, and named, is whole.

### 29.9 The helper is compiled once, and kept

Java runs classes and not source. The helper's source is in the
`zeno` file; the first run makes classes of it with `javac`, in the
folder this machine has for what can be made again (the registry's,
27), and later runs start those.

**Why.** Compiling takes about a second and starting takes a fifth of
one. Paying the second on every run would make a short program slow
for good.

**How it stays right.** The folder is named by a number worked out
from the source, so another version of Zeno makes its own. The
classes are made in a folder of the run's own and given their name
when whole, so two runs at once never share half of them. They are
compiled for Java 11, so a later Java runs them as they are.

**With no `javac`**, Java is given the source, which Java 11 and
later compile as they start. With no folder to keep them in, they are
made in a folder of this run's own and taken away after.

**Alternative rejected.** The classes inside the `zeno` file, ready
made: building Zeno would then need Java, and Zeno is built with
Rust and nothing else.

### 29.10 A name in brackets, where a word of Zeno is in the way

`System.in` does not parse (5.19c). On a class, and on an object that
has no items of its own, `thing["name"]` is `thing.name`:
`System["in"]`.

**Why this is safe to mean two things.** It is taken so only where
`[ ]` has no other meaning: a class has no items, and neither has an
object that is not an array, a list, a map or text. For JavaScript the
same writing is the language's own rule ([`node.md`](node.md)).

### 29.11 The bridge is kept out of the functions every program runs

Every function of `bridge.rs` that the rest of Zeno calls is marked
`#[cold]` and `#[inline(never)]`, and so is what letting go of a value
from another language calls.

**What happened.** With Java added, a sort on `zeno run --vm` took a
tenth longer than in 0.5.1 (3.63 s to 4.02 s for a million numbers,
best of 8 rounds each), while the count of instructions was 1 % lower.
No line of the VM had changed. The places that hand a value to the
bridge are `ops::item`, `ops::set_item`, `ops::field` and
`value::equal`, which every program runs through, and the compiler
had folded the bridge into them. So their code changed, and moved,
each time the bridge did: `ops::item` was 2170 bytes with JavaScript
added and 2129 with Java. It is 1800 with the bridge kept out, and
does not change when the bridge does.

**Why this is the fix and not a patch.** 26.11 promises that a
program which asks for no other language runs the code it ran before.
The source said so already; the compiled program did not. `#[cold]`
tells the compiler that these calls are rare, which they are in every
program without the import and cheap beside the trip to another
program in one with it.

**After it.** The same sort is within 2 % of 0.5.1. All six
benchmarks, both engines, timed in alternating rounds against 0.5.1,
are between 6 % faster and 4 % slower. The 4 % is nbody on the VM
(16.51 s to 17.08 s); about half of it was there before the bridge
was begun, and the rest is no more than this machine gives for one
build timed twice (24.29).

**What it does not fix.** Where the compiler puts the VM's own loop
still moves by a few bytes when code is added anywhere, and that
alone is worth a few percent on one benchmark or another. Stable Rust
has no way to pin it.

### 29.12 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to Java: lambdas, `Comparator`, `Runnable`.
- A class of Zeno that extends a class of Java.
- Saying the types of a call where two methods fit equally (29.4).
- Zeno's checker reading Java's types, which Java has.
- `java` in a built program, and in `--target java`, as 26.9 has it
  for Python.

## 30. The least C: `zeno build --minimal`

Partha asked (2026-11-18) for one more way to build: one that goes
past the checks and writes only the C the program itself needs, so that
the file is small and easy to read, with everything that is there now
kept as it is. `zeno build` writes about 3,000 lines of C for a program
of one line, because the whole runtime is pasted in front of it and
every operation goes through a function that checks it.

### 30.1 A new option, and the builds that were there do not change

`zeno build --minimal` writes the least C that runs the program. Six
things are done, each with its own section below: no check of any kind
(30.2), no place in the source carried along (30.4), only the parts of
the runtime the program uses (30.5), `print` as C's `printf` (30.6),
each statement written the short way (30.7), and the C compiler asked
for a small program (30.8). docs/minimal.md is the walkthrough.

**Why a new option.** He asked for what is there to stay. The C that
every other build writes is, byte for byte, what it was before this
chapter: 2,028 C files were compared, the 363 programs of the check
(30.10) built nine ways, with the compiler before and after.

**Why the word `minimal`.** It is his word for it ("the minimum code"),
and it says what the option is for, which is how `--fast` was named
(23.1). `--small` promises a small program, and it is the C that gets
small (30.11). `--unchecked` names one of the six things. `--bare` and
`--direct` say less than `minimal` does to someone who has not read
this.

**Why not `--target c`.** `--target` writes the program in another
language with the rules of Zeno carried along in a runtime (24.2),
checks and all. This is the opposite promise, and it is the same C
backend as `zeno build`, so it is an option of that.

### 30.2 No check of any kind: a mistake does what the C does

| | other builds | `--minimal` |
|---|---|---|
| `xs[i]` with `i` out of range | `IndexError` | reads or writes whatever memory is there |
| `ages["Eve"]` with no such key | `KeyError` | reads an item that is not there |
| overflow of `+ - *`, of `-n`, `abs(n)`, `**`, `sum` | `OverflowError` | no defined result |
| `n // 0`, `n % 0` | `ZeroDivisionError` | what the processor does: on a computer the system stops the program |
| `x / 0.0` | `ZeroDivisionError` | infinity, or NaN |
| `math.sqrt(-1.0)`, `math.log(0.0)`, `math.asin(2.0)` | `ValueError` | NaN or infinity |
| `u8(300)` | `ValueError` | 300 goes on as it is |
| `n << 70`, `n << -1` | `ValueError` | no defined result |
| `xs.pop()`, `min(xs)` of an empty list, a slice from past the end | an error | no defined result |
| `int(x)` of infinity or NaN | `ValueError` | the biggest int, the smallest, or 0 |
| a variable that became `none` again after it was checked | an error | used as if it held a value |
| `free(p)` twice | stops, and says so | no defined result |

**Why further than `--fast`.** `--fast` is about time. It leaves out the
checks that cost something in a tight loop and keeps the rest: a key
that is not there, a whole number divided by zero. `--minimal` is about
what is in the file. A check brings its message, the message is put
together from pieces of text, and text needs memory: one check left in
keeps `zeno_fail`, the error value, `zeno_join`, `zeno_str_int` and an
allocator in a program that adds two numbers. It is all of them or the
file is not small.

**Why a whole number divided by zero is not caught here, when `--fast`
catches it (23.1).** There the reason was that the check is nearly free
beside a division. Here the cost is not time. The table says plainly
what happens, and it is what a C programmer expects of `/`.

**What is not a check, and stays.** `-7 % 3` is 2 in Zeno and -1 in C,
and `-7 // 2` is -4 and not -3. A correct program relies on that, so
`%` and `//` are still the runtime's `zeno_mod` and `zeno_floordiv`,
each a few lines with the check taken out. `x // 8` and `x % 8` are
still a shift and a mask (23.5).

### 30.3 The errors a correct program can meet stay

`int("ten")` raises `ValueError`, a file that is not there raises
`FileError`, `raise` raises, `try` and `except` catch, and an error
that nothing catches stops the program and says what it was. Running
out of memory still stops the program and says so.

**Why.** These are not mistakes in the program. What a person types
and whether a file is there are known only when the program runs, and
the program was written to deal with them. A minimal build of a
correct program must do what the checked build does (30.10), and it
could not if these went.

### 30.4 No place in the source

A runtime function that can stop the program takes the line and the
column it was called from as its last two arguments, for the message.
In a minimal build no function has those two parameters and no call
passes them, and the table of file names is gone. An error nothing
caught prints its kind and its message:

```
error: uncaught ValueError: cannot turn "ten" into an int
```

**Why.** Two numbers at every call are code at every call, and they are
the first thing that makes the C look unlike C a person writes. With
the checks gone, the only reader left for them was an error the
program raised itself.

**What it costs.** That message does not say where. The checked build
does: build that way to find it.

**How it is done.** The emitter writes a mark in place of `line, col`
(a byte no C has in it), and the mark goes with the comma before it
when the file is put together. In the runtime the parameters and
arguments are taken out by name, token by token (`without_positions`
in src/minimal.rs); the test that compiles the whole runtime for each
kind of build holds that to being C.

### 30.5 Only what the program uses

The runtime and the program are cut into items (a function, a type, a
variable, a `#define`, an `#include`), each asked for by its name.
Starting from the statements at the top of the program, every item
that is named is kept, and every item those name, until nothing new is
named. The rest is not written. A header is kept when one of the names
it brings is used. Comments between items are dropped, since they
explain the runtime across all its builds; comments inside a function
stay with it. A function is declared ahead only if something written
before it names it.

**Why not leave it to the C compiler.** It already does this for the
machine code: an unused `static` function is not in the program of any
build, which is why the program shrinks much less than the C (30.11).
What was asked for is the file: C that can be read, reviewed, and
carried to another project.

**Why the program's own unused functions go too.** One rule, "what the
program uses". Every function Zeno writes is `static`, so nothing
outside the file could have called it.

**Why by name, and not with a C parser.** The runtime is ours and is
written one way. Three things hold the cutting to its word: a unit
test gives the whole minimal runtime of each kind of build to the C
compiler; `tools/minimal.py` reads the C of every build it makes with
the compiler's warnings on, and a function or variable left in unused,
or used and not declared, is a failure; and the programs then have to
run right.

**The marks.** What a minimal build leaves out of the runtime is
between `#ifndef ZENO_MINIMAL` and `#endif /* ZENO_MINIMAL */`, with
what stands in its place after `#else /* ZENO_MINIMAL */`. They are
decided when the C is written, as the marks of `ZENO_FIRMWARE` are, so
no built program has them in it, and every other build gets the text
between them unchanged.

### 30.6 `print` is `printf`

```zeno
print(f"{n} is prime")
print("total", total, "of", len(xs))
```

```c
printf("%lld is prime\n", (long long)z_n);
printf("total %lld of %lld\n", (long long)z_total, (long long)z_xs->len);
```

Words written in the program go into the format. A whole number is
`%lld`, text and a bool are `%s`, and `print` of words alone is `puts`.
`{n:5}`, `{n:<5}`, `{n:05}` and `{x:8.2f}` are `printf`'s own. A float
is `%s` of `zeno_float_text(x, (char[64]){0})`, which writes it into
bytes of the statement's own, because `printf` has no format for "the
fewest digits that read back as the same float". `{n:x}` and
`{reg:08b}` are written the same way by `zeno_radix_text`, and a
quantity is `%s ms`. What `printf` would print differently is left to
the runtime, and shown with `%s`: text lined up to a width (Zeno
counts characters, `printf` bytes), `^`, a float filled with zeros
(`printf` does not fill `inf`), and a list, a dict or an object.

**Why.** `print` in every other build turns each value into text first,
and text takes memory, so `print(n)` brought an allocator into a
program that otherwise has none. With `printf`, a program of numbers
has no runtime in it: `examples/primes.zeno` is 100 lines of C, and
hello is one `puts`.

**What it costs, measured.** `printf` is a large function. On Linux a
program whose `print` never ran it before has about 250 KB more of the
C library in memory while it runs (`ring`: 1,564 KB to 1,812 KB):
pages of the library that nothing had touched. What the program
itself asks for goes down (30.11). On a board nothing is paged, and
the function is in the image of the checked build as well, which
writes its error messages with `fprintf`; there the cost is the stack
`printf` uses while it runs. A program that prints words alone gets
`puts`, and has no `printf` in it at all.

### 30.7 Statements the short way, and what stays as it was

`x = (x + 1);` is written `x += 1;`, and `return (a * b);` is `return a
* b;`. The emitter puts every operation in brackets so that what is
around it cannot change its meaning; around a whole statement nothing
is left that could (`tidy` in src/emit_c.rs). The statements at the
top of the program are the body of `main`, unless the program has a
collector in it, which has to find the program's variables on the
stack below `main` (docs/memory.md).

**What stays.** Names keep their `z_`: a Zeno program may call a
variable `printf`, `main` or `int`. A whole number is still `int64_t`,
because that is what an int is in Zeno. A temporary is still written
where two values have to be worked out in the order Zeno gives them. A
list still holds `zeno_slot`s and not an array of `int64_t` (30.12).

### 30.8 The C compiler is asked for a small program

`-Os` in place of `-O2`. With `--fast` as well it is `-O3
-fno-math-errno`, since that was asked for by name.

### 30.9 What it goes with

Every kind of build that writes C: the collector, `--owned`,
`--no-collector`, `--firmware`, and `--memory` and `--fast` beside
them. `--release` adds nothing to it. `--llvm`, `--web` and `--target`
refuse it with a sentence that says why.

**Why not LLVM.** Nobody reads the IR, so the half of this that is for
a reader has no reader there, and the half that is for the machine
`--fast --llvm` already does.

**The smallest.** `--minimal --no-collector` or `--minimal --owned`. A
program that makes a list has to free it somehow, and with the
collector that is about 500 lines of C that no option can make small.

### 30.10 How it is held to its word

`tools/minimal.py` builds every program of the check of the targets
(24.9: the examples, the corner programs, every sample of the book)
both ways for each of the four kinds of build, and the two must print
the same, end the same way, and stop with the same message. A program
that a check stops has no defined result in a minimal build, so it is
found and left out: the C of the checked build is given a line that
writes a mark in `zeno_fail` and `zeno_bug`, where every check ends.
On 2026-11-18: 213, 193, 193 and 210 programs for the four kinds, all
the same, and 17 to 20 left out for each. It runs on GitHub on a push
that changes the C backend (.github/workflows/minimal.yml), on Linux
with gcc and on macOS with clang.

### 30.11 What it buys, measured

`python3 tools/minimal.py --sizes` makes the table in docs/minimal.md.
In short, for the examples:

- **The C** is 23 lines for hello, about 100 for a program of numbers,
  and 300 to 1,000 for a program with lists, objects and text, from
  about 3,000 every time. Over all the programs of the check it is 7%
  of the bytes with no collector and 14% with one.
- **The program** shrinks less, because the C compiler never put an
  unused function in it. Its code and constants (`text`, as `size`
  counts it) are a quarter to a third smaller for most of the examples:
  `ring` 8.1 KB to 4.5 KB with no collector, `words` 16.5 KB to 12.8
  KB. At the ends, `blink` loses 6% (it had almost nothing to lose) and
  `primes` 82%, 11.4 KB to 2.1 KB. The file on disk moves in steps of
  4 KB and often does not move at all.
- **Memory.** What the program holds from start to end changes little,
  unless the program stops needing the pool (`primes`: 34.8 KB to 0.6
  KB). What it asks for while it runs goes down wherever `print` made
  text: `thermostat` 1,360 bytes to 240.

### 30.12 Left for later

- A list of whole numbers as an array of `int64_t`, and an object's
  fields read without a slot, which is what a person would write.
- A top-level `let` of a number as `static const`, with its value.
- `%` as C's own where both sides are known not to be below zero.
- A `print` for a board with no `printf`.
- The uncaught error's place, for a build that wants only that back.

## 31. A field with the name of a type, in C

Found while `zeno build --minimal` was checked (2026-11-18):
`tools/targets/edge-names.zeno` ran with `zeno run` and every
`--target`, and `zeno build` wrote C for it that the C compiler
refused.

### 31.1 The parameter steps aside, and the field keeps its name

A class may have a field with the name of a class or an enum:

    class point {
        point: int
    }

Zeno has no rule against it, and `zeno run` runs it. In C a class is a
type `z_point`, and the function that makes an object had one parameter
for each field, called as the field is in the struct: `z_point`. Inside
that function the parameter hid the type, so `z_point *self` was read
as a multiplication. A field named as another class broke the list of
parameters itself, and a case of an enum that carries such a value
broke the same way. `edge-names.zeno` has it by another road: its class
`new_` is `z_new` in C, which is what its field `new` is.

**Decision.** Such a parameter is `z2_point`. The field stays
`z_point` in the struct, where C keeps the names of fields apart from
the names of types, so `self->z_point = z2_point;` is right.

**Why `z2_`.** It is how a second variable of one name is already
written (`z2_x`), so nothing new is to be learned when reading the C.
And no type can have that name: every type begins with `z_`.

**Why only where the names meet.** For every program without such a
field the C is what it was, byte for byte: 2,028 C files compared, the
363 programs of the corpus built nine ways, and only the nine of
`edge-names.zeno` differ. The names of all classes and enums are
gathered before the first class is written, because the type may be
written below the class that has the field.

**Why not an error.** "The entire language must be unambiguous and
intuitive": a name that is right for `zeno run` and wrong for `zeno
build` would be a rule of C showing through. Two classes that C would
know by one name are still refused (`same_in_c`), since there a name
would have to be made up for a type the program prints and compares.

## 32. A `try` on Windows, in C

Found while 0.5.2 was got ready (2026-11-18): the test
`a_minimal_build_prints_what_zeno_run_prints_for_a_correct_program`
passed on Linux and macOS and failed on Windows. The program it builds
stopped at its first caught error and said nothing.

### 32.1 Under MinGW a `try` is a plain jump

A `try` in C is `setjmp`, and an error is `longjmp` back to it (5.5i).
On Windows `setjmp` is a macro, and MinGW writes it as
`_setjmp(place, the frame of this function)`. `longjmp` then does not
only jump. It walks the stack back to that frame with the machinery
Windows has for the exceptions of C++ (`RtlUnwindEx`), so that the
functions it passes can clean up.

On GitHub's Windows machine, with gcc 15.2 and `-Os`, that walk failed.
The program of the test, built with `--minimal` and the collector,
ended with the number 0xC0000028 (Windows' "bad stack") where
`int("4x2")` is caught. A debugger showed the place: `longjmp`, then
`RtlUnwindEx`, then the stop. The same C built with `-O0`, `-O1` and
`-O2` ran to its end, and so did five examples with `-Os`. The same C
built by gcc 13 ran under Wine at every level.

**Decision.** Under MinGW for x86-64 the runtime says
`_setjmp(place, NULL)`. With no frame, `longjmp` puts the registers
back and jumps, and walks nothing. Every C build has these lines, and
they do something only there.

**Why.** A Zeno program has nothing for the walk to do: its C has no
clean-up code between a `raise` and its `try`. The walk can only go
wrong, and where it went wrong the program could not say so. A plain
jump is what `_setjmp` and `_longjmp` are on Linux and macOS (22.14),
and what the LLVM build has asked for on Windows since it first ran
there (12.8). So this makes the C build the same as
the other, and Windows the same as the other systems.

**Why not find what gcc 15 did.** It was looked for and not found from
here: no machine at hand has that compiler, and a build on GitHub's
takes ten minutes. The reason above does not depend on it. Whatever
made the walk fail, a program that does not walk cannot meet it.

**Why not only with `--minimal`.** `-Os` is where it was seen, and
only `--minimal` asks for `-Os`. But the checked build has the same
`setjmp` in the same functions, and nothing says `-O2` is safe by more
than luck with where the compiler put things. One way to jump, in
every build.

**What is left as it was.** 32-bit MinGW already asked for no walk
(`_setjmp3(place, NULL)` is its macro). Windows on ARM64 has only the
`setjmp` that walks, and other compilers on Windows say `setjmp` in
their own way, so those keep the macro. The trial workflow now builds
six programs with `--minimal` on the machine it tries, and says where
one that fails stopped.

## 33. A library written in Zeno

6.10 said of the methods of text and lists: "Once modules exist, what
can be written in Zeno will be." Modules have existed since chapter 7,
and since then Zeno has gained a VM, a second compiler and fifteen
other languages to write a program in. A function of the library was
by now written once for each: `math.log2` is in `builtins.rs`, in
`runtime.c`, and in thirteen other runtimes. That is why
[`missing.md`](missing.md) puts this first: every small gap of the
library costs that much, until the library can be written in Zeno.

This chapter is the way to do it, the first functions written that
way (6.21 had left them out "until something needs it"), and two
mistakes that it found. [`library-in-zeno.md`](library-in-zeno.md)
walks through the code.

### 33.1 A module that comes with Zeno may have a part written in Zeno

The folder `library/` holds one `.zeno` file for each such module:
`library/math.zeno`, `library/random.zeno`. The files are kept inside
the `zeno` program (`src/library.rs`), so there is nothing to install
beside it and nothing to find when a program runs.

`math` has both kinds of part. `math.sqrt` is built in, as before, and
`math.hypot` is written in Zeno. A program does not see the
difference: `import math`, then `math.sqrt(x)` and `math.hypot(x, y)`,
or `from math import sqrt, hypot`.

**Why inside `zeno`, and not a folder beside it.** A folder that has
to be found is a way for it not to be found: a `zeno` that was copied
to another machine, a folder of an older version. Every installer
would have had to carry it. The files are small text.

**Why one module can have both kinds.** `hypot` belongs with `sqrt`.
A second module, `math2` or `mathx`, would make the reader learn
which function lives where, for a reason that is about how Zeno is
built and not about mathematics.

**Turned down: writing these in Rust and C like the rest.** `hypot`
is one line of C. It is also a line in each of fifteen other
runtimes, each with its own test, and the answers would differ in
the last digit, because each language has its own `hypot`. Written in
Zeno it is the same arithmetic everywhere, so it prints the same
everywhere, and that is checked by the tests there already are.

### 33.2 The part is joined like a file of the program

`modules.rs` reads the part when a file of the program imports its
module, gives its names the module's name in front (`math.hypot`),
and puts its statements ahead of the program's own. From there on it
is a file like `shapes.zeno`: the checker checks it, the interpreter
and the VM run it, both compilers and every target compile it, and
none of them was changed for it.

The part begins with `strict`, so every type in it is written, as
every kind of build asks. It may keep things to itself with `private`.
It imports the built-in part of its own module (`import math`, for
`math.sqrt`), and nothing else.

In a message it is named `library/math.zeno`, with its own line
numbers, like any file. `zeno join` shows it, which is a way to read
the library.

**Why last among the files, and first among the statements.** A place
in a message is a file's number and a line. The parts are read after
every file of the program, so the program's files keep the numbers
they would have had. Their statements still go first: a part uses
nothing of the program's, and the top of any file may use the part.

### 33.3 Only what the program reaches is joined

Of a part's functions, the program gets the ones its files name, the
ones those name, and so on. A program that calls `math.gcd` has
`math.gcd` in it, and not `hypot`, `sinh` or `clamp`.

What is not a function comes whole when anything of the part is
reached: the four numbers of `random`.

**Why.** A program for a board pays for every function in it. A
library that came whole would be a reason to avoid it there, and
firmware is what Zeno is for. The C compiler would drop most unused
functions if asked, but the fifteen targets would not, and `zeno
build` shows its C to be read.

**How.** The stage that gives names their full names already visits
every use of a name. It now also notes which full names each function
of a part uses, and `Loader::join` follows those from what the
program's own files name.

### 33.4 A program that names nothing of a part is the program it was

A file that spells none of the names a part offers cannot be using
it, and the part is then not read at all. If a file does spell one
(`let clamp = 3`) and turns out not to mean the part's, the part is
taken off the end of the files again. Either way the joined program
is, to the last statement, what it was before parts existed.

**Why it matters.** "Nothing existing may change" is how every
feature since 0.1 has been added. Here it holds by construction for
every program that was accepted before: `math.hypot` and `import
random` were both refused. `tools/minimal.py` and the test
`a_program_that_names_nothing_of_a_part_is_the_program_it_was` hold
it there.

**The one thing that does change**, as for `json`, `web` and `python`
before it (26.11): `random` is now the name of a module that comes
with Zeno, so a file of a program called `random.zeno` can no longer
be imported under that name.

### 33.5 A part means the names that come with Zeno

A program may give `abs`, `len` or `max` a meaning of its own: they
are names, and not words of the language. Joined to such a program,
a part that says `abs(x)` would call the program's `abs`. What
`math.hypot` does would then depend on who calls it.

Two things keep that from happening.

1. **A part uses no such name where it can do without.** The part of
   `math` has its own private `size` in place of `abs`. `random`
   keeps its four numbers as plain whole numbers and cuts them to 32
   bits with `& 4294967295`, so it needs no `u32.wrap`.
2. **Where it cannot, the program is told.** `random.pick` needs the
   length of a list, and `len` is the only way to ask. A program that
   has a `len` of its own and reaches `pick` is refused, at its `len`:
   "this program uses `random.pick`, which is written in Zeno and uses
   the `len` that comes with Zeno. So the program cannot give `len` a
   meaning of its own here. Give this one another name". A program
   that does not reach `pick` keeps its `len`.

**Why a refusal, and not a fix.** The fix is a way for a part to say
"the `len` that comes with Zeno" that nothing can hide. That is a
change to how every engine looks a name up, and it is worth making
once, for the files of a program as well: an imported file has the
same trouble today, and is refused the same way (7.7). Until then
the refusal is honest, rare, and can be lifted without changing any
program.

### 33.6 `import random` goes at the top of a file

A module that comes with Zeno can be imported inside a function,
where the import of a file cannot (7.5). A part written in Zeno is joined to the file, as a file of the
program is, so its import belongs where theirs do. `import random`
inside a function is refused with a message that says so. `import
math` inside a function still gives the built-in part, and
`math.hypot` there says to move the import to the top.

### 33.7 What `math` gained

| | What it is |
|---|---|
| `math.hypot(x, y)` | the distance of the point (x, y) from (0, 0) |
| `math.sinh(x)`, `math.cosh(x)`, `math.tanh(x)` | the hyperbolic functions |
| `math.gcd(a, b)` | the greatest whole number that divides both |
| `math.clamp(value, low, high)` | the value, kept between the two |

**`hypot` takes floats.** `math.hypot(3, 4)` is refused, with the
message every function written in Zeno gives: write `3.0`. `math.sqrt`
takes a whole number because the checker has a rule for it by name. A
function written in Zeno has the rules of the language and no others,
and "an int does not become a float by itself" is one of them.

**`hypot` is the root of the sum of the squares, and exact where that
is.** `math.hypot(3.0, 4.0)` is `5.0`. Sides whose squares would not
fit in a float are first multiplied by 2**-600, and tiny ones by
2**600, which changes no digit of a float. *Turned down:* dividing
by the longer side, which is the usual way and gives 13.000000000000002
for (5.0, 12.0).

**`sinh` near zero is a series.** `(e**x - e**-x) / 2` takes one
number from another that is nearly equal, and loses most of its
digits. Below 0.25 the first six terms of the series are used. The
three functions are made from `math.exp`, so their last digit is the
machine's `exp`'s, as `exp`'s own is.

**`gcd` is never negative, and `gcd(0, 0)` is 0**, as in Python, C++
and Go.

**`clamp` is written once for every type that `<` compares**: whole
numbers, floats, quantities in one unit, text. The three are of one
type. The value is held against `low` first, so with `low` above
`high`, which is a mistake in the program, the answer is `low` for a
value below it and `high` otherwise. *Turned down:* an error for that
case, as Rust and Java give. A function written in Zeno that raises
must say `raises`, and then every `clamp` in every program would need
a `try`.

### 33.8 `random`

| | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `random.between(low, high)` | a whole number from `low` to `high`, both included |
| `random.number()` | a float from 0.0 up to 1.0, never 1.0 |
| `random.pick(items)` | one of the items of a list |
| `random.seed(n)` | starts the numbers again from `n` |

**The same numbers on every run, until the program seeds.** A program
that never calls `seed` gets the numbers of `random.seed(0)`.

*Why.* A test that fails must fail again when it is run again. A
simulation is compared with yesterday's. A board has nothing to make
a first number from. And it is one rule for `zeno run`, a compiled
program and every target, where "different each time" would be
fifteen ways of asking a machine for something unpredictable. C does
the same. Python, JavaScript and Go do not, and a game written in
Zeno has to seed itself. It has nothing to seed from yet: the time of
day is in [`missing.md`](missing.md), and `random.seed` of it will be
the line to write.

*This cannot be changed later* without changing what programs print,
so it is decided now and not left open.

**Why sfc32.** It needs four whole numbers of 32 bits, additions,
shifts and one `^`: no multiplication and no division, so it is quick
on a processor that has neither. It passes the usual tests of
randomness, which the short generators that C libraries use do not.
It is written with nothing but operators, so it is the same on every
engine. It is not for keys or passwords, and the file says so.

**`between` includes both ends**, so a die is `between(1, 6)`. The
ends can be given in either order. Every number is as likely as any
other: bits are drawn under a mask that just covers the span, and a
draw above it is thrown away, where the short way (`bits % span`)
makes the low numbers come up a little more often. `high - low` must
fit in an int, or the subtraction is an OverflowError like any other.

**`number` has 53 bits**, made from two draws as Python makes it, so
every float it can give is as likely as any other.

**`pick` of an empty list is an IndexError**: there is no item to
give.

**Left out for now.** `shuffle`, which takes items out of a list it
was only lent (5.15e). A seed from the machine. Numbers that follow
a bell curve.

### 33.9 Two mistakes this found

**Two files could not both import a module that comes with Zeno.**
`main.zeno` and `shapes.zeno` each say `import math`. Joined, the
program said it twice, and the checker answered "`math` is already
declared in this block". No example had two such files. Now, as the
files are joined, an import that an earlier file already made is
left out. Twice in one file is still refused. The part of `math`
imports `math` itself, so every program that used it would have met
this.

**A function of an imported file, used as a value, did not build.**
`let f = shapes.area` ran under `zeno run`, and `zeno build` wrote
`zeno_wrap_shapes.area`, which is not a name in C. The wrapper is now
named from the function's name in C, `zeno_wrap_z_shapes_area`. A
function of the first file keeps the name it had, so the C of every
program that built before is unchanged. `[1.0, 2.0].map(math.sinh)`
is how it was found.

**One thing seen and left.** A file can use `math` without importing
it, when another file of the program does: the joined program has
one set of names. It is the other side of the first mistake, and
mending it means the checker knowing which file a line is in.

### 33.10 What can be written this way next

What is only arithmetic and control: `factorial`, a search in a
sorted list, a queue. JSON in a compiled program (18.5) is text and
lists, and can be.

What cannot: anything that asks the machine. `program.exit`, the
environment and the time of day need each engine. And the methods of
text and lists stay built in, for the reason of 6.10: they are called
as `xs.insert(...)`, and they take items out of a list they were lent.

## 34. Ending a program, its environment, and the error stream

Three functions of the module `program`, each of which asks the
machine, so each was written once for every engine: `zeno run`, the
VM, C, LLVM and the fifteen target languages. A program that does not
use them is unchanged: they are three new names inside `program`, and
nothing else moved. Walkthrough: [`ending-a-program.md`](ending-a-program.md).

### 34.1 `program.exit(code)` ends the program, and is not an error

```zeno
import program

if len(program.arguments()) != 2 {
    program.warn("usage: copy <from> <to>")
    program.exit(2)
}
```

**The program ends there**, and whatever started it (the shell, a
script, `program.run`) is given `code`. What was printed is sent
first. Before this, a program could end in two ways only: at its last
line, with 0, or with an error nobody caught, with 1 (6.19). A tool
that a script calls has to be able to say "no such file" with one
number and "wrong words" with another.

**No `try` stops it, and no `except` sees it**, not even one that
names no kind. It is not an error: a program that asked to end has
not gone wrong. Python's `sys.exit` is an exception, and a bare
`except:` that was written to catch something else swallows it; that
is the kind of surprise Zeno is meant not to have. Inside both engines
it travels up as an error that no `try` catches does (a
`Control::Fatal` that says where the program ended, with the number
kept beside it, 34.5), so the language beside a program (`import
python`) is still told that the program is over. In C and LLVM builds it is
C's own `exit`, which also runs the memory report. Each target
language uses its own way to end at once (`os._exit` after the output
is sent in Python, `exit!` in Ruby, `std::_Exit` in C++), never one an
`except` written in that language could stop.

**`code` goes from 0 to 255.** That is what every system hands on: on
Linux and macOS, `exit(256)` arrives as 0, which would turn a failure
into a success. A number outside is a `ValueError`, raised where the
call is, as `char(0)` is; a number written down outside is found by
the checker before the program runs. A `--minimal` build has no
checks (30.2), and there the number is cut to its last eight bits, as
in C.

**It does not count as the end of a path.** A function that promises
an `int` still has to return one on every path, `program.exit` or not.
**Why.** Java, Go and C do the same. The rule "every path returns"
stays one a reader can check without knowing which calls end the
program, and the cost is one line in a rare case.

**In a test** (`zeno test`), a program cannot end in the middle of the
run: the test fails, with "the program ended here, with
`program.exit(2)`", and the next test runs. **In a page**, the program
cannot end either: the turn that is running stops, and the page stays,
with its buttons. **In a firmware build** it is allowed: an uncaught
error there already ends with `exit(1)`, and what ending means on a
real board is for the board's runtime to say (missing.md, item 8).

### 34.2 `program.environment(name)` gives `str or none`

```zeno
let home = program.environment("HOME")
if home is none {
    print("HOME is not set")
}
```

**`none` when the environment does not say**, which a program must
handle (`str or none`, as `input()` gives). A name that no environment
can hold (empty, or with `=` or a zero byte in it) is `none` too, and
the machine is not asked: some systems would refuse it with an error,
and C would read only the part before the zero. A value that is not
UTF-8 is read as the words on the command line are, with U+FFFD where
a byte cannot be read.

**A function, and not a dict of everything.** A dict would be a copy
taken when the program started, of names the program never looks at,
and it would have to be made in every target. One question, one
answer.

**It only reads.** Setting a variable changes nothing for the program
itself, only for programs it starts, and C's `setenv` is not safe
beside other threads. If `program.run` ever needs to give a program an
environment, that will be a word of `run`'s.

**The word is `environment`**, whole, as Zeno's names are (1.4), not
`env` or `getenv`.

**A firmware build refuses it**: a board has no environment, and a
value the build needs is a `const`. **A page has none**, and gets
`none`. A program built for WebAssembly sees what its host gives it:
`tools/run-wasi.js` gives it Node's environment, `wasmtime` gives
nothing unless asked with `--env`.

### 34.3 `program.warn(text)` writes one line on the error stream

```zeno
program.warn(f"cannot read {path}, going on without it")
```

**One `str`**, and a line end after it. `print` takes any values, and
showing every kind of value is a long piece of each backend; an
f-string already turns anything into text, so one `str` loses nothing
and costs fifteen short functions instead of fifteen long ones.

**What was printed before it is sent first**, so that on a screen that
shows both streams the lines keep the order the program wrote them in.

**The word is `warn`.** Ruby and Perl have a `warn` that does exactly
this. `program.error(text)` reads as if it raised an error, which it
does not. `print(text, to: errors)` would make `print` the one built-in
that takes a named argument for where its output goes, and every
backend's `print` more complicated, for a rare need.

**In a page**, where there is one place for text, the line is shown
with the rest. **In a firmware build** it goes where an uncaught
error's message goes.

### 34.4 How the three are held to each other

`tools/targets.py` now holds every target to `zeno run` on two more
things: the number the program ended with (it compared only "0 or
not" before), and the lines written on the error stream before any
error. Every program is started with `ZENO_TARGETS=yes`, so that
`tools/targets/edge-ending.zeno` can read a variable whose value is
known. Two changes came with that. `go run` ends with 1 whatever the
program ended with, so Go programs are built first and then run, as
C++ and Rust ones were. And `tools/run-wasi.js` hands the program
Node's environment instead of an empty one.

In `cargo test`, both engines give a `Ran`: what was printed, what was
warned, the error if any, and the number at the end. A test sets the
environment the way it sets what is typed (`with_environment`), and
that environment goes to the built programs it runs as well.

### 34.5 The end travels as an error no `try` catches

**Decision.** Inside `zeno run` and the VM, `program.exit(3)` keeps 3
aside, for the thread the program runs on, and stops the program with
`Control::Fatal`, the kind no `try` catches, with the message "the
program ended here, with `program.exit(3)`". At the end of the run,
`Ran::ended` finds the 3 and makes it a run that went well, ending
with 3. A page's turn does the same, and the page stays. A test that
calls a function that ends the program shows that message, as it did.

**Why.** It first had a kind of its own, `Control::Exit`, beside
`Control::Raise` and `Control::Fatal`. Counted before 0.6.0, the VM ran
1 to 3 % more instructions than in 0.5.2 on every benchmark (fib
+2.1 %, loop +3.1 %, sort +2.7 %), and the whole difference was inside
its loop, at lines that had not changed (`let base = frame.base`
alone ran 3.9 million more on fib 25). The loop is one large function,
and a sixth kind of `Control` changed how the Rust compiler kept its
values in registers. Without it the counts are those of 0.5.2 again.
What a program does is the same either way: nothing catches the end,
everything above it is told, and the number reaches the shell.

**The other choice.** Keeping `Exit` and finding another change that
gave the loop back its registers would have been luck, and the next
change anywhere could undo it. Carrying the end in a kind that already
exists leaves the loop as it was in 0.5.2.

### 34.6 On Windows a built program asks for the environment in UTF-16

C's `getenv` answers on Windows in the machine's code page, so a
value in Tamil on a machine set up for English came out of a built
program as question marks, where `zeno run` printed it. Windows keeps
the environment whole, in UTF-16, and `program.environment` now asks
it (`GetEnvironmentVariableW`) and turns the answer into UTF-8, as
`program.arguments` does for the command line. The three functions of
Windows are declared inside the function that uses them, so that a
`--minimal` build, which keeps only the functions a program uses,
keeps them with it. **Turned down: `_wgetenv`**, which is Microsoft's
C library's own and reads a copy made when the program started.

### 34.7 What the VM reaches outside itself sits in a box of its own

`program.warn` gave the VM one more field, the text it collects for
the tests, and the board had grown with its inputs, ports and
converter. Both sat in the VM before the stack and the frames, which
every instruction reads, and pushed them 48 bytes further on. With
that, `bench/loop.zeno` ran 6% slower by the clock than in 0.5.2
while running the same instructions to the last digit: callgrind
showed the two builds' inner loop identical but for those two
offsets. It was measured, not guessed: with the output, the warnings,
the board, the page and the keyboard moved into one `World` behind a
pointer, the same program is within 1.5% of 0.5.2 by the clock, and
the others are level or faster (nbody 4% faster).

So the rule: what an instruction reads on every step (the stack, the
frames, the handlers) stays together at the front of the VM, and what
only a call of a built-in reaches goes in the box, where it can grow
without moving anything.

## 35. A case of an enum can stand for a number

```zeno
enum Reply {
    Ack = 6
    Nak = 21
}

let byte: u8 = u8(Ack)        # 6, to send
let reply = Reply(byte)       # Reply or none, from what came back
```

Every protocol, every register field and every error code is a number
with a name. Before this, a program kept the numbers in `const`s and
the meaning in an enum, and wrote the `match` between them by hand,
once for each direction. Walkthrough: [`enum-numbers.md`](enum-numbers.md).

### 35.1 `Ack = 6`, for every case or for none

**The number is written out**, a whole number with or without a minus,
in any base Zeno reads (`0x15`, `0b1010`). A `const` or a sum is not
taken: the list of numbers is meant to be read off the page, as the
table in a datasheet is.

**Every case has one, or none does.** C numbers the cases it is not
told about (one more than the case before), which makes the number of
a case depend on where it is in the list: adding a case in the middle
changes the numbers after it, and a message sent by the old program
means something else to the new one. In Zeno nothing has a number
that was not written. **Why not a number for every enum, counted from
0?** The same reason: a number that nobody wrote cannot be relied on,
so it is better not to have one at all.

**Only a case that carries nothing.** A `Fault(code: int)` is not one
number; giving it one would say that every fault is the same.

**No two cases the same.** `Reply(6)` has to give back one case. C
allows two names for one number; Zeno has `const` for a second name.

**The number is an int**, the size Zeno counts in. A case that has to
fit a `u8` is turned into one with `u8(Ack)`, which is checked like
every conversion: a number too big for a `u8` is an `OverflowError`
there.

### 35.2 `int(Ack)` gives the number, `Reply(6)` gives the case or `none`

**Both ways are conversions, written as conversions are.** `int(x)`
and `u8(x)` already turn a value into a number, and the name of a type
called like a function already makes a value of that type (a class).
So `int(Ack)` and `Reply(6)` need nothing new to be read. **Turned
down: a field, `Ack.number`.** A case is not an object, and a field
would read as if it could be changed. **Turned down: `Ack as int`.**
Zeno has no `as`, and does not need a second way to convert.

**`Reply(6)` gives `Reply or none`**, because most numbers are no
case at all, and a byte that came over a wire can be anything. The
checker makes the program look at the `none` before it uses the case,
as it does for `input()` and `program.environment`. **Turned down:
raising a `ValueError` for a number that is no case.** Not knowing a
code is the ordinary case for a program that reads from outside, not
a mistake, and `none` makes the program say what it does then.

**`int(Ack)` cannot fail**, and `u8(Ack)` fails only as `u8(n)` does.

**A plain enum without numbers is refused in both**, and the message
says how to give it numbers. A case is not secretly a number in Zeno,
as it is in C.

**Comparing a case with a number is still refused** (`Ack == 6`): a
`Reply` and an `int` are different things, and `int(Ack) == 6` says
which one is meant.

### 35.3 How it is built: two functions written beside the enum

The checker knows which calls these are, since it knows that `Ack` is
a case of an enum with numbers and that `Reply` is one. It notes each,
as it notes a `count += 1` on a sized number (10.27), and `checked`
rewrites the program. Beside the enum, in the same block, it writes

```zeno
function Reply..number(value: Reply) -> int {
    match value {
        case Ack { return 6 }
        case Nak { return 21 }
    }
}
function Reply..case(number: int) -> Reply or none {
    if number == 6 { return Ack }
    if number == 21 { return Nak }
    return none
}
```

and `int(Ack)` becomes `int(Reply..number(Ack))`, `Reply(6)` becomes
`Reply..case(6)`. No program can write a name with two dots in a row,
so the names are no one else's, and an enum declared inside a function
gets its two functions inside that function.

**Why not in each engine.** Every engine, every build and all fifteen
target languages can already run a function with a `match` and an
`if`. Written this way, the feature is the same everywhere from the
first day, with nothing to keep in step: `tools/targets/edge-enum-numbers.zeno`
passes in all of them unchanged. An enum whose numbers no call uses
gets no functions, so a program that only writes the numbers, as
documentation, builds to the same code as before.

**What it costs.** `Reply(n)` tries the cases one after another, which
for the dozen cases of a protocol is as fast as a table. An enum of
hundreds of cases would want a table or a `switch`, which the C
compiler may make of the `if`s on its own.

### 35.4 Left for later

**A loop over the cases** (`for reply in Reply.cases`), which other
languages have and which a menu or a test of every code wants. It
needs a list of an enum's cases as a value; it is the next thing for
this chapter. **A case that is a set of bits** (`Read | Write`), for a
register of flags: that is a different thing from one number per case,
and wants a type of its own.

## 36. Bytes

```zeno
import files

let frame: list[u8] = [0x7E, 0x01, 0x00, 0xFF]
files.write_bytes("frame.bin", frame)
let back = files.read_bytes("frame.bin")     # list[u8]
print(back[0])                                # 126
```

A firmware image, a capture from a logic analyser, a record a board
wrote to its flash: none of these is text, and until now Zeno could not
open them (6.16). This chapter is the first of three about bytes. It
gives a file as its bytes. The second stores a `list[u8]` one byte to
an item in C and LLVM (5.13a), and the third gives a list a fixed
length. Walkthrough: [`bytes.md`](bytes.md).

### 36.1 `files.read_bytes` gives a `list[u8]`, and `files.write_bytes` takes one

**A byte is a `u8`, and a file of bytes is a `list[u8]`.** Zeno has had
both since 0.1, so nothing new has to be learned: an item is a number
from 0 to 255, `len` is the size of the file, `for b in bytes` walks
it, and every method of a list works. **Turned down: a `bytes` type of
its own**, as Python and Go have. It would be a second kind of list,
with its own methods to learn and its own rules for what goes in. What
a `bytes` type buys is a compact list, and that is a question of how a
`list[u8]` is stored, which the second part of this chapter answers
for every `list[u8]`, not only the ones that came from a file.

**Two functions with names of their own**, beside `read` and `write`.
**Turned down: `files.read(path, binary: true)`.** What a call gives
back would then depend on the value of an argument, and the checker
would have to know it; `read_bytes` says on the page what it gives.

**Everything the file holds, as it holds it.** No byte is changed, and
none is refused: a zero, a byte that is no UTF-8, a `"\r\n"` all arrive
as numbers. The errors are those of `files.read`: no file, or one that
cannot be read (a folder, or a file this program may not open), as a
`FileError` that every kind of build can catch. There is no third,
because nothing is required of the content.

**`write_bytes` makes the file, or replaces what was in it**, as
`files.write` does, with one byte for each item. The list is a
`list[u8]`, so its items fit in a byte, and a number written out that
does not fit is refused before the program runs (`256 does not fit in
a u8 (0 to 255)`). A list of `int`s is refused too: it may hold
anything, and turning it into bytes would have to drop what does not
fit. `[u8(n) for n in numbers]` says where the check is. The one list
whose items are not known until the program runs, one that came from
`json.parse`, is looked at item by item, and an item that is no byte is
a `ValueError` that names it.

**The list is new at each call**, so it can be kept by an owner in a
build with no collector: `let frame: owned list[u8] = files.read_bytes(path)`.

**How it is built.** `zeno run` and the VM read the file with Rust's
`std::fs::read`. C and LLVM call `zeno_files_read_bytes` in
`runtime.c`, which reads in pieces of 512 bytes into a list with room
for the whole file, and in a firmware build says whether it worked, as
`files.read` does. Each target language uses its own way of reading a
file as bytes (`list(f.read())` in Python, `File.binread(path).bytes`
in Ruby, `os.ReadFile` in Go).

### 36.2 A `list[u8]` is stored one byte to an item

In C and LLVM every list was an array of eight-byte slots, so a file of
a megabyte, read with `read_bytes`, took eight megabytes. Now a
`list[u8]` keeps one byte for each item. Nothing in the language
changes: the same program prints the same thing, and only the memory
it takes is different (an 8 MB file read and written back takes 13 MB
in all, where it took 64 MB).

**Every `list[u8]`, not only the ones from a file.** `[1, 2, 3]` where
a `list[u8]` is wanted, `[u8(n) for n in numbers]`, a field
`payload: list[u8]`, a `map` whose function gives a `u8`: each is
stored packed. A program cannot tell the difference, so there is no
choice to make and nothing to write. **Turned down: a `bytes` type**
(36.1), and **turned down: `packed list[u8]`**, a word that asks for
it. Both would put a question of storage on the page that the compiler
can answer alone, and the second would leave the slow way as the one a
beginner meets first.

**Only `list[u8]`.** A byte is what files, protocols and buffers are
made of; a list of `u16` or `i32` is rarer and takes eight bytes an
item still. Packing them is the same work again for each width, and
waits until a program asks for it.

**How it is built.** The runtime keeps one struct for a list,
`zeno_list`, with a length, the room and the items. For a `list[u8]`
the items are bytes, read through `ZENO_BYTES(list)`, and a set of
functions does for them what the list functions do for slots:
`zeno_bytes_of`, `zeno_bytes_append`, `zeno_bytes_at`, `_pop`,
`_insert`, `_copy`, `_concat`, `_slice`, `_str`, `_eq`, `_find`,
`_contains`, `_reverse`, `_clear`, `_sort`, `_sort_by`, `_sum` and
`_best`. A byte goes into and comes out of them as an `int64_t`, so the
code around them does not change. `sort` is a counting sort, since
there are only 256 values; `find` and `contains` are `memchr`; `==` is
`memcmp`.

The checker marks each place a list is made whose type is `list[u8]`
(a list written out, a comprehension, a call such as `read_bytes`), and
the emitters make a packed list there. The kind the emitters share
gains `Kind::Byte`, which appears only as the item of a list: an item
read out of one is an `int` again, as a field of a small type is
(5.13a). A packed list and a list of slots never meet: where one would
be stored as the other the emitter stops with an error, so that a
place the checker did not mark is found by the tests and not by a
program that prints the wrong numbers. The one comparison between them
that a program can write, `bytes == [1, 2, 3]` where the right side is
a `list[int]`, has its own function, `zeno_bytes_eq_ints`.

The interpreter, the VM and the fifteen target languages are as they
were: there a list of numbers is already the language's own.

### 36.3 `[0] * 64` repeats a list

A buffer starts as so many zeros, and writing sixty-four of them out is
no way to say it. `list * n` makes a new list with the items of `list`,
`n` times over, as in Python: `[0] * 64`, `[0x7E, 0x00] * 3`. Where a
`list[u8]` is wanted the numbers written in it must fit in a byte, as
in any list written out, and the new list is stored packed (36.2).

**One way round.** `3 * [0]`, which Python also takes, is refused with
a message that shows `[0] * 3`. Two spellings of one thing is one too
many (principle 1).

**Not for lists of lists, dicts or objects.** `[[0] * 3] * 3` is the
best-known trap in Python: the three rows are one row, and setting
`grid[0][0]` sets all three. A list holds such values by sharing them,
so `*` would always make that trap, and it is refused with a message
that shows the comprehension, `[[0] * 3 for i in range(3)]`, which
makes each row. Numbers, text, bools, enum values and `none` are never
changed in place, so repeating them is safe.

**A count below zero is a `ValueError`**, where Python quietly gives an
empty list. A negative count is a mistake in the program, and an empty
list would carry it further before anything showed it. A count of zero
gives an empty list.

**How it is built.** The checker types `list * int` as the list, and
refuses the cases above. `zeno run` and the VM build the list in
`ops.rs`. C and LLVM call `zeno_list_repeat`, or `zeno_bytes_repeat` for
a list of bytes, which is one `memcpy` for each repeat; with no
collector a list of text takes its own copies, as `+` does. The target
languages each have their own way in the `mul` of their runtime
(Python's own `*`, Ruby's `Array#*`, a loop elsewhere).

### 36.4 `list[u8, 64]`: a list of a fixed length

```zeno
var buffer: list[u8, 64] = [0] * 64
buffer[0] = 0x7E
buffer.append(1)      # error: `append` would change how many items this list has
print(buffer[64])     # error: 64 is outside a list of 64 items
```

A buffer in firmware nearly always has a size that is fixed when the
program is written: a frame of 8 bytes, a block of 512, a ring of 64.
C writes `uint8_t buffer[64]`, Rust `[u8; 64]`, Go `[64]byte`. In Zeno
it is `list[u8, 64]`: a list that always has 64 items.

**The length is part of the type, and is a number written in it.**
`list[u8, 64]` reads as "a list of u8, 64 of them", and a number in the
`[ ]` can never be mistaken for a type. **Turned down: a word of its
own, such as `array[u8, 64]`.** It would be a second kind of list, with
its own name to learn, for what is a list that cannot grow. Everything
a list does that leaves its length as it is works the same way.
**Turned down: `[64]u8` or `u8[64]`**, the order of Go and C: Zeno
writes a type's name first and what it holds after (`list[u8]`,
`dict[str, int]`), and a length is one more thing it holds.

**What gives one a value.** A list written out with exactly that many
items (`[0x7E, command, 0, 0x7F]`), `[0] * 64`, or another list of the
same type and length. The count is checked before the program runs:
`this list has 2 items, and a list[u8, 8] always has 8`. A list whose
length is only known when the program runs (`[0] * n`, a `list[u8]`
from somewhere else) is refused, with a message that says so.

**What it does.** Everything a list does that leaves the length as it
is: an index, `xs[i] = v`, `len`, `for`, `in`, `==`, `find`, `sort`,
`reverse`, `slice`, `map`, `filter`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `+` (which
makes a new, ordinary list), printing. `append`, `pop`, `insert` and
`clear` are refused, with a message that says to give an item a new
value instead. A position written as a number is checked before the
program runs: `buffer[64]` on a `list[u8, 64]` is an error then, not an
`IndexError` later.

**Where it can go.** A list of a fixed length goes where one of the
same type and length is wanted: a variable, a parameter, a field, what
a function gives back, an item of a `list[list[u8, 4]]`. It does not
go where an ordinary `list[u8]` is kept, such as a `let` that says
`list[u8]` or a field of that type: whatever held it there could
append to it, and the first holder would find a list longer than its
type says. The message says to write `list[u8, 64]` there, or copy the
items with `.slice(0)`.

**A function that never changes the length can be given one.** This is
the case that matters most: `checksum(data: list[u8])` should take a
buffer as well as any other list. The checker reads the function: if
it only reads its `data`, gives items new values, walks it, or passes
it on to a function that does the same, a list of a fixed length goes
there. If anything in it could change the length (`data.append`, or
keeping `data` in a variable, a list or a field, or returning it, or
handing it to a function the checker cannot read), the message names
that line: ``this list always has 8 items, and `pad` may change how
many its `data` has: it calls `data.append` (line 11)``. The same holds
for a generic function such as `first[T](xs: list[T])`. **Turned down:
refusing every function that takes a `list[u8]`**, which would make
each library function be written twice, and **turned down: a check
when the program runs**, which would turn a mistake the checker can
see into an error that waits for the program to reach it, and would
need a mark on every list in all fifteen target languages.

**How it is built.** The checker has one more type, `Ty::Fixed`, the
item and the length. Whatever only looks at a value (the arguments of
`print`, `len` and the other built-ins, an index, a loop, the object of
a method) sees it as the list it is, so none of that had to change.
The places that keep a value see the length, and `src/lengths.rs`
reads a function's body to answer whether it changes the length of a
parameter. Every engine and every build stores a list of a fixed length
as a list: the length was made sure of before the program ran, so
nothing is left to check while it runs. A `list[u8, 64]` is packed one
byte to an item, as any `list[u8]` is (36.2).

### 36.5 Left for later

**A list of a fixed length that takes no block from the pool.** Today
`list[u8, 64]` in a build with no collector is a block from the pool,
as any list is. Since its length is known, its items could sit inside
the object that has it as a field, or on the stack of the function that
makes it, with nothing to give back. That is the next step for this
type.

**Text from bytes, and bytes from text** (the UTF-8 of a `str`, and a
`str` from bytes that are UTF-8), which a protocol that carries a name
wants. It is a pair of functions with an error for bytes that are not
text, and waits until a program asks. **`files.append_bytes`**, for a
log of records, the same. **A file read in pieces**, for a file too big
to hold, waits for cleaning up at the end of a block, as it does for
text.

## 37. The libraries of Ruby

The first language of the second version (26.1): `import ruby`, for
the library that comes with Ruby and for gems. [`ruby.md`](ruby.md)
is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for JavaScript
(28) and Java (29): Ruby runs beside the program, they talk over a
socket, numbers and text cross and everything else stays, what Zeno
gives is a copy, a value from there is not a condition, the types are
known when the program runs, and nothing changes for a program that
does not ask. What follows is what Ruby made different.

### 37.1 `ruby.require` loads, and `ruby.constant` names

```zeno
ruby.require("date")
let Date = ruby.constant("Date")
```

**Why two functions, where Python has one.** In Python `import` gives
the module, and everything is reached from it. In Ruby `require`
gives nothing: it loads a file, and what the file brings are
constants that every program can then name. One library can bring
several (`net/http` brings `Net::HTTP` and `URI`), and many constants
need no library at all (`Math`, `File`, `Kernel`). A `ruby.module`
that guessed the constant from the name of the library would be right
for `date` and wrong for `net/http`, `yaml` (`YAML`) and
`active_support`.

**Why these names.** `require` is the word Ruby has, so it is the one
a person looks for. `constant` is what Ruby calls every name that
begins with a capital letter, a class, a module and `RUBY_VERSION`
alike, so one function covers them. It takes the name as Ruby writes
it, `"Net::HTTP"`.

**`require` gives none.** Ruby's gives `true` the first time and
`false` after, which says nothing a program of Zeno needs.

### 37.2 A call has brackets

In Ruby `day.year` is a call. In Zeno `thing.name` with no brackets
is the method itself, to be called later, as it is for a value of
JavaScript (28.6) and Java (29.3), and that rule holds for a value of
Ruby: `day.year()` calls, and `day.year` is the method.

**Why not call it as Ruby does.** A dot that sometimes calls is the
ambiguity the language was written to be without: `words.push` would
have to mean "call with nothing" or "the method" by a rule the reader
cannot see. With brackets every call in a Zeno program looks like a
call, whichever language answers it. Python, JavaScript and Java
already agree with Zeno here, so Ruby is the one that bends.

The method not called yet prints as a sentence that says so, since
the commonest mistake is to leave the brackets off as Ruby allows.

### 37.3 `send` for the names Zeno cannot write

`empty?`, `sort!`, `+`, `class` and `raise` cannot follow a dot in
Zeno. They are reached through `send`, which is Ruby's own method for
calling a method by its name: `words.send("empty?")`.

**Why not let `?` and `!` into a name after a dot.** `?` and `!` are
not part of any name in Zeno, and letting them in for one module
would change what the lexer reads for every program, which 26.11
rules out. It would also not reach the operators or the words.

**Why not the name in brackets, as for Java (29.10).** In Java an
object that has no items has no use for brackets. In Ruby almost
everything has `[]`: an Array, a Hash, a String, a Struct, a class
(`Hash["a", 1]`). `words["empty?"]` already means something there.
`send` means one thing, and is what a Ruby programmer would write.

Where a name has no method and the same name with `?` or `!` has, the
error says how to write it.

### 37.4 A symbol stays in Ruby; `ruby.symbol` makes one

`:up` and `"up"` are different values in Ruby, and a Hash keeps them
apart. If a symbol arrived as a str, the program could not give it
back as what it was, and `hash[key]` with a key Ruby gave would look
under the wrong key. So a symbol is one of the values that stay, and
`ruby.symbol("up")` is how a program writes `:up`.

**In a copy it is its name.** `ruby.copy` makes plain data of Zeno
(26.5), and a dict has keys that are str or int. A Hash with symbol
keys is the commonest Hash in Ruby, so the copy would be refused for
most of them if a symbol could not be a key. As a value it is copied
the same way, so that one rule covers both.

**No looking under both.** `ages["bob"]` does not also try `:bob`.
