A Hash can hold both keys, and then which one was meant would be a
guess.

### 37.5 Text and bytes are one String

Ruby has one class for both. A String comes across as a str when it
is text: as it is when Ruby has it in UTF-8, turned into UTF-8 when
it is in another encoding, and read as UTF-8 when Ruby has no
encoding for it (`ASCII-8BIT`), which is what a socket, `Net::HTTP`
and `File.binread` give. Bytes that do not read as UTF-8 stay in
Ruby.

**Why read the unlabelled bytes as text.** Most of what Ruby hands
out without an encoding is text: the body of a web page, the output
of a program. If those stayed in Ruby, the first thing most programs
do, fetch something and look at it, would give a value that `len` and
`+` refuse.

**What it costs.** Whether such a String arrives as a str depends on
what is in it, where everywhere else it depends on the kind of value:
the bytes of a file that happens to hold only text arrive as a str.
Python has `bytes` and JavaScript has `Buffer`, so they have no such
case. Nothing is lost by it, because a str given back to Ruby is the
same bytes. A program that must have bytes whatever they are reads
them through something that stays in Ruby: `File.open(name, "rb")`,
and its `each_byte()`.

### 37.6 An exception of Ruby is an error of Zeno

`ZeroDivisionError` and `KeyError` have Zeno's kinds of the same
name. `IndexError` and `StopIteration` are `IndexError`,
`ArgumentError` is `ValueError` (it is what Ruby raises for a value a
method cannot use, `Integer("x")`), `Errno::...` and `IOError` are
`FileError`, and the rest are `Error` with the name Ruby gave in
front. `RuntimeError` is the exception `raise "text"` makes, and its
name says nothing, so the message is the text alone, as for a plain
`Error` of JavaScript (28.8).

`ArgumentError` is also what Ruby raises for the wrong number of
arguments. That is a mistake in the program and not a value, but Ruby
does not tell the two apart, so neither can Zeno.

### 37.7 A loop goes through what `each` gives

`for item in thing` takes everything `thing.each` gives, as Ruby's
own `for` does, and of a Hash its keys, as for a dict.

**Why `each` and not `to_a`.** They are the same for most things and
differ for some: a table of `csv` gives its rows to `each` and its
header as well to `to_a`. A loop is `each`.

**Something with no end is refused.** `1..` and `loop` would be gone
through forever before the loop began (26.12). A Range with no end and
anything whose size is infinite raise `ValueError` and say what to
write (`first(n)`).

### 37.8 A library is looked for from the folder of the program

As for Python and JavaScript (28.9): the folder of the `.zeno` file
is the first place `require` looks, so a `helper.rb` beside the
program is `ruby.require("helper")`. A `Gemfile` there is the one
Bundler uses, when the program requires `bundler/setup` and
`BUNDLE_GEMFILE` does not already name another.

**Why Bundler is not required for the program.** A `Gemfile` beside
a program does not say that the program must run under it, and under
Bundler every gem that the `Gemfile` does not name is hidden. A
program of Ruby says `require "bundler/setup"` when it wants that,
and so does a program of Zeno.

### 37.9 Left for later

- A block: a function of Zeno given to `map`, `each`, `File.open`.
  It is the callback that 26.12 leaves, and Ruby needs it more than
  the others.
- A loop with two names over a Hash, giving the key and the value.
  It gives a count and the key, as over the list of keys that the
  loop takes. The same holds for a dict of Python and a Map of Java.
- A class of Zeno that inherits from a class of Ruby.
- `ruby` in a built program, and in `--target ruby`, as 26.9 has it
  for Python.
- Rubies before 3.1 and other Rubies (JRuby, TruffleRuby) are not
  tested. The helper uses nothing newer than Ruby 2.6.

### 37.10 On Windows the helper is a file

Everywhere else Ruby is started with `-e` and the helper as one word.
On Windows a program is handed its command line as one text and cuts
it into words itself, and Ruby cuts it by rules of its own: a `\`
followed by spaces and then a `"` takes the `"` out of the count, and
a word with `*` or `{` in it is looked up as the name of a file. The
helper arrived cut short at a line that ended in `\`, Ruby stopped on
a syntax error, and Zeno said there was no Ruby. So on Windows the
helper is written once into the folder for what can be made again
(`registry::cache`), under a number worked out from it, and Ruby is
given the file. **Turned down: only mending that line**, which was
done too: the next line of the helper to trip a rule nobody knows by
heart would bring the fault back, and only on a machine no test here
runs on. **Why not a file everywhere:** `-e` needs no folder to write
in, and works.

## 38. The libraries of PHP

The second language of the second version (26.1): `import php`, for
what comes with PHP and for Composer packages. [`php.md`](php.md) is
the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for the others (28,
29, 37): PHP runs beside the program, they talk over a socket,
numbers and text cross and objects stay, what Zeno gives is a copy, a
value from there is not a condition, the types are known when the
program runs, and nothing changes for a program that does not ask.
What follows is what PHP made different.

### 38.1 `php.type`, `php.callable` and `php.constant`, because PHP keeps the three apart

In Python everything a module has is reached with a dot from the
module. PHP has no value for a module, a class or a function: a class
is named by `new` and `::`, a function by being called, a constant by
being written. Each lives in its own table, and one name can be in
all three (`count` is a function, and many classes have a method and
a constant called that). So there is one way in for each.

**Why these names.** `type` is the word Java's module uses for a
class (29.1), and `class` cannot follow a dot. `callable` is what PHP
itself calls a value that can be called (`is_callable`,
`Closure::fromCallable`), and `function` is a word of Zeno.
`constant` is PHP's own `constant()`. Each takes the name as PHP
writes it, with its namespace: `"Carbon\\Carbon"`, `"Shop\\total"`,
`"DateTime::ATOM"`.

**`php.require(path)`** reads a file of PHP that is not in a package,
from the folder of the program, as `require_once` does. It gives
none, as Ruby's (37.1).

### 38.2 An array of PHP crosses whole

An array of PHP is a value and not an object: given to a function it
is copied, as a list of Zeno is not. It is what a list and a dict are
in PHP, both at once. So it comes across as one of them, whole: a
list where its keys are 0, 1, 2 and so on in order, a dict for any
other. `explode(",", "a,b")` gives a list of Zeno, which `append` and
`len` and everything else of Zeno work on.

**Why not leave it in PHP, as a list of Python stays (26.5).** A list
of Python is an object: two holders see one list, and changing it is
seen by both, so a copy would not be the same thing. An array of PHP
is never shared, so a copy is exactly what PHP would hand to another
function. Leaving it would only make every result of PHP's functions,
nearly all of which are arrays, go back to PHP for each item.

**An empty array is a list.** PHP cannot tell `[]` from an empty map.
A list is the commoner, and an empty list and an empty dict print
differently but are both empty.

### 38.3 A function that changes its argument is given a variable

`sort(&$array)` and `preg_match($p, $text, &$matches)` change what
they are given and give back something else. Given a list of Zeno,
they would change the copy PHP made of it, and nobody would see it.
`php.variable(value)` is a variable that lives in PHP. Given to such a
parameter, PHP changes it, and `.value` reads it after.

**A list given where a variable is wanted is an error**, before the
function is called. PHP knows which parameters are written `&$`, so
the helper asks it. A program that gave a list and saw nothing happen
would have no way to find out why.

**Why not change the list of Zeno after the call.** Zeno would have
to say which argument came back changed, for every call to every
function, and write it into a list the program may not expect to
change. `php.variable` says it at the line.

### 38.4 Classes, functions and methods are values the helper makes up

`php.type("DateTime")` gives a value that the helper made for the
class, since PHP has none. Calling it is `new`. A dot after it is
the constant of that name, or the static property, or the static
method. A dot after an object is the method of that name, or the
property.

**The method before the property.** PHP lets a class have both with
one name, and a dot in Zeno is one thing. A method is what a program
of PHP more often reaches by a name, and the property is still
reached with the name in brackets, `thing["name"]`, which on an
object that has no items of its own is the property first.

**A name in brackets for the words of Zeno.** `Size::from` and a
property `for` cannot follow a dot. As for Java (29.10) the name in
brackets reaches them: `Size["from"]("l")`. An object of a class
that has items of its own (`ArrayAccess`) keeps its brackets for
them.

### 38.5 Named arguments are PHP's

`name=value` is PHP 8's `name: value`, by the name of the parameter.
This is why PHP 8 is the oldest PHP the module says it works with:
the rest of the helper would run on 7.4.

### 38.6 A warning of PHP is an error of Zeno

PHP reports most of what goes wrong in its functions by a warning on
the screen and a value of `false`: `file_get_contents` of a file that
is not there. A program of Zeno would go on with the `false`, and
fail somewhere else. So the helper turns a warning into an error, and
the error has the kind of what the warning says: `FileError` for a
file, `Error` for the rest. A notice and a deprecation only advise,
and PHP prints them as it always does. `@` before a call in PHP,
which hides its warning, has no form in Zeno, so a warning is not
hidden.

`DivisionByZeroError` is `ZeroDivisionError`. `ValueError`,
`InvalidArgumentException`, `DomainException` and `JsonException` are
`ValueError`. `OutOfBoundsException` and `OutOfRangeException` are
`IndexError`. Everything else is `Error`, with PHP's name for it in
front, but for the plain `Exception` and `Error`, whose name says
nothing.

**What it costs.** PHP has no exception of its own for a file, so
whether a warning or a `RuntimeException` is a `FileError` is read
from its text: "Failed to open stream", "No such file or directory",
"Permission denied" and a few others. These are the system's words,
which PHP passes on, and are the same in every PHP 8.

### 38.7 Bytes that are not text stay in PHP

A string of PHP is bytes. Where they read as UTF-8 they are a str,
as for Ruby (37.5), and bytes that do not stay in PHP. There an item
is a byte as an int, `len` is how many, and `for` goes through them,
since a program that kept bytes wants them as numbers.

### 38.8 The helper's names begin with `zeno_` and `Zeno`

A Composer package puts its functions and classes into the one
program PHP runs, beside the helper's. PHP refuses a second function
of one name, so a package with a `keep` or a `back` would stop the
helper from starting. Every function of the helper begins with
`zeno_`, and every class with `Zeno`.

### 38.9 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to PHP: `array_map`, `usort`,
  `preg_replace_callback`. It is the callback that 26.12 leaves.
- A class of Zeno that extends a class of PHP.
- `php` in a built program, and in `--target php`, as 26.9 has it
  for Python.
- Only PHP 8.3 is tested. PHP 7.4 would run all but named arguments,
  and is not tried.

## 39. The libraries of Lua

The third language of the second version (26.1): `import lua`, for
Lua's own library and for modules from LuaRocks. [`lua.md`](lua.md)
is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for the others
(28, 29, 37, 38). What follows is what Lua made different.

### 39.1 `lua.require` and `lua.global`

`lua.require(name)` is Lua's `require`, which gives the module, as
Python's `import` does. So unlike Ruby's (37.1) it gives what was
loaded. `lua.global(name)` is what every program of Lua has without a
`require`, `string`, `table`, `os`, and is named as Node's (28.2),
which is the same thing.

### 39.2 Lua is talked to over named pipes

Every other helper connects back over a socket of this machine. Lua
comes with no sockets, and the one library that gives them, LuaSocket,
is written in C and has to be built for each Lua. What Lua does have
is `io.open`, and on Linux and macOS a named pipe is a file it can
open. So Zeno makes two pipes with `mkfifo`, in a folder only this
user can open, and Lua opens them as files: one Lua writes and Zeno
reads, one the other way. The names are removed as soon as both ends
are open, so once Lua has started there is nothing to clean up.

**Why not stdin and stdout, which every Lua has.** The helper leaves
the screen and the keyboard to Lua (26.3): a library that prints, or
asks, works as it would in a program of Lua. On stdout the lines
would be mixed with what Lua prints, and a module written in C prints
around anything the helper could put in the way.

**Windows has no such pipe.** Its named pipes are not files that
`io.open` can make, so there the helper uses LuaSocket if it is
installed, and says so if it is not. The same is done where `mkfifo`
is not there. The rest of the bridge does not know which it is: a
link is something to read lines from and something to write them to.

### 39.3 A function gets `self` when it is a method

Lua writes `object:name(x)` and `module.name(x)`, and only the colon
gives the function its object. Zeno has one dot, and the call cannot
say which is meant. The function can: one written
`function Class:name()` has a first parameter called `self`, and Lua
5.2 and later say what a function's parameters are called. A function
read from a table is given the table when its first parameter is
`self`.

Lua 5.1 cannot say, and neither can a function written in C. For
those, a function that the table has from its metatable is a method,
and one the table holds itself is not. This is how Lua makes an
object: its methods are in the class, which is the metatable's
`__index`, while a module is a plain table that holds its functions.
A function read from a userdata, a file or a socket, is always given
it, as their methods are all called with a colon.

**When the rule is wrong**, the name in brackets is Lua's own
`t["name"]`, which gives the function as it is, and the program
passes the object itself: `p["length"](p)`.

**Why not a second way to write a call, such as `p.call("length")`.**
Zeno's dot already means the method of an object for every other
language, and almost every call of a library is told apart by the
rule. A second form would have to be written at each of those calls,
for the few the rule gets wrong.

### 39.4 Several values are a list

A function of Lua gives any number of values. None is `none`, one is
that value, and several are a list of Zeno with all of them:
`string.find("hello", "l")` is `[3, 3]`.

**Why not the first only, as Lua does in an expression.** What comes
second is often what the call was for: the count of `gsub`, the
captures of `find`, the next position of `string.unpack`. Lua's own
`local a, b = f()` takes them all, and Zeno has no such assignment.

**`nil` and a message is an error.** This is how most functions of
Lua say they failed (`io.open`, `os.rename`, `load`), and what a
program of Lua passes to `assert`. Given back as `[none, "message"]`,
it would be a list, which is not `none`, and a program that tested the
result would go on. When the first of two or more values is `nil` and
the second a string, the call raises `Error` with that message, and
`FileError` when a number comes third, which is the number of the
system that Lua's file functions give. A single `nil` is still `none`:
`string.find` with no match.

### 39.5 A table stays in Lua, and counts from 1

A table is shared in Lua, as a list of Python is, so it stays (26.5).
Its items are where Lua has them, and `t[1]` is the first. `lua.copy`
makes a list of a table whose keys are 1 to its length, and a dict of
any other.

**Why not shift the index by one.** `t[1]` in Zeno would then be
`t[2]` in Lua, and a key that is a number would mean one thing in a
table that is a list and another in one that is not. Everything a
program reads about Lua says `t[1]`. The list that `lua.copy` makes is
Zeno's, and counts from 0 as every list does.

**`for` over a table** gives the items of a list and the keys of any
other, as Zeno's own `for` does for a list and a dict. **Over a
function** it is Lua's generic `for`: the function is called until it
gives `nil`, which is what `string.gmatch` and `io.lines` give.

### 39.6 Numbers

Lua 5.3 and later know whether a number is an integer, and it arrives
as what it is. Before 5.3, and in LuaJIT, every number is a float, and
a whole one within 2^53 arrives as an int, as in JavaScript (28.3).

### 39.7 Named arguments are a table of options

As for JavaScript (28.4): Lua has no named arguments, and a library
takes a table of options last instead. `f(1, loud=true)` is
`f(1, {loud = true})`.

### 39.8 An error of Lua is an `Error`

Lua's errors are values with no kind, usually a string, so every
error of Lua is an `Error` with the value as its message. The
position that Lua puts in front of a message names the helper when an
error is raised from a function of Lua's library, so that position is
taken off. The one other kind is the `FileError` of 39.4.

### 39.9 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to Lua: `table.sort(t, f)`, callbacks.
- Windows, which needs LuaSocket and was not tried.
- `lua` in a built program, and in `--target lua`, as 26.9 has it for
  Python.

## 40. The libraries of C# and .NET

The fourth language of the second version (26.1): `import csharp`, for
the types that come with .NET and for packages of NuGet.
[`csharp.md`](csharp.md) is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as
it does for the others, and .NET is close to Java (29): classes,
methods of one name that take different things, a helper that has to
be compiled. Where Java decided a question the same way, 29 has the
reason, and what follows is what .NET made different.

### 40.1 The module is `csharp`

**Why not `dotnet`, which is the runtime and the command.** Every
other module is named for the language its libraries are written in,
and the name is what a person reads in the documentation of a library:
"a library for C#". F# and Visual Basic run on .NET too, and what they
make is used the same way, but nearly every package of NuGet is
written in C# and documented with it. `cs` is the target of
`zeno build --target cs` (24), which writes a program, and is the
wrong word for using a library.

`csharp.type(name)` is named as Java's (29.1), and calling it is
`new` (29.2). `csharp.assembly(path)` is Java's `java.jar`: an
assembly is what .NET calls a .dll.

### 40.2 A type is named as C# writes it

`"List<int>"`, `"Dictionary<string, List<int>>"`, `"int[]"`, `"int?"`,
and `"string"` for `System.String`. .NET's own way to write a
generic type, `"System.Collections.Generic.List`1[System.Int32]"`, is
what `Type.GetType` takes, and nobody writes it in a program.

**A name with no namespace is looked for in the namespaces a new
project of C# has without a `using`**: `System`,
`System.Collections.Generic`, `System.IO`, `System.Linq`,
`System.Net.Http`, `System.Threading`, `System.Threading.Tasks`.

**Why, when Java's types need the whole name (29.1).** For Java the
packages looked in would have been a list Zeno chose. This list is
C#'s own: every project made by `dotnet new` since .NET 6 has these
namespaces without asking (its "implicit usings"), so a person who
writes C# already writes `File`, `Math` and `List<int>` with no
namespace. A name that is not found with its namespace is tried there
only after, so a whole name always means what it says.

### 40.3 Of several methods, the arguments choose, and a named argument is a parameter

The choice is Java's (29.4), with C#'s order: an int of Zeno fits an
`int` before a `long` and both before a `double`; a list fits an array
or a `List<T>` as well as its items fit theirs, a class before an
interface; `int?` takes what `int` takes, one step later. Two that fit
as well are an error that lists both.

**A named argument is given to the parameter of that name**,
`Math.Round(2.567, digits=1)`. C# has named arguments of its own,
unlike Java (29) and Lua (39.7), so `name=value` means in Zeno what
`name: value` means in C#. The message that says no method fits lists
each with the names of its parameters, so the names can be found.

**A method that hides one of its base class's** (`new` in C#) is the
one there is: `JObject.Parse` and `JToken.Parse` take the same
arguments, and C# calls the first on a `JObject`.

**A generic method is given its types from the arguments**:
`Task.FromResult(7)` is `Task.FromResult<long>(7)`. A type that no
argument says is `object`. Writing the types in the call, as C# can,
is the rejected alternative of 29.4.

### 40.4 A `Task` is waited for

A method that takes time, such as one that reads the network, gives a
`Task`, and C# writes `await` before the call. Zeno waits for it, and
the call gives what the task gave: `none` for a plain `Task`.

**Why not give the `Task`.** Zeno has no `await` for a value of
another language, and a `Task` that is not waited for does its work
while the program goes on, or not at all if the program ends first.
Every library of .NET that reads a file or the network has methods
that end in `Async`, and each would need a second call to be of use.

### 40.5 Numbers go as `long`, and are made what the parameter is

Every whole number of Zeno arrives as a `long`, and becomes `int`,
`short`, `byte` or an enum when the method takes one and it fits, as
C# turns `5` into what it is given to. A float becomes a `float` or a
`decimal` the same way. Every whole number that comes back and fits 64
bits is an int, and a `decimal` stays in .NET, since a float of Zeno
would change it.

**Why not Java's rule (29.5)**, `Integer` when it fits: that was for a
collection that takes `Object`. A collection of .NET says its type
(`List<int>`), and the number is made that type when it is given.

### 40.6 A package is found from the project beside the program

.NET has no folder that every package goes to, as pip and npm have,
and NuGet installs a package only into a project. So the program uses
the project beside it: `dotnet new classlib` and `dotnet add package`
in its folder (or one above), and Zeno reads `obj/project.assets.json`,
which `dotnet` writes and which names each .dll of each package, and
of every package it needs, and where NuGet keeps it. A type is then
found in them by its name, as in .NET's own.

**Why not a name and a version in the program, as
`csharp.package("Humanizer.Core", "3.0.10")`.** The packages a package
needs, and which of their versions, are worked out by NuGet, and the
file that NuGet writes is the answer. Zeno would otherwise have to
work them out as NuGet does. It also leaves the project as .NET has
it: `dotnet` builds it, updates it and lists what it has, and the code
of C# beside the program is built into it (`csharp.assembly` of its
`bin` folder).

**Why not install what is missing.** No other module installs
anything (26), and a program that fetches from the network when it is
run is a program that does something it does not say.

### 40.7 The helper is built once with `dotnet build`, and kept

As Java's (29.9): the source is in the `zeno` file, the first run
builds it in the folder for what can be made again, under a number
worked out from the source, and later runs start what was built. .NET
takes some seconds where `javac` takes one, so this matters more.

**It is built for the .NET that builds it**, read from
`dotnet --version`, and it may run on a later one (`RollForward`).
.NET cannot compile a single file as it starts, as Java 11 can, so
where it cannot be built `dotnet run` is started instead, which says
why: there is no SDK, only the runtime.

### 40.8 An exception of .NET is an error of Zeno

`IOException` and those under it, and `UnauthorizedAccessException`,
are `FileError`; `KeyNotFoundException` is `KeyError`;
`IndexOutOfRangeException` and `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` are
`IndexError`; `ArgumentException` and `FormatException` are
`ValueError`; `DivideByZeroException` is `ZeroDivisionError`;
`OverflowException` is `OverflowError`. Every other is `Error`. The
message begins with .NET's name for it, as Java's does (29.7).

**Why more than Java's three.** .NET has an exception of its own for
each of these, where Java's `ArithmeticException` was two kinds. Each
means in .NET what the kind means in Zeno, by .NET's own description.

### 40.9 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to .NET: an event, a `Func<T>`, the
  lambdas of LINQ.
- An extension method called with a dot on its object.
- What a method puts back in an `out` or `ref` parameter.
- `csharp` in a built program, and in `--target cs`, as 26.9 has it
  for Python.

## 41. `f32`: a float of 32 bits

```zeno
let gain: f32 = 0.1
var total: f32 = 0.0
for i in range(10) {
    total += gain
}
print(gain, total)          # 0.1 1.0000001
let wide: float = total     # an f32 goes where a float is wanted
```

Most boards with a float unit (a Cortex-M4F, an M33, an ESP32) have one
of 32 bits. A `float` of 64 bits is done there in software, many times
slower, and a sensor's reading, a filter's coefficient or a PID gain
never needed 16 digits. `f32` is a float of 32 bits, as C's `float`,
Rust's `f32` and Java's `float`. It is the fifth item of
[`missing.md`](missing.md). Walkthrough: [`f32.md`](f32.md).

### 41.1 The name is `f32`

**`f32`, beside `u8` and `i32`.** A sized type in Zeno is named by what
it holds and how many bits: `u` for a whole number without a sign, `i`
with one, and now `f` for a float. Rust and Zig spell it the same.
**Turned down: `float32`**, Go's, which is longer and breaks the
pattern; **`single`**, C#'s and Pascal's, which says nothing to anyone
who has not met it; and C's own `float`, which Zeno already uses for the
64-bit one.

### 41.2 A sum of `f32`s is an `f32`, and a sum with a `float` is refused

**An f32 with an f32, or with an int, gives an f32.** `+ - * /` are done
in 32 bits, and `// % **` in 64 and rounded once to 32, which is the
same answer to within the last bit and the same in every engine. An int
beside an f32 is turned into a float and then into the nearest f32, so
`gain * 3` is an f32. A comparison compares the two f32s.

**Why not "arithmetic gives an int" (2.8a)?** A sized whole number is a
way to store a number, and the danger is a sum that wraps; doing the sum
in an `int` takes that danger away. An f32 is a way to *compute*: the
point is that the board's float unit does the sum. Making every sum a
`float` would put the sums back in software, which is the thing `f32`
is for avoiding.

**An f32 with a float is refused before the program runs**, with a
message that says what to write:

```
error: `+` between f32 and float would have to choose between 32 bits and 64. Write `f32( )` around the float to work in 32, or `float( )` around the f32 to work in 64
```

Either answer is a guess. C picks 64 bits silently, so a single `1.5`
in a filter written in `float`s turns the whole sum into software
`double`s, which is a classic slow bug on a microcontroller. Picking 32
bits silently would throw away digits the float had. The principle is
"one meaning" (4), and here the program has to say which one.

A **written** float is not a float value, and adapts (41.4): `gain +
1.5` is an f32 sum.

### 41.3 An `f32` goes where a `float` is wanted

**Every f32 is exactly a float**, so nothing is lost, and asking for
`float( )` each time would be noise: an f32 is given to a function that
takes a `float`, put in a `float` variable, or returned as one, and is
widened on the way. This is the rule of sized whole numbers (2.8c),
which go where an `int` is wanted.

**A `list[f32]` is not a `list[float]`**, for the reason a `list[u8]` is
not a `list[int]`: lists are shared, and whoever held it as a
`list[float]` could put a float in it that is not an f32. The message
says to copy it, `[float(x) for x in readings]`.

### 41.4 A written float is rounded to the nearest `f32`

**`let gain: f32 = 0.1` needs nothing more.** A number written in the
program where an f32 is wanted, or beside an f32 in a sum or a
comparison, is made the nearest f32 before the program runs. 0.1 has no
exact f32, as it has no exact float, and the nearest one is what anyone
writing 0.1 there means. **Turned down: C's `0.1f`**, a mark on every
number in a filter, which says nothing the type does not.

**A written number too big for an f32 is an error before the program
runs**: `let a: f32 = 1e39` says `1e39 does not fit in an f32, whose
largest is about 3.4e38`. A written number too small becomes the
nearest f32, which may be a subnormal or 0, as in every language.

**A float value is not rounded by itself.** `let a: f32 = x`, with `x` a
`float`, is refused, and the message says to write `f32(x)`. Most
floats are not f32s, so the rounding is a step the program should show.

### 41.5 `f32(x)` makes one

**`f32(x)` takes an int, a float or an f32** and gives the nearest f32.
A float too big for an f32 is an `OverflowError`, a `try` can catch, as
a whole number too big for a `u8` is a `ValueError` for `u8(n)`;
`f32(inf)` is inf and `f32(nan)` is NaN, which are f32s. An int is first
made a float, as everywhere: `f32(16777217)` is `16777216.0`.
`float(x)` and `int(x)` take an f32.

### 41.6 `math` works in 64 bits

**`math.sqrt(gain)` gives a `float`.** The functions of `math` take a
float, and an f32 goes in by 41.3. Each gives the same answer in every
engine and target, because each language's 64-bit `sqrt`, `sin` and the
rest agree, and not all of them have 32-bit ones. `abs`, `min`, `max`
and `sum` keep an f32 an f32: they choose or add, and `sum` adds in 32
bits, one item at a time.

### 41.7 What a build writes

**C writes `float`.** A sum of two f32s is C's `float` sum, a field is
four bytes, and `-O2` uses the float unit's own instructions. Division
by zero is a `ZeroDivisionError`, as for a float, except in a minimal
build, which has no checks.

**LLVM keeps an f32 in a `double` and rounds after each step.** For `+
- * /` this is the same answer bit for bit: a double has more than
twice the bits of an f32 and two more, so rounding the exact double
answer to 32 bits gives the answer a 32-bit unit gives. It kept the
backend's slots and calls unchanged.

**Every target language** has a type for an f32 in its runtime and does
the same rounding: Go's `float32`, Java's and Kotlin's `Float`, C#'s
`float`, C++'s own tag, Rust's `f32`, and a small class with the value
in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Ruby, PHP, Lua and Dart, which
round with their own 32-bit tools (`struct`, `Math.fround`, `pack`,
`string.pack`, `Float32List`). `tools/targets/edge-f32.zeno` holds them
all to `zeno run`.

### 41.8 An `f32` is printed with the fewest digits that read back as it

**`print(gain)` shows `0.1`**, not `0.10000000149011612`: the shortest
number that, made an f32 again, is the same f32, then written as a float
is. That is what Rust, Java and C# print for one. `print(float(gain))`
shows every digit of the float it is, for when that matters.

### 41.9 Left for later

- `json.write` of an f32, and `f32("0.5")` from text.
- A format such as `{x:.2}` with no `f` after it, for an f32.
- `math` in 32 bits (`sqrtf`), when a program shows it is too slow.
- `pointer[f32]` and a register that holds an f32.
- An f32 field in LLVM takes eight bytes, where C takes four.
- A generic function copied for `T = f32` that changes a number written
  once in it rounds it for every copy.

## 42. `u64`: a whole number of 64 bits with no sign

```zeno
function fnv(text: str) -> u64 raises OverflowError {
    var h: u64 = 0xcbf29ce484222325
    for c in text {
        h = h ^ u64(c.code())
        h = u64.wrap(h * 0x100000001b3)
    }
    return h
}
let hash = fnv("hello")
print(f"{hash:016x}")             # a430d84680aabd0b
print(u8.max, i16.min, u64.max)   # 255 -32768 18446744073709551615
```

A hash (FNV, CRC-64, xxHash), a random generator (xorshift, PCG), a
counter of microseconds since boot, a 64-bit register, a file offset
past 8 exabytes: each is a whole number of 64 bits with no sign, and
Zeno's `int` has a sign. `u64` is that number, as C's `uint64_t`, Rust's
`u64` and Go's `uint64`. With it come the limits of every whole type,
`u8.max` to `u64.max`, which Rust spells `u8::MAX`. It is the sixth
item of [`missing.md`](missing.md). Walkthrough: [`u64.md`](u64.md).

### 42.1 The name is `u64`, and there is no `i64`

**`u64`, beside `u8`, `u16` and `u32`.** The pattern of 2.8 names a
whole type by its sign and its bits. Rust and Zig spell it the same.
**Turned down: `uint64`** (Go), longer and outside the pattern, and
**`ulong`** (C#), which says nothing of the size.

**There is no `i64`.** It would be a second name for `int`, which is
already a signed number of 64 bits, and two names for one type is two
meanings (4): a reader would ask how they differ. `int.max` and
`int.min` are its limits.

### 42.2 A sum of `u64`s is a `u64`, checked

**`+ - * // % **` between two u64s give a u64**, and a result past
18446744073709551615 or below 0 is an `OverflowError`, as an `int` sum
past its end is (2.4):

```
the result is too big for a u64
the result is below 0, and a u64 never is
```

`/` gives a float, as it does for ints. `& | ^ ~ << >>` work on the
bits; a shift is 0 to 63, and `<<` that pushes a 1 off the top is an
`OverflowError`, as for an int.

**Why not "arithmetic gives an int" (2.8a)?** That rule makes `u8 + u8`
an `int` so that the sum cannot wrap. An `int` cannot hold half the
numbers a `u64` holds, so the sum would fail where the u64 did not.
The answer stays a u64 and is checked instead.

**Why checked, when C and Go wrap?** For the reason ints are (2.4): a
silent wrap is a wrong number that looks right. A program that wants
the wrap says so with `u64.wrap` (42.6), and a reader sees it.

### 42.3 A `u64` meets only a `u64` or a written number

**A u64 with an int value, a float, or any other type is refused before
the program runs**, with a message that says what to write:

```
error: `+` between u64 and int would have to choose between a u64 and an int. Write `u64( )` around the int to work in u64s, or `int( )` around the u64
```

Either guess can be wrong. Making it a u64 fails when the int is
below 0; making it an int fails when the u64 is past `int.max`. C picks
unsigned silently, so `-1 < x` is false for every unsigned `x`, one of
its best known traps. The principle is "one meaning" (4), and here the
program says which.

**A written number adapts**, as it does for f32 (41.4): `h * 3`,
`h == 0`, `h > 1000` and `[h, 7, 8]` need nothing more, and the list is
a `list[u64]`. A written number below 0 beside a u64 is an error before
the program runs (`-1 does not fit in a u64`).

A u8, u16 or u32 does not mix with a u64 by itself either, because
their sums are ints (2.8a). `u64(x)` never fails for one, and the
message says so.

### 42.4 Conversions say what they check

| Write | Gives | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `u64(n)` | a u64 | `n` is below 0: `OverflowError` |
| `int(x)` | an int | `x` is past `int.max`: `OverflowError` |
| `u8(int(x))` and the like | that type | it does not fit |
| `float(x)` | the nearest float | never |
| `str(x)` | its digits | never |

**A u64 does not go where an int is wanted by itself**, though a u8
does (2.8c): every u8 is an int, and half of the u64s are not. The
message names the conversion. **A u64 does not go where a float is
wanted** either: a float holds 53 bits exactly, so most u64s past 2**53
would change, and the program should show the step.

### 42.5 A written number past `int.max` is a u64

**`let x: u64 = 18446744073709551615` is written as it reads.** The
lexer reads a whole number up to the largest u64, and the checker
accepts one past `int.max` only where a u64 is wanted:

```
error: 18446744073709551615 is too big for an int (-9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807). Only a u64 holds it: write it where a u64 is wanted, as in `let x: u64 = 18446744073709551615`
```

A number past the largest u64 says so, in decimal or hex:
`this number is too big. The largest whole number Zeno holds is
18446744073709551615, the largest u64`. This replaces the lexer's old
"number is too large", which said nothing of where the end is.
**Turned down: a mark such as Rust's `5u64` or C's `5ULL`**, a mark on
each number that says nothing the type does not.

### 42.6 `u64.wrap` keeps the low 64 bits

**`u64.wrap(h * 0x100000001b3)` is the multiplication cut to 64
bits**, which is what a hash or a random generator means; `u64.wrap(a +
b)`, `u64.wrap(a - b)` and `u64.wrap(a << n)` are the same for those
operators. **`u64.wrap(n)` of an int keeps its 64 bits read with no
sign**: `u64.wrap(-1)` is `u64.max`. This is the rule of `u8.wrap`
(2.8b), the same word for the same idea, and Rust's `wrapping_mul`.

**Why a wrapper around the sum, and not a function `wrapping_mul(a,
b)`?** The sum reads as a sum, and the one word at the front says
everything inside wraps. **Turned down: Go's and C's silent wrap**
(42.2), and a separate type that always wraps (Rust's `Wrapping<u64>`),
which hides the wrap at each use.

### 42.7 Every whole type has `.max` and `.min`

**`u8.max`, `u8.min`, `i8.max` ... `u32.max`, `int.max`, `int.min`,
`u64.max` and `u64.min`.** Each is the number of its type: `u8.max` is
a u8 of 255, and `u8.max + 1` is the int 256 by 2.8a. Before this, a
program wrote 255 or 2147483647 by hand, and a digit wrong in one is
hard to see. Rust spells it `u8::MAX`; Zeno
already reads `.` as "of", and `max` and `min` are the words Zeno uses
for the larger and smaller (`max(a, b)`). **Turned down: C's
`UINT8_MAX`**, a name in capitals for each type, and Java's
`Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

The floats have no `.max` yet (42.10).

### 42.8 What a build writes

**C writes `uint64_t`.** `+ - *` are checked with the compiler's
`__builtin_add_overflow` and its two friends, which are one instruction
and a branch. `--release`, `--fast` and `--minimal` drop the checks and
wrap, as they do for ints, so the C there is C's own `+`. `--firmware`
carries the `OverflowError` as a value, as for every error.

**LLVM keeps a u64 in an `i64`**, which has no sign of its own, and
uses the unsigned instructions: `udiv`, `urem`, `icmp ult`, `lshr`,
`uitofp`. The checks call the same runtime functions as C.

**Every target language** has a u64 in its runtime: Go's `uint64`,
Rust's `u64`, C#'s `ulong`, Kotlin's `ULong`, C++'s own tag over
`uint64_t`; Java's `long` with its unsigned methods
(`Long.compareUnsigned`, `Math.unsignedMultiplyHigh`); a small class
over a big whole number in Python, Ruby, JavaScript, TypeScript (a
`BigInt`) and Dart (a `BigInt`); and a class over the 64 bits in PHP
and Lua, which have only signed ints and do the unsigned steps by hand
(Lua's `math.ult`, PHP's sums in pieces of 32 and 16 bits). `tools/targets/
edge-u64.zeno` holds them all to `zeno run`.

### 42.9 A u64 prints its digits, and `x` its bits

**`print(h)` shows the decimal digits**, all twenty of
`18446744073709551615` when it is the largest. `{h:x}`, `{h:X}` and
`{h:b}` show the bits with no sign, so `{u64.wrap(-1):x}` is
`ffffffffffffffff`; `{h:016x}` pads with zeros, as a hash is shown.
`{h:d}`, a width, `<` `>` `^` and `{h:.2f}` work as for an int.

### 42.10 Left for later

- A u64 as a key of a dict, in `range( )`, or as an index. Each is
  refused before the program runs today; `int( )` makes one an int.
- `pointer[u64]` and a register of 64 bits.
- `json.write` of a u64 (a `ValueError` today), and `u64("123")`.
- A u8, u16 or u32 going where a u64 is wanted by itself. Each fits,
  so this is safe; it needs the sized types' sums to have a type
  first.
- `float.max`, `float.min` and `f32.max`.
- `u8(x)` and `u8.wrap(x)` straight from a u64, without `int( )` between.
- A u64 field in a firmware struct is 8 bytes in C; packed layouts of
  registers are item 9 of [`missing.md`](missing.md).

### 42.11 The new numbers cost the old ones nothing

f32 and u64 each brought a test to the top of every `a + b`, and arms
for `none`, `u64` and the pins to the test of `a == b`. Counted by
`bench/run.py --count`, a program of strings ran 0.85% more
instructions in the VM than in 0.5.2 and one of trees 0.54% more,
though neither has an f32 or a u64 in it. Two causes, both found with
callgrind and not guessed from timings:

- `value::equal` grew too big for the compiler to copy into each
  operator, so every `==` became a call. It is now two parts: the
  common pairs (int, string, bool, `none`) in a small part that is
  copied in, and every other pair in a second part that is called.
  The answers are the same for every pair.
- The two tests for f32 and u64 asked four questions of every
  operator. They are now one question per side (f32 and u64 sit next
  to each other in `Value`, so "is it either" is one comparison), and
  the work for them lives in its own function, `narrow_binary`.

After both, against 0.5.2, the VM ran fib, loop and sort to the same
count within 0.03%, strings 0.07% fewer, trees 0.08% more and nbody
0.13% more.

The interpreter (`zeno run` with no `--vm`) showed the same thing a
third time: fib ran 0.8% more instructions, every one of them in
`ops::binary`, which had grown. The VM had long answered two ints and
two floats itself before calling it. That short part is now
`ops::fast_binary`, `ops::binary` tries it first for whoever calls,
and the long part is `binary_rest`. The interpreter's fib went from
12,888 million instructions to 12,499 million, 2.2% fewer than in
0.5.2, and the VM's counts did not move.
The rule stays that a feature a program does not use costs that
program nothing (decision 34.5 is the same lesson for `program.exit`).

## 43. Units made of units: `V * A` is `W`

```zeno
let supply = 3.3 V
let draw = 20 mA
let power = supply * draw
print(power, power.mW)          # 0.066 W 66 mW
print(supply / draw)            # 165 ohm
print(1 / 2 ms)                 # 500 Hz
print((5 W * 2 h).Wh)           # 10 Wh
```

Units are what Zeno has that C does not (1.15), and until now they
stopped at the sums a firmware program does every day: the power a
board draws, the resistor for a current, the energy a battery gives,
the frequency of a period. A program took the numbers out, multiplied,
and put a unit back by hand, which is the very slip units exist to
catch. It is the seventh item of [`missing.md`](missing.md).
Walkthrough: [`units-made.md`](units-made.md).

### 43.1 A closed list of what units make

**Zeno makes a unit from two others only when the pair is on a list:**

| Write | Gives |
|---|---|
| voltage `*` current, either way round | power |
| current `*` resistance, either way round | voltage |
| power `*` time, either way round | energy |
| power `/` voltage, power `/` current | current, voltage |
| voltage `/` current, voltage `/` resistance | resistance, current |
| energy `/` time, energy `/` power | power, time |
| a number `/` time, a number `/` frequency | frequency, time |
| time `*` frequency, either way round | a plain number |

These are Ohm's law, power and energy, and periods, which are nearly
all the sums with units in a firmware program. Any other pair is
refused before the program runs, and the message lists these.

**Why a list, and not an algebra of dimensions?** An algebra (F#, the
`uom` crate of Rust, Boost.Units) makes `m * m` a unit of its own, and
`V * s / m` too, and then needs a name for each answer or shows it as
`kg*m^2*s^-3`. That is a feature the size of the rest of the units, and
most of what it makes has no name a firmware engineer would use. A list
keeps 1.15's rule that every unit has a name on the list, so a typing
slip is still an error, and it says in one table what works. A pair can
be added to the list later without changing any program that works
now. **Turned down: making a unit for a pair that is not on the list**,
because a `V * V` in a program is far more often a slip than a sum.

### 43.2 The answer is in the unit with no prefix

**`3.3 V * 20 mA` is `0.066 W`, and `.mW` makes it `66 mW`.** Each side
is first put in the unit of its kind with no prefix (`V`, `A`, `ohm`,
`W`, `J`, `s`, `Hz`), the numbers are multiplied or divided, and the
answer is in that unit of its own kind.

**Why not the "finer unit" of 1.15?** "Finer" compares two units of
one kind, and here the answer is a third kind. A rule from the prefixes
(`mV * mA` is `uW`) would need units that are not on the list, and two
programs that work out the same power would print it in two units. One
rule, the same every time, is "no prefix"; `.mW` says the rest, as
`.ms` does for time.

`J` is the energy with no prefix. A program that wants watt-hours
writes `.Wh`, as it writes `.ms`.

### 43.3 Time times frequency is a plain number

**`10 ms * 1 kHz` is `10.0`**, the number of cycles, as `1 s / 1 ms` is
`1000.0` by 1.15. A count of cycles has no unit on the list, and a
float is what it is.

### 43.4 A number over a time is a frequency

**`1 / 2 ms` is `500 Hz`, and `1 / 1 kHz` is `0.001 s`.** Only time and
frequency turn over: `1 / 2 V` has no unit on the list and is refused.
A unit binds to its number, so `1 / 2 ms` needs no brackets.

### 43.5 Every engine and build, the same digits

The interpreter, the VM, C, LLVM and all fifteen target languages
scale each side the same way, `x * times / over` with the same numbers,
and then multiply or divide once, so they print the same digits. In C
and LLVM the scales are known when the program is built, and a sum is
one or two instructions; a quantity is still a `double` with its unit
known only to the compiler. Division by zero is a `ZeroDivisionError`,
except where a build has no checks.

### 43.6 Left for later

- More pairs: charge (`mAh`, for battery life), speed (`m / s`),
  `rpm` and `Hz`.
- A unit a program names itself.
- `sum` of quantities, which still wants `+` in a loop (1.15).

## 44. The libraries of C, Go and Rust

The third version of using other languages' libraries (26.1):
`import c`, for a library of C, and for a library of Go or Rust built
with the C interface each of them has. [`c.md`](c.md) is the
walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here too: nothing changes for a program
that does not ask, the helper runs beside Zeno and not inside it, and
what can be refused is refused with a message that says what to do.
What follows is what C made different.

### 44.1 The module is `c`, and it has one function

**`c.library(library, declarations)`.** Every other language could be
asked what a thing is: Python has `dir`, Java has reflection. C cannot.
A library of C knows the names of its functions and nothing of what
they take or give, and that is only in the header. So the program
says it, and the words it says it in are the ones it would copy from
the header: `"double cbrt(double x);"`. That is one thing to learn
for a person who knows C, and nothing new to learn for the library.

**Why not read the header itself.** A header is written for the C
preprocessor: macros, `#ifdef`s for each system, other headers it
includes. Reading it right is the work of a C compiler, and the whole
of `<stdio.h>` is hundreds of declarations a program does not use.
The program declares the few it calls, and may still `#include` the
header, so that the compiler checks that the two agree (44.3).

**Why `c` and not `native` or `ffi`.** The module is named for the
language its libraries are written in, as `python` and `csharp` are
(40.1). Go and Rust come through it because what they give C is a
library of C (44.6).

### 44.2 The library is named as the compiler would be told it

One text or a list: a bare name is `-l` (`"z"` is `-lz`), a name with
`/` or the ending of a file (`.c`, `.so`, `.a`, `.o`, `.dylib`,
`.dll`) is a file, found from the program's folder, and a word that
starts with `-` goes to the compiler as it is. `none` is the C
library every program has. A person who has built with the library
in C already knows what to write.

**Why a `.c` file may be given.** A board's firmware has C already
(a checksum, a protocol), and testing it from a Zeno program on the
computer, with no board, is the first thing a firmware engineer will
want. Building it with the rest costs nothing more.

### 44.3 The C compiler works out the types

Zeno writes a small file of C with a function for each declaration,
which takes the arguments from a table and calls the real one, and
builds it with the library. What a type is (a whole number with a
sign or without, how many bytes, a float, a pointer) is worked out
from that file by the compiler, with `_Generic`, so that `uLong`,
`size_t` and `time_t` are known on this machine exactly as C knows
them, and a declaration that disagrees with an included header is the
compiler's error.

**Why not libffi.** It does the same at run time, but it is one more
thing to have installed, and it believes the declaration without a
header to check it against. A C compiler is there already wherever
`zeno build` is used.

**It is built once.** The result is kept in Zeno's cache, under a
number made from the declarations, the files given and when they last
changed. The first run takes about half a second; the next is
immediate.

### 44.4 The library is loaded by a helper in C

As for every other language, the library runs in a helper beside the
program ([`bridge.c`](../src/bridge.c), built once and kept), spoken
to over the same lines (26.3). A fault in C (a pointer that is
wrong, memory that is not there) stops the helper, and Zeno stops the
program with an error at the line that called it, instead of
crashing with no word of where.

**What it costs.** A call goes to the helper and back: under a
tenth of a millisecond, which is nothing for a checksum of a frame and too much
for a call in a loop of a million. The calls with no cost are the
ones `zeno build` makes (44.8).

### 44.5 Values go across as C would take them

- A number is checked to fit the type the function takes, and is an
  `OverflowError` if it does not, as `u8(300)` is. A `uint64_t`
  above the top of `int` comes back as `u64` (42).
- A `str` given for a `char *` (or any pointer to bytes) is copied
  with the `\0` C expects. A `char *` given back is copied into a
  `str`, or a list of bytes if it is not UTF-8.
- A list given for a pointer is lent: copied into memory of the type
  it points to, and copied back into the list afterwards, unless the
  pointer is to `const`. That is how a buffer is filled.
- Any other pointer given back is kept as it is: given back to C,
  compared with `==`, printed. Zeno never looks inside it and never
  frees it: a library that hands out memory has a function to free
  it, which the program calls, as it would in C. `NULL` is `none`.

**Why lend a copy, and not the list's own memory.** A list of Zeno
is not laid out as an array of C is (its items are values, which may
be of any size), and a list may change length while C holds it. A
copy for the length of a call is the one that cannot go wrong.

### 44.6 Go and Rust come in through C

A library of Go built with `-buildmode=c-shared` or `c-archive`, or
of Rust built as a `cdylib` or `staticlib` with `extern "C"`
functions, is a library of C, and `c.library` takes it. There is no
`import go` or `import rust`: neither has a way to load a library and
ask it for its functions at run time, as Python or Java do, and both
of them build the C interface well. Building it is done by their own
tools (`go build`, `cargo`), which a person who writes Go or Rust
already uses.

### 44.7 What is refused, and why

- **A function that takes `...`**, such as `printf`: the types of what
  it takes are not in its declaration. The message says to declare it
  with the types the program gives, or to write a function of C that
  calls it.
- **A function given as an argument** (a callback): a function of
  Zeno lives in Zeno, and C would call it from inside the helper.
  It can come later (44.9).
- **A struct given or given back whole**, not through a pointer: its
  fields would need a type of Zeno for each struct. A pointer to one
  is fine, and is kept as any other pointer is.

### 44.8 Nothing changes for a program that does not ask

`import c` itself starts nothing; the first `c.library` builds and
starts the helper. Every function that does it is out of the way of
the rest of Zeno (`#[cold]`, never inlined), so that the speed of a
program without it does not move.

**The one thing that does change**, as in 26.11: `c` is now the name
of a module that comes with Zeno. A file of the program called
`c.zeno` can no longer be imported as `import c`, and a package cannot
be called `c`. One test had three files called `a`, `b` and `c`
importing each other; it now calls the third one `d`, and that, with
the message that lists the modules, is the only line of the tests
from before that changed.

`--target` refuses `import c` with a message, as it refuses `import
python`. `zeno build` takes it (44.10).

### 44.9 Left for later

- A function of Zeno given to C as a callback.
- Structs by value, with a class of Zeno for each.
- The address of a variable (`&huart2`), which for now a function of C
  gives.
- Reading the declarations from a header, for a library with many
  functions.
- `zeno build --llvm`, which writes LLVM and not C.

### 44.10 `zeno build` calls C as C does

Partha asked for it next, for a vendor's HAL on a board, and it is the
place where `import c` costs nothing: the C that `zeno build` writes
calls the declared function by its name, with no helper and nothing in
between, and the C compiler links the library in. Every build does it:
`--firmware`, `--no-collector`, `--owned` and `--minimal`.

**What made it possible: the checker knows the declarations.** When
the library and the declarations are written out as texts in
`c.library(...)` (nearly always), the checker reads them, as `zeno run`
does, and gives each function a type: `int` for a whole number of C,
`u64` for `uint64_t`, `float`, `bool`, `str or none` for a `char *`
given back, and a new type, a C pointer to `thing`, `or none`, for any
other pointer given back. So a wrong argument is found before the
program runs, in `zeno run` too, and the C build knows what to write.
A declaration worked out while the program runs still works with
`zeno run`, unchecked, and `zeno build` asks for it written out.

**Why a name only a header gives is a whole number.** Zeno does not
read headers (44.1), so it cannot know what `uLong` or
`HAL_StatusTypeDef` is. Nearly every such name passed by value is a
whole number or an enum; a few are floats, and those few have names
headers share (`float32_t`). The C compiler sees the real type and
says so if the two disagree, and a pointer to such a name is kept as a
pointer, whatever it points to. **Turned down: asking the C compiler
first**, as `zeno run`'s stubs do. The checker would then need a
compiler, and for a board, the board's compiler and its headers, just
to say whether a program is right.

**The same answers as `zeno run`.** A number is checked to fit the
type the function takes, with the same message; a list is lent, copied
in and back; text given back is copied. A test holds every build to
what `zeno run` prints (`emit_c::tests`). Two differences, both of C:
a `list[u8]` given for bytes is handed over where it is, with no copy,
which a program cannot tell apart from the copy and back; and text
that is not UTF-8 is printed as the bytes it is, where `zeno run`
shows `\u{fffd}`. `tools/minimal.py`, which holds `--minimal` to what
the checked build does, builds the libraries in as `zeno build` does.

**A file of C may not be the build's own C.** `zeno build modbus.zeno`
writes `modbus.c`, and the example's checksum was in `modbus.c` too:
the first build would have written over it. The build now refuses,
and says which file, and the example's file is `crc.c`.

### 44.11 A declaration with no `(` is a value

A HAL is used through its constants as much as its functions:
`GPIOA`, `GPIO_PIN_5`, `GPIO_PIN_SET`, `HAL_OK`. They are macros or
constants of an `enum`, which no library holds as a symbol, so they
cannot be looked up as a function is. `"uint16_t GPIO_PIN_5;"` says
there is a value of that name and type, and `hal.GPIO_PIN_5` reads it
by its name, as C would: in `zeno run`, in the stubs, which are
compiled with the header; in `zeno build`, where it is written.

**Not declared again.** C cannot declare a macro (`uint16_t
GPIO_PIN_5;` would become `uint16_t ((uint16_t)0x0020);`), so a value
is only read, and the header declares it. A variable of the library's
own file of C, with no header, is written `extern`, as C writes it,
and is declared as it is written.

### 44.12 No `import cpp`

C++ was the one big language left. It is skipped, for now and on
purpose:

- **Firmware libraries are C.** The HAL of every chip vendor, CMSIS,
  FreeRTOS, lwIP, FatFs: all C. What firmware needs is in 44.10.
- **The C++ interface is not one thing.** Names are mangled
  differently by each compiler, classes and templates have no form a
  program outside C++ can call, and a library built by one compiler
  cannot always be called by another. Every language that uses C++
  libraries (Python, Rust, Go) mostly does it through a layer of C.
- **That layer already works here.** A library of C++ with `extern
  "C"` functions is a library of C, and `c.library` takes it, as it
  takes Go and Rust (44.6).

### 44.13 A missing function is said the same way on every system

A declared function the library does not have is found on Linux when
the stubs are loaded, and the helper says "the library `m` has no
`name`, which was declared". The linkers of Windows and macOS find
it earlier, when the stubs are built, and what they say names a
temporary file that is different each time. Their lines ("undefined
reference to", "undefined symbol:", `"_name", referenced from:`) are
read, and when the name is one the program declared, the error is the
one Linux gives. Any other complaint of a linker is still shown as it
was said.

## 45. Inputs: a pin the program reads

```zeno
from board import input_pin, pull_up, led

let button = input_pin(2, pull_up)    # pressed joins pin 2 to ground
if button.is_low() {
    led.on()
}
print(button, button.is_high())       # InputPin(2) true
```

Until now a pin could only be driven: `is_on()` read back what the
program had written, and 3.15b kept inputs off the list for 0.1
because they want a real board. A board that cannot read a button is
not much of a board, and it is the first half of item 7 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md). Walkthrough: [`inputs.md`](inputs.md).

### 45.1 An input is a type of its own

**`input_pin(2)` gives an `InputPin`, and `pin(2)` still gives a
`Pin`.** An `InputPin` has `is_high()`, `is_low()` and `number`. It
has no `on`, `off` or `toggle`, and a `Pin` has no `is_high`; each is
an error before the program runs that names what to write instead.
Underneath, an input pin is its number, as a pin is (3.15), and costs
what an `int` costs.

**Why two types?** An output is driven and an input is read, and on
the hardware a pin is one or the other at a time. Rust's
`embedded-hal` splits them the same way, into `OutputPin` and
`InputPin`. Driving a button's pin is a short circuit waiting to
happen, and the checker can see it. **Turned down: a mode set while
the program runs**, as Arduino's `pinMode(2, INPUT)`. The mode then
lives in the board and not in the program, and `on()` of an input is
found on the bench.

### 45.2 It is read with `is_high` and `is_low`

**An input says `is_high()` and `is_low()`, and not `is_on()`.** A
button usually joins its pin to ground, with a pull-up holding the pin
high the rest of the time, so a pressed button reads low. "On" would
then mean the opposite of "pressed", or of "high", depending on who
reads it. High and low are what the data sheet and the scope say, and
they mean one thing. Both are given so that a test reads as it is
meant: `if button.is_low()`, and not `if not button.is_high()`.

**`is_on()` of a `Pin` stays as it is.** For an output, "on" is what
the program drove it to, and nothing that works today changes.

### 45.3 The pull is said where the pin is made

**`input_pin(2, pull_up)`, `input_pin(2, pull_down)`, or
`input_pin(2)` with nothing pulling it.** `pull_up` and `pull_down`
are values of the `board` module, of the type `Pull`, as `led` is a
value of the type `Pin`. They are imported like anything else
(`from board import pull_up`, or `board.pull_up`), a function can take
a `Pull` and pass it on, and one prints as its name.

**Why there?** The pull is set in the same register write that makes
the pin an input, and the schematic decides it once: a button with no
resistor of its own needs the pull-up, for as long as the board is on.
**Turned down:**

- **A word of the call** that is not a value, as `register(u8, ...)`
  takes a type. A program's own variable called `pull_up` would then
  mean one thing in the call and another outside it.
- **A str**, `input_pin(2, "up")`. A typing slip would be found when
  the program runs, if at all.
- **A `bool`**, `input_pin(2, pull_up=true)`. Two of them would let a
  program ask for both pulls at once.
- **An enum with the cases `up` and `down`.** An enum's cases are
  names of their own in Zeno (`Ack`, not `Reply.Ack`), so it would
  take two common words from every program that imports it.

A `Pull` is the str of its name underneath, so printing one, comparing
two and keeping them in a list work as they do for any str. The
checker keeps a `Pull` and a `str` apart.

### 45.4 A fifth function in the board layer

**A compiled program that makes an input pin calls
`zeno_board_input(pin, pull)`**, with 0 for nothing, 1 for a pull-up
and 2 for a pull-down, and reads the pin with `zeno_board_read`, as
`is_on` already does. With ST's HAL it is one `HAL_GPIO_Init`.

**Only such a program calls it.** The part of the runtime that does is
marked `#ifdef ZENO_INPUT_PINS`, and the build keeps it only when the
program makes an input pin. So a board header written for the four
functions (5.12) still builds every program that reads no pin, and
the C of such a program is what it was before, line for line. A
program that does read one, built over such a header, gets the C
compiler's message naming `zeno_board_input`, which is the function to
write. **Turned down: asking every header for the fifth function**,
which would break every header there is for a feature most of their
programs do not use.

### 45.5 On a computer nothing presses the button

**On the simulated board a pull-up reads high, a pull-down low, and a
pin nothing pulls keeps the level it had** (they all start low, as
before). That is what a pin with nothing wired to it does, near
enough. **Making an input prints nothing.** The lines the simulated
board prints are what the program drives, as a logic analyser on an
output shows it; a pull is weak, and is not driven.

So under `zeno run` a button is never pressed. A board of one's own
(5.12b) can press it: the test
`a_button_is_pressed_on_a_board_of_its_own` builds
`examples/doorbell.zeno` over a header whose button is down for three
reads, and the bell rings once. That is how firmware is tested on a
desk. **Turned down for now: pressing a button under `zeno run`**,
from a file of times and levels. It is worth having, and wants its own
design: what the file looks like, and whether the clock moves by
itself while a program waits for a press.

### 45.6 Nothing changes for a program that reads no pin

`led`, `pin`, `register`, `Pin` and every line the simulated board
prints are as they were, and so is the C of every program that makes
no input pin. `board` gains `input_pin`, `pull_up` and `pull_down`,
and Zeno gains the type names `InputPin` and `Pull`; a program's own
class of either name comes first, as one called `Pin` does (3.15).
`--target` builds still refuse the `board` module.

### 45.7 Left for later

- Pressing a button under `zeno run` (45.5).
- Waiting for an edge, and an interrupt when one comes: item 7 of
  [`missing.md`](missing.md), with the rule for a variable an
  interrupt shares.
- Debouncing in the library: a press read twice, some milliseconds
  apart.
- `button` as a value of the board, as `led` is, for boards that have
  one.
- An `InputPin` as a key of a dict, which a `Pin` cannot be either.
- Running it on a real board. The STM32 sketch in
  [`board.md`](board.md) gains its fifth function, and like the other
  four it has not been tried on hardware.

## 46. A serial port

```zeno
from board import serial

let port = serial(1, 115200 baud)
port.write("ready\n")
let byte = port.read_byte()           # u8 or none
if port.has_byte() {
    port.write_bytes([0x06])
}
```

A serial port is how a board talks: to a terminal on a desk, to a GPS
module, a modem, another board. It is the second part of item 7 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md), after inputs (45), and the one that list
put first among the rest. Walkthrough: [`serial.md`](serial.md).

### 46.1 A port is a type of its own, and a number underneath

**`serial(1, 115200 baud)` gives a `Serial`**, which has `write`,
`write_bytes`, `read_byte`, `has_byte` and `number`, and prints as
`Serial(1)`. As a pin is (3.15), a port is a kind of its own to the
checker and its number in the built program, so it costs what an
`int` costs, and a list of ports, a port in a field and a function
that takes one all work. A port the board does not have is a
`ValueError`, as a pin is: the simulated board has ports 0 to 3.

### 46.2 The speed has a unit: `baud`

**`serial(1, 9600)` is refused**: the message says to write
`9600 baud`. Two bare numbers side by side do not say which is the
port and which the speed, which is the reason `sleep(500)` is refused
(3.15a). `baud` joins the list of units (1.15) as the one unit of a
kind of its own, so a speed in `Hz` is refused too. A speed of 0 or
below is a `ValueError`.

**Why not `Bd`, or `kBd`?** Data sheets write "115200 baud", and the
speeds a port is set to are written out in full, so one unit with no
prefixes is enough. **Left for later: `1 / 9600 baud`**, the time of
one bit, which would join the list of units made of units (43.1).

### 46.3 Text and bytes are sent by two methods

**`port.write(text)` sends the bytes of the text's UTF-8, and nothing
else: no line end is added. `port.write_bytes(bytes)` sends a
`list[u8]` as it is.** A port only looks at the list, so in a build
where a list has one owner it is lent for the call.

**Why two?** It is how `files.write` and `files.write_bytes` already
are (36.1), so neither is a guess, and the checker can say which one
was meant. **Turned down: one `write` that takes either**, which would
need a rule for a list written in place (`[1, 2]` is a `list[int]`
until something says otherwise). **Turned down: adding a line end**,
as `print` does. A protocol decides its own line ends (`\r\n` for a
modem), and a port that added one would be wrong for half of them.

### 46.4 `read_byte` waits; `has_byte` does not

**`port.read_byte()` gives the next byte, waiting for it, as a
`u8 or none`. It is `none` only when no byte can come any more.
`port.has_byte()` says whether a byte has come that has not been read,
without waiting.** A console, a modem or a protocol reads in order and
can wait, and is shortest written with `read_byte`; a loop that also
blinks a light asks `has_byte` first. These are Arduino's
`Serial.read()` and `Serial.available()`, and MicroPython's
`uart.read(1)` and `uart.any()`.

**Why `none` and not a byte that never comes?** On a board no more
bytes is never, so a firmware program can treat `none` as the end. On
a computer it is the end of what was typed (Ctrl-D, or the end of a
file piped in), and a program that reads lines stops there, as one
that reads `input()` does (23). **Turned down: `read_byte` giving
`none` for "nothing yet"**, which would make every reader a loop with
a wait in it, and a reader on a computer spin for ever once the input
ended.

**Left for later: `read_line`, a timeout, and reading many bytes at
once.** A line is a few lines of Zeno over `read_byte`
(`examples/console.zeno`), and the library written in Zeno (33) is
where it can go once a board has been tried.

### 46.5 Four more functions in the board layer, for a program with a port

```c
#define ZENO_SERIALS 4                                       /* how many ports */
void zeno_board_serial_open(int port, double baud);          /* set its speed */
void zeno_board_serial_write(int port, const uint8_t *bytes, size_t count);
bool zeno_board_serial_ready(int port);                      /* no waiting */
int  zeno_board_serial_read(int port);                       /* waits; -1: no more */
```

**Only a program that makes a port calls them**, by the rule of 45.4:
the part of the runtime that does is marked `#ifdef ZENO_SERIAL_PORTS`
and kept only for such a program. A board header written with four
functions, or five, still builds every program with no port, and the C
of every such program is what it was. Writing takes a buffer and a
count and not a byte at a time, because a board's driver (ST's
`HAL_UART_Transmit`, a DMA) sends a buffer.

### 46.6 On a computer every port is the terminal

**What a port sends is written out as it is, with no line of its own,
and what it reads is what is typed, a byte at a time.** That is a
serial monitor: the window where a firmware engineer reads what a
board says and types back. The end of what was typed is the end of the
port: `read_byte` gives `none` and `has_byte` is `false`. A terminal
hands over a line at a time, so on a computer `has_byte` waits for the
next line, where on a board it never waits.

**Turned down: a line for each write, as the pins have** (`pin 7 on`).
A pin's level is an event a logic analyser shows; the bytes of a port
are text, and a line around every `write("hel")` would cut a sentence
in pieces. Every port of the simulated board is the one terminal, so a
program with two ports sees both there; a board of one's own (5.12b)
keeps them apart, and is how the tests wire a port back to itself.

### 46.7 Left for later

- `read_line`, a timeout, and reading many bytes at once (46.4).
- `1 / 9600 baud` as the time of one bit (46.2).
- Parity, stop bits, flow control. The board header sets them; 8N1 is
  what nearly every port is.
- A byte arriving by interrupt, with the rule of item 7 for what an
  interrupt may share.
- Running it on a real board, with ST's HAL underneath, as in
  [`serial.md`](serial.md). Like the rest of the board layer it is a
  sketch until then.

## 47. Reading a voltage: an analog pin

```zeno
from board import analog_pin

let sensor = analog_pin(0)
let level = sensor.voltage()          # 1.65 V
if level < 1200 mV {
    print("low")
}
print(sensor.count(), "of", sensor.max_count)    # 2048 of 4095
```

A thermistor, a potentiometer, a battery through a divider, a current
through a shunt: most of what a board measures arrives as a voltage on
a pin, read by its analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). It is the third
part of item 7 of [`missing.md`](missing.md), after inputs (45) and the
serial port (46). Walkthrough: [`analog.md`](analog.md).

### 47.1 An analog pin is a type of its own

**`analog_pin(0)` gives an `AnalogPin`**, which has `voltage()`,
`count()`, `max_count` and `number`, and prints as `AnalogPin(0)`. It
is the pin's number underneath, as every pin is (3.15). It has no
`on` and no `is_high`: those belong to a `Pin` and an `InputPin`, and
the message says which to make. Three types for three things a pin can
be is the rule of 45.1 carried on: the checker knows which a pin is.

### 47.2 `voltage()` is in volts, and `count()` is the converter's own number

**`sensor.voltage()` gives a quantity in `V`.** Units are what Zeno
has that C does not (1.15), and this is where a firmware program meets
its first real one. `level < 1200 mV`, `level * 20 mA` (a power, 43)
and `level.mV` all work, and `level < 1200` is refused.

**`sensor.count()` gives the number the converter counted, an `int`,
and `sensor.max_count` the count that stands for the whole reference**
(4095 for 12 bits). A program that wants a share, as for a
potentiometer, writes `sensor.count() / sensor.max_count`, and one
that does its own sums on counts, as C code does, can.

**Why both?** A voltage is what the reading means, and a count is what
was measured; a lookup table for a thermistor is indexed by count, and
a battery is compared in volts. **Turned down:**

- **A bare count only**, as Arduino's `analogRead`. `512` means
  nothing until one knows the bits and the reference, and those are
  the board's, not the program's.
- **A float from 0 to 1 only**, as Mbed's `AnalogIn.read()`. It has
  no unit to check, and the program multiplies by the reference by
  hand, which is the slip units are for.
- **`read()`**, which does not say what comes back.

The voltage is the count's share of the largest count, times the
reference, worked out in that order by every engine and build, so the
whole scale is the reference exactly and they print the same digits.

### 47.3 The board says its bits and its reference, and has two functions

```c
#define ZENO_ANALOG_BITS 12           /* the converter counts 0 to 4095 */
#define ZENO_ANALOG_REFERENCE 3.3     /* the volts its largest count stands for */
bool zeno_board_analog(int pin);      /* make the pin one the converter reads; false if it cannot be */
int  zeno_board_analog_read(int pin); /* what it counts on the pin now */
```

**Only a program that makes an analog pin calls them**, by the rule of
45.4 (`#ifdef ZENO_ANALOG_PINS`), so a header without them still
builds every other program. **A pin the converter cannot read is a
`ValueError`** ("pin 7 of this board cannot read a voltage"): on most
chips only some pins reach the converter, and the board is what knows
which.

### 47.4 On a computer nothing is wired

**On the simulated board a pin that is high reads the whole reference
(3.3 V, a count of 4095) and one that is low reads 0 V.** Every pin
can be read, the converter has 12 bits, and making an analog pin
prints nothing, as making an input prints nothing (45.5). It is what a
voltmeter on the pin would show: a pin the program drove high, or one
a pull-up holds, is at the supply. A board of one's own (5.12b) feeds
real readings: the test `a_voltage_is_read_on_a_board_of_its_own` has
a 10-bit converter against 5 V that reads a ramp.

### 47.5 Left for later

- Feeding a voltage to a pin under `zeno run`, with pressing a button
  (45.5): one design for both.
- Averaging, a sample time, and choosing the reference. The board
  header sets them.
- Reading several pins in one sweep, and a reading by interrupt.
- A voltage written out: a DAC, and PWM, which is next.
- A temperature from a thermistor, in the library written in Zeno.

## 48. A PWM signal: a pin switched on for a share of the time

```zeno
from board import pwm_pin

let lamp = pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz)
lamp.duty(0.25)               # on for a quarter of each millisecond

let servo = pwm_pin(10, 50 Hz)
servo.pulse(1500 us)          # on for 1.5 ms of each 20 ms
```

A pin is only ever high or low. Switched fast by a timer of the chip,
it dims a lamp, sets the speed of a motor and tells a servo its angle,
with no work from the program between two changes. It is the fourth
part of item 7 of [`missing.md`](missing.md), after inputs (45), the
serial port (46) and reading a voltage (47). Walkthrough:
[`pwm.md`](pwm.md).

### 48.1 A PWM pin is a type of its own, made with its frequency

**`pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz)` gives a `PwmPin`**, which has `duty(share)`,
`pulse(time)` and `number`, and prints as `PwmPin(9)`. It is the pin's
number underneath (3.15). It has no `on` and no `off`: a `Pin` has
those, and the message says that all the time on is `duty(1.0)`. It is
the fourth thing a pin can be, by the rule of 45.1.

**The frequency is given when the pin is made, and it has a unit.**
`pwm_pin(9, 1000)` is refused: "the frequency of a PWM pin has a unit,
as in `pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz)`". A frequency worked out from a period,
`1 / 20 ms`, is one too (43). **Why when it is made?** The frequency
belongs to the wiring: a servo wants 50 Hz and a lamp wants more than
the eye sees, and neither changes while the program runs. A timer is
set up once with it. **Turned down:** a frequency with a default, as
Arduino's `analogWrite` has (490 Hz on some pins and 980 Hz on others,
which nobody remembers), and a frequency set by a method after the
pin is made, which leaves a pin with no frequency in between.

**A new pin is off all the time**, as a new `Pin` is low. A frequency
of 0 Hz or less is a `ValueError`.

**One pin has one signal.** Making a second `PwmPin` for a pin that
has one starts the signal again, off, at the new frequency, and both
values then drive it, as two `pin(9)` drive one pin.

### 48.2 `duty` takes the share of the time on, from 0.0 to 1.0

**`lamp.duty(0.25)` is on for a quarter of the time.** A float, since
a share is a number with no unit, and 0.0 to 1.0 since that is what a
share is. Outside that range is a `ValueError` that says the range and
gives an example. **Turned down:**

- **A count from 0 to 255**, as `analogWrite(pin, 64)`. The 255 is one
  timer's width and means nothing on another, and `64` does not say
  "a quarter" to anyone reading.
- **A percentage, 0 to 100.** Zeno has no `%` unit, and `duty(25)`
  beside `duty(0.25)` would be the ambiguity the language is built to
  keep out. A program that thinks in percent writes `duty(25 / 100)`.
- **Clamping** a share above 1.0 to 1.0. A wrong sum would then run a
  motor at full power in silence.

The name is the word on the data sheet: the duty cycle.

### 48.3 `pulse` takes the time on in each period

**`servo.pulse(1500 us)` is on for that long in each period.** A servo
and an electronic speed controller are told a time, not a share: 1 ms
to 2 ms, whatever the period. Without `pulse` the program would write
`duty(1500 us * 50 Hz)`, and must then know the frequency in two
places. The time has a unit, and a bare number is refused. A time
below zero or longer than one period is a `ValueError` that says how
long the period is.

`pulse(t)` is `duty(t * frequency)` and nothing more. The two are two
ways to say one thing, and each is the plain way for one kind of
device.

### 48.4 One function in the board layer

```c
bool zeno_board_pwm(int pin, double hertz, double duty);
```

**It starts or changes the signal on a pin, and answers false if the
pin cannot make one.** On most chips only the pins a timer reaches
can, and the board is what knows which, so making such a pin is a
`ValueError`: "pin 7 of this board cannot make a PWM signal". Making a
pin calls it with a duty of 0, and `duty` and `pulse` call it with the
same frequency and the new share. The runtime keeps each pin's
frequency and checks every range, so the board sees a pin it has, a
frequency above 0 and a duty from 0 to 1.

**One function, not three** (open, set, close): every call carries the
whole signal, so a board has nothing to remember, and one that must
set up its timer can do it when the frequency changes. **Only a
program that makes a PWM pin calls it** (`#ifdef ZENO_PWM_PINS`), by
the rule of 45.4.
