### 48.5 On a computer each change is printed

**The simulated board prints a line when a signal changes**: `pin 9
pwm 0.25 at 1000 Hz`, and `led pwm 0.5 at 2500 Hz` for the LED's pin.
It is the line `pin 9 on` (5.12a) for a pin that is partly on. Setting
the duty a pin already has prints nothing, as turning on a pin that is
on prints nothing, and so making a pin that has no signal yet prints
nothing. A pin that was
on is turned off first, with its own line, since a timer takes the pin
over. Every pin can make a signal there. Reading such a pin, with
`is_on()`, says off: the simulated board has no time in which the pin
would be high.

### 48.6 Left for later

- Reading back the duty and the frequency of a pin.
- Changing the frequency of a pin that is made (a buzzer playing a
  tune), which today is a second `pwm_pin`.
- The timer's resolution: a board with an 8-bit timer rounds `0.001`
  to nothing, and the program is not told.
- Two pins of one timer that must share a frequency, complementary
  outputs and dead time for a motor bridge.
- A voltage from a real DAC, and a tone.
- A trial on a real board. The board function is written for the
  simulated board and for test boards only.

## 49. A ticker: a steady beat the program keeps time by

```zeno
from board import ticker

let beat = ticker(10 ms)
while true {
    let came = beat.wait()        # until the next tick: 1 when on time
    step()
}
```

A loop that ends with `sleep(10 ms)` takes 10 ms and the time its work
took, so it runs slow, by a different amount each round. A control
loop, a sampler and a clock need rounds that are the same length
whatever the work takes, and need to know when a round ran over. It is
the fifth part of item 7 of [`missing.md`](missing.md), the "timer"
there. Walkthrough: [`ticker.md`](ticker.md).

### 49.1 A ticker is made with its period, and is a type of its own

**`ticker(10 ms)` gives a `Ticker`**, which has `wait()`, `ticks()`,
`restart()` and `period`, and prints as `Ticker(10 ms)`. Its ticks are
one period apart, counted from when it is made: the first is one
period later. The period has a unit, and a bare number is refused:
"the period of a ticker has a unit, as in `ticker(10 ms)`". A period
of no time or less is a `ValueError`.

**Why not `timer`?** `Timer` is already what `web.every` gives, a call
that waits and can be stopped ([`web.md`](web.md)). And on a
microcontroller "a timer" is five things: it makes PWM (48), counts
pulses, measures them, wakes the chip and keeps a beat. The name says
which one this is. Go and Mbed call theirs a ticker too.

**Why in `board` and not in `time`?** `time` is in all fifteen target
languages, and a ticker there would have to be written fifteen times
before it was any use. It is built for the loop of a firmware program,
where the other parts of `board` are, and a program on a computer
imports it from there the same way.

### 49.2 `wait()` and `ticks()` both say how many ticks have come

**`beat.wait()` waits for the next tick. `beat.ticks()` never waits.
Each gives the number of ticks that have come since the program last
took them, and takes them.** `wait()` gives 1 when the loop kept up
and more when it was late; `ticks()` gives 0 when no tick has come.

```zeno
if blink.ticks() > 0 { led.toggle() }      # a loop with several beats
seconds += second.ticks()                  # a clock that loses nothing
if beat.wait() > 1 { late += 1 }           # a loop that knows it ran over
```

**Why a count and not a `bool`?** A count is the whole truth: a clock
adds it and stays right, and a control loop multiplies it by the
period and has the time that went by. A `bool` would lose the ticks
that came while the program was busy. **Turned down:**

- **Running the late ticks one after another**, as `last += interval`
  does on an Arduino. A program that fell behind would then run its
  loop in a burst, with no waiting, to catch up, which is the last
  thing a motor wants. The program is told how late it is and decides.
- **Dropping late ticks in silence**, as Go's `Ticker` does. That a
  round ran over is what a firmware engineer most needs to know, and
  is what C code most often does not check.
- **`ticks()` that only looks**, with a second call to take them. Two
  calls leave a moment between them in which a tick can come.

Zephyr's `k_timer_status_get` and `k_timer_status_sync` are the same
pair. The ticks stay where they were due: taking them late does not
move the next one, so a loop does not drift.

**`beat.period` is the time from one tick to the next, in `ms`**, the
unit `now()` counts in, so `came * beat.period` is the time that went
by.

### 49.3 `restart()` starts the period again

**`idle.restart()` makes the next tick one period from now and forgets
the ticks that had come.** It is how a ticker measures quiet: a
program restarts it at each byte or each press, and `idle.ticks() > 0`
then says that nothing came for a whole period. That is a timeout and
a debounce, which 45.7 and 46.7 left open.

### 49.4 It asks the board for nothing new

**A ticker is kept on the board's clock and its sleep**
(`zeno_board_now` and `zeno_board_sleep`, 5.12), so a board header
with the first four functions runs it. **Why not a hardware timer
each?** A chip has a handful, and PWM takes some. Comparing with one
clock gives a program as many beats as it wants, at the clock's
resolution. A sleep may end a little early, so `wait()` reads the
clock again until the tick has come.

Only a program with a ticker keeps this part of the runtime
(`#ifdef ZENO_TICKING`, by the rule of 45.4), so the C of every other
program is what it was.

### 49.5 A board keeps a fixed number of tickers

**Sixteen, unless the board header says another number with
`ZENO_TICKERS`.** Each is two doubles in a table. Making one more is a
`ValueError`: "this board keeps 16 tickers, and this would be one
more. Make each ticker once, outside any loop". **Why a fixed table?**
A firmware build with no collector has no `malloc`
([`pool.md`](pool.md)), and a number
underneath is what every other value of the board is (3.15). A ticker
is not given back, so one made in a loop uses the table up, and the
message says so. `zeno run` keeps the same sixteen.

### 49.6 On a computer

The clock is the computer's, and a ticker prints nothing: there is no
line to show, as there is none for `sleep`. A program in a page cannot
`wait`, as it cannot `sleep`, and is told to ask with `ticks()`.

### 49.7 Left for later

- A function the board runs at each tick: an interrupt, which is next.
- Giving a ticker back, and one tick only (`after`).
- A ticker in the fifteen target languages.
- A period finer than the board's clock and sleep can keep.
- A trial on a real board.

## 50. Interrupts: the board counts, and the program asks

```zeno
from board import falling, input_pin, pull_up

let button = input_pin(2, pull_up)
let press = button.interrupt(falling)

while true {
    press.wait()              # the chip sleeps until the button goes down
    ring()
}
```

A pulse from a wheel sensor lasts a millisecond, and a program that
looks at the pin now and then misses most of them. A chip's answer is
the interrupt: the hardware notices the edge itself, whatever the
program is doing. It is the last part of item 7 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md), which asked for "a safe way to share a
variable" with an interrupt, "and the rule should be one sentence".
Walkthrough: [`interrupts.md`](interrupts.md).

### 50.1 An interrupt is made from an input pin and an edge

**`button.interrupt(falling)` gives an `Interrupt`**, which has
`wait()`, `edges()` and `number`, and prints as `Interrupt(2)`. From
then on the board counts those edges of the pin. **`rising`, `falling`
and `either` are values of the `board` module, of the type `Edge`**,
as `pull_up` is a `Pull` (45.3), so a function can take one and a str
in their place is refused.

**Why from an `InputPin`, and not `interrupt_pin(2, falling)`?** The
pin is still read: a program that counts presses also asks whether the
button is down now. And what holds the pin is said once, where the
input is made. An `Interrupt` is the pin's number underneath (3.15),
and it is a type of its own so that `wait()` exists only on a pin
whose edges are being counted, which the checker then knows (45.1).

**One pin has one interrupt.** A second `interrupt( )` on a pin starts
the count again with the new edge, as a second `pwm_pin` starts the
signal again (48.1). A chip has one such setting a pin.

### 50.2 `wait()` and `edges()` both say how many edges have come

**`press.wait()` waits for an edge. `press.edges()` never waits. Each
gives the number of edges counted since the program last took them,
and takes them**, as `wait()` and `ticks()` do for a ticker (49.2), for
the same reasons: a count loses nothing, and a `bool` would.

```zeno
print(turns.edges(), "turns this second")     # a rate, with a ticker
if press.edges() > 0 { ring() }               # a loop that does other things
press.wait()                                  # nothing else to do: sleep
```

### 50.3 The program's own code never runs inside an interrupt

That is the rule, in one sentence. **The board counts what happened,
and the program asks for the count when it chooses to.** There is no
function of the program that the hardware starts by itself, so there
is no variable shared with one, and nothing to get wrong.

**Why not a function that runs when the edge comes**, as C, Arduino
and Rust have?

- **The shared variable.** In C the handler and the loop both write
  `count`, the programmer marks it `volatile`, and `count += 1` in the
  loop still loses an edge that lands between its read and its write.
  No compiler sees it, and it shows up once a week. Rust refuses it,
  with critical sections and its ownership rules through the whole
  language; in Zeno owning is one way to build a program, not the
  language.
- **The runtime.** A handler that joins two strs, or appends to a
  list, while the program is half-way through doing the same, breaks
  the pool both draw from. Refusing that needs the checker to know of
  every function whether it could allocate or raise, which is the
  ground of item 9.
- **What a handler is for.** Nearly every handler in firmware does one
  of two things: counts, or sets a flag for the loop to see. Counting
  is both. The board's own handler is two lines of C that cannot be
  wrong, and it is written once, in the board header.

**What this gives up:** an answer inside the interrupt itself, within
microseconds of the edge: bit-banging a protocol, or reading the
second line of an encoder at the edge of the first. Those stay in C,
which a firmware build calls directly (44.10).

**Also turned down: functions run between two statements of the
program**, an event loop, as a page has (`web.every`). It is safe, but
the compiler must then place the points where they may run, in four
engines, and it is one answer to item 14 (tasks), which should be
designed whole. It can be layered on counting later without changing
it.

### 50.4 Three functions in the board layer

```c
bool zeno_board_interrupt(int pin, int edge);   /* count from now on: 1 rising, 2 falling, 3 either */
int  zeno_board_edges(int pin);                 /* how many since last asked; start again from none */
int  zeno_board_edges_wait(int pin);            /* the same, after waiting for at least one */
```

**Why is the wait the board's, and not a loop over
`zeno_board_edges` and a sleep?** Looking at the count and going to
sleep must be one step, or an edge that lands between the two is slept
through. On a Cortex-M that is: interrupts off, look, `WFI`,
interrupts on. The board knows how its chip does it. **A pin with no
interrupt is a `ValueError`** ("pin 7 of this board cannot count its
edges"), and only a program with an interrupt calls the three
(`#ifdef ZENO_INTERRUPTS`, 45.4).

### 50.5 On a computer the program drives its own edges

**Nothing is wired to the simulated board, so the edges counted are
the ones the program drives on that pin itself**, with `pin(2).on()`,
as if a wire joined the two. It is the rule of 47.4, where a pin the
program drove high reads as 3.3 V. Making an input with a pull is not
an edge.

**A `wait()` with no edge counted is a `ValueError` there**: "the
board says no edge can ever come on pin 2, so the program would wait
for ever". Nothing can drive a pin while the program waits, and a
message is kinder than a program that hangs. The board function says
it by answering 0, which a real board never does.

### 50.6 Left for later

- A function of the program run for each edge, with item 14.
- Waiting for the first of several: an interrupt or a ticker. Today a
  loop asks each and sleeps a little in between.
- When an edge came: the width of a pulse, which a chip's timer can
  capture.
- Debouncing a button in the board. Today the program does it, with a
  ticker (49.3).
- Interrupts of a serial port or a converter. A board header may use
  them inside its own functions already.
- Pressing a button under `zeno run` (45.5).
- A trial on a real board.

### 50.7 The interpreter keeps the board behind a pointer, and what the clock said about `loop`

Before 0.7.0 went out, `zeno run` was timed against 0.6.0, as every
release is. `bench/loop.zeno` took 3 to 5% longer, and ran the same
instructions to the seventh digit (84,061,204,209 where 0.6.0 ran
84,061,205,164). Building each commit since 0.6.0 put it at this
chapter's: the commit before it is level.

**What was changed.** The interpreter held the board inside itself,
between its other fields, and this chapter gave the board two more
tables, 576 bytes. The VM had the same trouble in 0.6.0 and keeps what
a program reaches outside itself in a box (34.7). The interpreter now
keeps the board in one too. That gave back about one part in a
hundred, and no more.

**What was measured, and left.** The rest is not in what the code
does. Three things say so:

- The same build, started under names of four lengths, takes 9.80 to
  10.39 seconds: where things land in memory moves the time by 3%
  either way, for 0.6.0 as for this one.
- A simulation of the cache (cachegrind) finds the same reads and the
  same writes in both, and next to no misses in either.
- With both versions built another way, so that no branch crosses a
  32-byte boundary (`-C llvm-args=-x86-branches-within-32B-boundaries`),
  every branch of the interpreter lies somewhere else, in both. The
  difference is then 1%: 10.13 and 10.25 seconds, each the mean of
  four names.

So the time is lost in where the code of the interpreter's loop
happens to lie for this processor (an Intel Xeon of the Emerald
Rapids kind), and which branch it is was not found. Another
processor, or the next change anywhere in Zeno, puts things
elsewhere. The builds that are released are made by another linker
for another C library, and their code lies differently again.

**That option is not turned on for the release.** It was made for a
fault of older Intel processors, which this one does not have, and
here it only served to move the code. It was tried for ten minutes on
one machine and one benchmark, it makes every build larger, and what
it does to the other five benchmarks and to the VM was not measured.
If `zeno run` is ever to be made steadier by the clock, how its code
is laid out is the first thing to look at, and it is written down
here for that.

| `zeno run`, seconds | 0.6.0 | 0.7.0 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| fib | 3.10 | 3.07 | −0.9 % |
| loop | 33.39 | 34.51 | +3.4 % |
| sort | 14.86 | 14.41 | −3.0 % |
| strings | 3.22 | 3.24 | +0.7 % |
| trees | 24.45 | 24.35 | −0.4 % |
| nbody | 58.31 | 58.32 | 0.0 % |

## 51. One step to a board: `zeno build --board`

```sh
zeno build --board boards/qemu-cortex-m3 examples/blink.zeno
```

```
Wrote blink.c
Built blink.elf for the board in `boards/qemu-cortex-m3`.
Run it with: qemu-system-arm -M lm3s6965evb -nographic -semihosting -kernel blink.elf
```

Item 8 of [`missing.md`](missing.md) is "one step from a `.zeno` file
to a board", and has three parts: the cross-compiler in the same
command, a runtime with no `printf` and no `exit`, and checks without
GCC's built-ins. This chapter is the first part. It was built first
because it is what lets the other two be tried: before it, nothing
Zeno wrote had ever run on a processor other than the computer's.
Walkthrough: [`board-build.md`](board-build.md).

### 51.1 `--board` names a folder, and the folder says how

**A board is a folder with a file called `zeno.board` in it, and
`zeno build --board <folder>` builds the program for it.** The file
names the board's C compiler, its flags, the files of C that are built
with every program, the linker script, and the command that runs or
loads the result:

```
compiler "arm-none-eabi-gcc"
flags "-mcpu=cortex-m3" "-mthumb"
header "board.h"
sources "startup.c" "system.c"
script "link.ld"
link "-nostartfiles" "-Wl,--gc-sections"
run "qemu-system-arm" "-M" "lm3s6965evb" "-nographic" "-kernel"
```

**Why a folder.** Decision 5.12c turned cross-compiling down, because
"those tools exist, differ for every vendor, and are what a firmware
engineer already has set up", and a `--target thumbv7m` would be "a
second, worse copy of each of them". That reason still holds, and the
folder respects it: Zeno knows no processor, no flag and no vendor.
It reads the names of the tools the engineer already has, and types
the command they would have typed. What 5.12c did not weigh is that
the command is long, is the same for every program on a board, and
was typed again for each one.

**Why not on the line**, as [`missing.md`](missing.md) first had it
(`zeno build --cc arm-none-eabi-gcc`, with the flags in
`zeno.package`). A line with a compiler, six flags, two files and a
linker script on it is the command 5.12c already had. And the flags
are not the program's: the same program is built for two boards, and
one board runs many programs. Written in `zeno.package` they would be
copied into every program, and a program for two boards would need two
packages. The header with the board's functions (5.12b) already lives
apart from the program. The flags, the startup file and the linker
script belong beside it.

**Why the file is read as `zeno.package` is** (8.1): one lexer, so a
comment starts with `#` and text is written as in a program. **Each
word in quotes is one word of the command**, and no shell reads the
line, so a path with a space in it needs no second kind of quoting,
and the same file works on Windows.

**Why a path and not a name** (`--board nucleo`). A name needs a place
where names are looked up, and there is none yet (51.9). A path is
what the engineer's own board will always be.

### 51.2 Eight lines, and one of them must be there

`compiler` is the only line a board must have. `about`, `compiler`,
`header`, `script` and `run` are said once; `flags`, `sources` and
`link` any number of times, and the words add up in the order written.

**A file is named as it is in the board's folder** (`header`,
`sources`, `script`), wherever the command is typed, so a board can
be moved and shared whole. **A file that is named and not there is
said before anything is built**, by its name, and so is every other
mistake in the file, with its line. A cross-compiler's own message for
a missing linker script is three lines about `ld`.

**Why `flags` and `link` are two lines.** `-mcpu` must be said when
compiling and when linking; `-nostartfiles` only means something when
linking. One compiler command does both here, so one list would work
today. Two lists say what each word is for, and stay right if the two
steps are ever run apart.

**Why `header` is a line of its own and not `-DZENO_BOARD=...` under
`flags`.** It is the one flag Zeno itself defines the meaning of
(5.12b), a file that must exist, and the difference between a board
with pins of its own and one with the simulated pins. A board with no
`header` line gets the simulated board, which is what makes the
emulated board of 51.6 so small.

### 51.3 A build for a board has no collector

**`--board` builds the C that `--no-collector` builds**: every list
and object has one owner, and memory comes from a pool whose size is
fixed when the program is built (5.9). `--collector` with `--board` is
refused, with the reason.

**Why.** The collector takes its memory from the system 64 KB at a
time, and first looks for garbage when 4 MB are in use (22.5). That
is right for a computer and cannot fit a chip that has 64 KB in all. A
collector made for a chip is a piece of work of its own (51.9). Until
it exists, building one in would give a program that links and then
stops at its first list.

**Why not leave the choice to the line**, so that `--board` alone gave
an ordinary build and `--board --no-collector` this one. Because the
shorter command would then be the one that does not work. The option
that names a chip gives the build made for a chip.

**`--minimal`, `--release`, `--fast` and `--memory` go with it** and
mean what they mean elsewhere. **`--llvm`, `--web` and `--target` are
refused**: the board's compiler is handed C, and those write something
else. (clang can make code for a chip from IR; nobody has asked.)
**`--board` belongs to `build` alone**: `zeno run` and `zeno check`
with it are refused, because a board changes nothing in what they do.

### 51.4 What the compiler is asked, and in what order

```
<compiler> -O2 <flags> -I<folder> [-DZENO_BOARD="<header>"]
    -o <name>.elf <name>.c <sources> [-T <script>] <link>
    <the libraries of C the program declares> -lm
```

One command compiles and links. **Zeno's own flag comes first and the
board's after it**, so the board has the last word: with `flags
"-Os"`, GCC takes the later `-Os` over the earlier `-O2`. **The
board's folder is on the path of headers**, so the header is found by
its plain name, and it and the sources can include the vendor's
headers beside them. **The libraries of C a program declares with
`import c` are built in** as in every C build (44.10): a vendor's HAL
is C, and this is where it meets the board. Only the hint to the
loader about where a library lies (`-Wl,-rpath`) is left out, since a
chip has no loader.

**The compiler is the board's, and `CC` is not read.** `CC` says which
compiler builds for this computer, and many people have it set. A
board build that obeyed it would hand ARM flags to the computer's
compiler.

**When the compiler is not installed**, the C has been written, and
the message gives the whole command, to run once it is.

### 51.5 The program is `<name>.elf`, and `run` is shown, not run

**The file is `<name>.elf`**, whatever the processor: it is what a
cross-compiler writes, what QEMU, OpenOCD, pyOCD and gdb read, and a
`.bin` or a `.hex` is one `objcopy` away from it. It also cannot be
mistaken for the program `zeno build` makes for the computer, which
has no ending.

**`zeno build` prints the board's `run` command with the program in
it, and does not run it.** The program is the last word, or stands
where a word says `{program}`, since some tools take a sentence
(`"program {program} verify reset exit"`).

**Why not run it.** For QEMU it would be harmless. For a real board
`run` writes to the chip's flash, and `build` has never changed
anything but files in the folder it is typed in. Doing it in the same
command is an option for later, and one that should be asked for by
name (51.9).

### 51.6 The board that comes with Zeno needs no hardware

**[`boards/qemu-cortex-m3`](../boards/qemu-cortex-m3) is the board
QEMU emulates as `lm3s6965evb`**: an ARM Cortex-M3 with 256 KB of
flash and 64 KB of RAM. The folder is four files: `zeno.board`, a
linker script, `startup.c` (the table of vectors, the first values of
the variables, a millisecond clock on the SysTick timer, then `main`)
and `system.c` (the handful of functions newlib leaves to a system).

**Why an emulated board first.** Nothing in Zeno has run on hardware,
and that needs a board on a desk ([`missing.md`](missing.md)). An
emulated chip needs nothing, runs in the tests of every change, and
still differs from the computer in the ways that matter to the C: a
processor of 32 bits under whole numbers of 64, no floating point in
the processor, another C library, a start with no system before it,
and 64 KB. **Why this one**: of the Cortex-M boards QEMU has, it is
the one with the most emulated (pins, serial ports, timers, a
converter), which the next steps will use.

**It has no `header`: its pins are the simulated ones**, a line of
text for each change, as under `zeno run`. That is what lets every
example be compared with the computer byte for byte. The simulated
board sleeps and reads the clock with two POSIX functions
(`nanosleep`, `clock_gettime`); the folder says the board has them
(`-D_POSIX_TIMERS=1`) and `system.c` supplies them on the SysTick
clock. So the runtime needed no third family beside "Windows" and
"everything else" (5.12).

**What a program prints goes out of the first serial port**, which
QEMU joins to the terminal, and what it reads comes in from it. **The
message of an error nothing caught goes to the debugger** (ARM
semihosting, which QEMU answers), and so does the end of the program,
with its answer: QEMU ends with 0, or with 1 after an error. On a real
board with a probe attached the same two calls reach the debugger on
the desk. So a test can tell what was printed from what went wrong,
and knows when the program is over, with nothing added to Zeno's C.

**The clock is real.** `sleep(500 ms)` takes half a second of QEMU's
time. A clock that only moved when the program slept (as in the test
of 5.12b) would be quicker and would hide the one thing a start-up
file most often gets wrong, its interrupt.

### 51.7 Every program, on the board and on the computer

**`tools/board.py` builds each example, each sample of the book and
each corner program of `tools/targets/` twice, with `--no-collector`
for the computer and with `--board` for the Cortex-M3, and the two
must do the same**: print the same text, end the same way, and stop
with the same message. Then again with `--minimal`, for the programs
no check stops. On the day it was written: 228 of 228 in the build
that checks, and 212 of 212 in the minimal one.

Left out, and counted: a program a build with no collector refuses; a
program with words on its line or with files; and a program that
reads what is typed to its end, which a serial port does not have.
**A number with a fraction may differ after its fifteenth digit.**
`cosh(1.0)` is `1.5430806348152437` from the computer's C library and
`1.543080634815244` from newlib: the next number along. Both are
within the last place, the function is the C library's and not Zeno's,
and holding them to one answer would mean writing the mathematics
again. Zeno's own printing of a float is the same on both: in the
first run of the check, which made no such allowance, this was the
only number in any program that differed.

The workflow `board` runs it on a push that changes the C backend, the
runtime or a board. `cargo test cortex_m3` is the short form, one
program with every part of a board in it, and skips the run where the
tools are not installed.

### 51.8 Found on the way

- **A list that is the default of a field was freed while the object
  still held it**, in every build with no collector, since those
  builds exist. `class Bag { items: list[str] = [] }`, made as
  `Bag()`: the list was made beside the call and freed when the
  statement ended. Two samples of the book did this, and
  `tools/minimal.py` had counted them as passing, because the checked
  build and the minimal build both ended with the same signal and so
  "did the same". The board did not: its memory is laid out otherwise,
  and it printed something else. **A place that keeps what it is
  given (a field, a `take` parameter) now owns the default made for
  it**, as it owns a `[]` written in the call, and `tools/minimal.py`
  fails a program that the system stops, but for three that are meant
  to end that way.
- **`PRIx64` is not there on every C library.** The runtime printed a
  register's address with it, and the newlib that Ubuntu ships does
  not define it for this compiler. It is `%llx` with a cast now, which
  is C99 everywhere.
- **`main` is given its two arguments by the board's start-up**, a
  name and no words, because the program's `main` takes them when the
  program asks for its arguments.

### 51.9 Left for later

- The rest of item 8: `print` and the end of the program through
  functions of the board, so that no C library is needed, and the
  checks without GCC's built-ins.
- A header for the emulated board that drives its real registers, as
  a second board: the pattern for a real one, tried as far as QEMU
  emulates it.
- A collector made for a chip (51.3).
- `--board` by name, a `board` line in `zeno.package`, boards as
  packages in the registry, and the emulated board carried inside the
  `zeno` program, which today needs a copy of the repository.
- Loading the program in the same command, asked for by name (51.5),
  and a `.bin` or `.hex` beside the `.elf`.
- `--llvm` for a board.
- An end to what is typed over a serial port, so that a program that
  reads to the end can be tried on a board.
- A trial on a real board.

## 52. `print`, and the end of a program, through the board

A build for a board (chapter 51) still stood on a C library. `print`
was `fwrite` to a stream, the message of an error was `fprintf`,
`input` was `fgetc`, and a program that stopped called `exit`. On a
computer those four are given. On a chip somebody has to bring them:
`boards/qemu-cortex-m3` does it with newlib and a file of the
functions newlib leaves open, and `hello` took 9,772 bytes of flash
there, most of it the C library's streams. A board with a vendor's
library and no streams at all could not be built for.

This chapter is the second part of item 8 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md). **A board's header may now bring the four
itself, and then nothing in the runtime writes, reads or stops through
the C library.** `hello` takes 936 bytes.

```c
#define ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS

static void zeno_board_print(const char *bytes, size_t count) { ... }
static void zeno_board_warn(const char *bytes, size_t count)  { ... }
static int  zeno_board_typed(void)                             { ... }
static void zeno_board_stop(int status)                        { ... }
```

Nothing in the language changes, and nothing a program prints
changes, on a computer or on a board.

### 52.1 Four functions, and one line that says the board has them

A program reaches outside itself in four ways, pins aside. It prints
(`print`, the question of `input`). It says something beside what it
prints: a warning (`program.warn`, 34.3), and the message of the error
that stops it. It reads what is typed (`input`). And it ends before
its last line: `program.exit(code)` (34.1), or an error.

| the board writes | for | what it must do |
|---|---|---|
| `zeno_board_print(bytes, count)` | `print`, `input`'s question | send these bytes where printed text goes |
| `zeno_board_warn(bytes, count)` | `program.warn`, an error's message | send them where a person looks for trouble |
| `zeno_board_typed()` | `input` | the next byte typed, after waiting for it, or -1 if none can ever come |
| `zeno_board_stop(status)` | `program.exit`, an error | the program is over; 0, the number it gave, or 1 after an error |

**Why bytes and a count, and not one character at a time.** A serial
port with a queue, a USB endpoint and a debugger's channel all take a
run of bytes at once, and a call for each character is a cost a board
cannot take back. A board that can only send one writes the loop
itself, in three lines. **Why a count and not text that ends in a
zero**: the runtime knows the length already, and the board would
count it again.

**Why `warn` is a function of its own.** A computer has two streams so
that what a program prints can go to a file while what goes wrong
stays on the screen (34.3). A board has the same two readers: the
thing the program talks to, and the engineer. A board with one wire
writes `zeno_board_warn` as a call to `zeno_board_print`, and that is
then a choice somebody made.

**Why -1 from `typed`.** `input` gives `none` when nothing more can be
typed, and reading a file on a computer ends. A serial port never
ends, so a board on one never answers -1 and `input` waits. A board
with nothing to read from answers -1 at once.

**Why one line says it, `#define ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS`, and the four are
not simply looked for.** C cannot ask whether a function exists. And
the headers that were there before this chapter have pins and a clock
and no printing: without the line they build as they did, on the C
library (the rule of 45.4: what was written before a part existed
still builds). **Why all four together, and not each when the program
uses it**, as the parts of the board are (45.4). A program that never
calls `input` still must not pull in `fgetc`, and a board that prints
by itself and reports its errors through `stderr` is a board whose
errors go nowhere. The four are one decision, "this board has no
streams", and one line makes it.

### 52.2 The runtime has one way out

Every place in `runtime.c` that wrote to a stream, read from one or
called `exit` now goes through five functions at the top of the file:
`zeno_out`, `zeno_out_now` (what was printed is to be seen before a
wait), `zeno_say`, `zeno_typed` and `zeno_stop`. They are written out
once, below the board, in two halves: the board's four, or the C
library's.

**The messages no longer go through `fprintf`.** There were under
twenty of them (`error: out of memory`, the uncaught error with its
file and line, the memory pool that is full, the report of
`--memory`), and between them they used `%s`, `%d` and `%zu`.
`zeno_sayf` does those three in under forty lines.
`fprintf` does everything, and on newlib everything is 20 KB of
flash, in every program that can fail, which is every checked one.

**On a computer nothing changes.** The same bytes go to the same
stream in the same order: what was printed is still pushed out before
anything is said on the error stream, so the two keep their order on
a screen. All the tests that were there pass as they were.

**One place stopped a program with `abort`**: the memory lent to a
function of C for a list (44.10), when there was none to lend. On
newlib `abort` raises a signal, which asks for a system with
processes, and `examples/modbus.zeno` did not link for the second
board. It says `error: out of memory` and stops with 1 now, as every
other place that runs out does, on a computer too.

**What still asks the C library for something on such a board**:
copying and measuring memory (`memcpy`, `memset`, `strlen`, which
every compiler for a chip brings), and a number with a fraction,
which `snprintf` makes into text and `strtod` reads. A float in a
program still costs 28 KB of newlib. That is the next part (52.9).

### 52.3 A program that reaches its last line returns from `main`

`zeno_board_stop` is called by `program.exit` and by an error.
**A program that simply ends is not stopped: `main` returns 0**, as
any C program does, to whatever called it, which on a board is the
start-up file.

**Why not call `zeno_board_stop(0)` there too.** The start-up file
calls `main` and has to say what comes after it in any case, for C
that was not written by Zeno as well. A second way to the same place
would be a second thing to get wrong. The header and the start-up file
are one board, and on the board that comes with Zeno they share one
function (`board_stops`).

### 52.4 `--minimal` for a board never writes `printf`

A minimal build writes `print` as `printf` (30.6), and only what the
program uses. For a board that is changed in two ways.

**In a build for a board, `print` goes through the runtime's
`zeno_print`, and not to `printf`.** On a computer `printf` is free:
it is in a library every program shares. On a chip it is copied into
the program, and newlib's is 20 KB. The first run of the size table
after 52.2 showed it: with `fprintf` gone from the runtime, the build
that checks had become smaller than the minimal one on the board with
a C library (`examples/buffer.zeno`: 15,888 bytes checked, 33,584
minimal), and the whole difference was `printf`. And a board that
prints by itself has no `printf` to call at all.

**Why for every board, and not only for one whose header says
`ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS`.** One rule, "a build for a board", needs no
reading of the header's C, and is the smaller program on both kinds
of board.

**For a board with a `header` line, both halves of 52.2 are written
and the header chooses**, as in a checked build. Zeno would have to
read the C of the header to know which half is wanted, and the line
may stand in a file the header includes. **The header is kept in such
a build even when the program touches no pin**, since it is where the
line is, and it may count on the sized numbers (`uint32_t` and the
rest), `bool`, `size_t` and `ZENO_LED` without including anything. In
a checked build the whole runtime stands above the header, so this
was always true there.

**A minimal build for a computer is as it was, byte for byte**: `print`
is `printf`, only the C library's half is written, and
`print("Hello")` is still one `puts`.

### 52.5 A second board: the same chip, on its own registers

**[`boards/lm3s6965evb`](../boards/lm3s6965evb) is the chip QEMU
emulates, with a header of its own.** `board.h` is the board layer
written for real: a pin is a bit of a GPIO port, the clock is the
SysTick timer, a serial port is a UART, `print` goes out of UART0, and
a warning and the end of the program go to the debugger
(semihosting). `startup.c` asks the C library for nothing.

| | pins | `print` | C library under it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `boards/qemu-cortex-m3` | simulated: a line of text for each change | newlib's `fwrite` | newlib, whole |
| `boards/lm3s6965evb` | the chip's ports A to G | the board's UART0 | `memcpy`, `strlen`; `snprintf` only for a float |

**Why keep the first.** Its simulated pins print what a computer
prints, so every example with a pin in it can be held to the computer
byte for byte (51.7), and it is the proof that a board with no header
and a full C library still builds. The second is the proof of this
chapter, and the pattern for a real board.

**The pins are numbered port by port**, 0 to 7 for PA0 to PA7 up to
48 to 55 for port G, because that is the order of the data sheet and
needs no table. **The LED is pin 13 to a Zeno program, as everywhere
(5.12b), and PF0 on this board**, where the board's LED is. PB5, which
the numbering would make 13, is not reached. That is the price of
`led` meaning the same in every program.

**What is tried, and what is not.** QEMU emulates the processor, the
SysTick timer, the direction and the level of every pin, and the data
and the flags of the UARTs. A program that drives a pin and reads it
back, sleeps, prints, reads a line and stops with an error does all of
that through the same registers a real chip has, and the tests hold
it to the answers. QEMU does not emulate a pull-up (an input with one
reads low there), the speed of a UART, or the clocks of the ports.
**Those lines are written from the data sheet and have been run
nowhere. None of the folder has run on the chip itself.**

**Two functions stay for the C library's sake**, in `startup.c`:
`_sbrk`, the memory `snprintf` takes while it makes a float into text,
and `__assert_func`, what newlib calls if it finds a fault in itself.
Newlib's own `__assert_func` prints with `fprintf`, which would bring
every stream back into any program with a float in it. The linker
leaves both out of a program that has none.

**The UART holds one byte at a time.** The chip can queue sixteen,
and turning the queue on empties it, in QEMU as on the chip: a byte
typed before the program started would be lost. A board that is sent
bytes faster than its program reads them wants the queue and an
interrupt (52.9).

### 52.6 What it buys, measured

Flash and RAM in bytes, `arm-none-eabi-gcc` 13.2 with newlib 4.4, the
build that checks:

| program | before this chapter | `qemu-cortex-m3` | `lm3s6965evb` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hello.zeno` | 9,772 | 9,472 | 936 |
| `blink.zeno` | 29,984 | 29,984 | 3,996 |
| `signal.zeno` | 31,296 | 31,016 | 4,844 |
| `buffer.zeno` | 35,536 | 15,888 | 7,464 |
| `modbus.zeno` | 34,520 | 14,452 | 9,720 |
| `words.zeno` | 38,432 | 18,704 | 10,408 |
| `primes.zeno` | 38,568 | 33,032 | 25,360 |
| `tour.zeno` | 50,184 | 44,504 | 36,840 |

The first column is the only board there was, `qemu-cortex-m3`, the
commit before. **The second column is the same board now: with
`fprintf` out of the runtime (52.2), a program that shows no float
lost 20 KB there too**, with a whole C library still under it.
`blink` did not move on that board, because its simulated pins print
with `printf`. `hello` and `blink` take 20 bytes of RAM on the second
board.

The last two rows show a float, and
28 KB of what is left is `snprintf`, `strtod` and the memory they
ask for.

A program of whole numbers and text carries `memcpy`, `memset` and
`strlen` of the C library and nothing else. `blink` is larger than
`hello` because `sleep(500 ms)` counts in a `double`, and this
processor does that in software.

In the minimal build `buffer` went from 33,584 bytes to 13,776 on the
first board when `print` stopped being `printf` there (52.4). A
program with a float in it has that machinery anyway, and pays a
little for the change: `primes` went from 30,304 to 31,880, and 1 KB
of RAM for the room where a number is made into text.

### 52.7 How it is held to its word

- **`a_board_can_print_read_and_stop_by_itself`** runs on a computer,
  under every kind of build and the minimal ones, with a header that
  crosses the streams: what is printed comes out of the error stream,
  a warning out of the other, and the number a program stops with is
  40 more than it gave. Nothing reaches the C library's side.
- **`a_program_prints_through_the_registers_of_a_cortex_m3`** runs on
  the emulated chip: the LED and pins driven and read back, the clock,
  a serial port, numbers of 64 bits, a float, a list, a warning, a
  line typed to `input`, and a division by zero that stops it with
  its file and line. Checked and minimal.
- **`tools/board.py` tries every program on both boards** (51.7). On
  the day this was written: 228 of 228 programs on `qemu-cortex-m3` and 208 of 208
  on `lm3s6965evb` in the build that checks, and 212 of 212 and 193
  of 193 in the minimal one. On the board with pins of its own
  a program that uses the `board` module is left out and counted: a
  simulated pin prints a line when it changes, and a real one does
  not.

### 52.8 `--memory` does not go with such a board yet

The report of `--memory` is written as the C library ends the program
(`atexit`), and a board that stops itself does not end that way.
**The C says so when it is compiled** (`#error`), and the build stops
with that line, so nobody waits for a report that cannot come. On a
board with no `ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS` it works as before.

### 52.9 Left for later

- A float made into text, and read, without `snprintf` and `strtod`:
  the last 28 KB of C library in a program for a board.
- The checks without GCC's built-ins (the rest of item 8).
- The report of `--memory` through the board (52.8).
- An analog pin, a PWM pin and an interrupt in the header of
  `boards/lm3s6965evb`: the chip and QEMU have a converter and timers.
- The UART's queue and an interrupt for what comes in (52.5).
- A board that runs alone, with no debugger: its warnings out of a
  serial port, and a loop or a reset where the program stops.
- A trial on a real board.

## 53. A float and its digits, with no C library

Three things in the runtime were done by the C library: `print(x)`
of a float found its digits with `snprintf` and `strtod` in a loop,
`{x:.2f}` was `snprintf`, and `float("2.5")` was `strtod`. On a
computer those are given. On a chip they are the largest thing in the
program: 28 KB of flash on an ARM Cortex-M3 for the first float a
program shows (52.6), with the memory `snprintf` asks for while it
works.

This chapter is the third part of item 8 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md). **The runtime now does all three itself,
with whole numbers, and exactly.** `snprintf`, `sprintf`,
`strtod`, `strtof` and `atoi` are not called anywhere in it.
`primes.zeno` takes 7,884 bytes on that chip, where it took 25,360.

Nothing in the language changes. What a program prints changes in two
places, and in both a build now prints what `zeno run` always did
(53.2, 53.4).

### 53.1 Whole numbers, in rows of 32-bit words

A float is a whole number times a power of two: 0.1 is
3602879701896397 / 2^55. Its digits in base ten are worked out
exactly, and exact sums on the smallest and the largest floats take
whole numbers of more than a thousand bits. The runtime keeps such a
number as a row of 32-bit words with its length beside it, and has a
dozen small functions for them (`zeno_big_times`, `zeno_big_shift`,
`zeno_big_compare` and their like): multiply by a small number, add,
subtract, compare, double, halve. Every row is on the stack of the
function that uses it, of a size fixed when the C is compiled. No
memory is asked for.

**Why whole numbers.** Sums on floats are rounded, and a method that
rounds on the way gives now and then another last digit, which is the
one thing this code is for. With whole numbers the answer is the same
on every processor, with or without floating point of its own.

**Rejected.**
- *A smaller `printf`* (newlib has one, and vendors have theirs).
  Each rounds its own way and none gives "the fewest digits", so the
  loop round `snprintf` and `strtod` would stay, and what a program
  prints would depend on the C library under it.
- *The fast methods with tables* (Grisu, Ryu). They are several times
  faster and carry tables of powers of ten, some 10 KB of them in
  Ryu, on a chip where flash is what this chapter is about.
- *`__int128`.* 32-bit compilers do not have it.

### 53.2 The fewest digits that name a float

The rule is the one of 24.21 and does not change: the fewest digits
that read back as this float and no other; of two such texts the
nearer; of two equally near the one that ends in an even digit.

The method is Steele and White's, in the form Burger and Dybvig gave
it ("Printing Floating-Point Numbers Quickly and Accurately", 1996).
Each float owns a stretch of the number line: every number nearer to
it than to the float on either side. Digits are taken off the front
of the float's exact value one at a time, and after each the code
asks whether what is written so far, or that with its last digit one
higher, already lies inside the stretch. The first time one does, it
stops.

**One answer changes, and it is the build that was wrong.** The C
tried each length in turn with the float's exact value rounded to
that length, and took the first that read back. But the fewest digits
are not always the rounded ones. A power of two has the float below
it half as far away as the float above, so its stretch reaches twice
as far up as down:

```zeno
print(2.0 ** -44.0)
```

`zeno run` printed `5.684341886080802e-14`, 16 digits, which reads
back as that float. The exact value rounded to 16 digits ends in
`...801`, which is below the stretch, so a build went on to 17 and
printed `5.6843418860808015e-14`. A build now prints what `zeno run`
prints. It can only happen to a float that is exactly a power of two:
46 of the 2,098 there are had another text.

**The C++ and Lua targets had the same fault**, because their
runtimes find the digits the way the C did, with their own `%.16e`.
They keep that way, which is short, and at each length now try the
rounded digits and then the digits one step higher: the stretch of a
power of two reaches further up than down, so those are the only
other ones that can name it. JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby
and Rust were right already. `tools/targets/edge-floats.zeno` prints
all 2,098 powers of two, on every target.

Which power of ten a float is under is guessed from its bits with
whole numbers too (`two * 78913 >> 18` is `two * log10(2)` near enough
for every float), and put right by one comparison. There is no call
to `log10` or `ceil`.

### 53.3 An `f32` takes the same road

The rule of 41.8 does not change: each length from 1 digit to 9,
rounded from the exact value, until one reads back as the same f32.
`zeno_f32_text` asks the same function for digits with that rule,
where it called `snprintf`, `strtof` and `strtod`. `zeno_f32_shown`,
which gave the float with those digits, is gone: nothing needs it.

### 53.4 `{x:.2f}` is exact, and a NaN is `NaN`

The float is split into its whole part and what is after the point.
The whole part is divided by 1,000,000,000 until nothing is left,
which gives its digits nine at a time. What is after the point is
multiplied by ten once for each decimal, and what comes out over the
point each time is the next digit. What is left at the end says which
way the last digit goes: up when it is over half, and to the even
digit when it is exactly half, as before (`{0.125:.2f}` is `0.12`).

**One answer changes.** A float that is not a number printed as the C
library writes it, `nan` or `-nan`, where `zeno run` prints `NaN`:

```zeno
let x = float("nan")
print(f"{x:.2f}")
```

A build prints `NaN` now, and `inf` and `-inf` as before. Text is
made the same way on Linux, macOS, Windows and a chip, whatever their
C libraries do with a NaN.

### 53.5 `float("2.5")` gives the nearest float, however long the text

What is accepted does not change: a sign, then `inf`, `infinity` or
`nan` in capitals or not, or digits with a point anywhere and `e` and
a power after them; blanks around it. `1.` and `.5` are floats; `.`,
`1e`, `1_000.0`, `0x10` and `nan(1)` are a `ValueError`.

The digits are gathered into a whole number `n` and a power of ten.
For most text that is all there is to do: with no more than 15 digits
and a power no more than 22, `n` and the power are both floats
exactly, and the processor's one multiplication or division gives the
nearest float by itself (Clinger, 1990). Any other text is `n`
divided by a power of ten, or multiplied by one, as whole numbers: a
long division gives 64 bits of the answer and says whether anything
was left, and the 53 a float keeps are rounded from that, to even on
a tie. The smallest floats, which keep fewer bits, come out of the
same division.

**No more than 770 digits are kept**, with a note of whether any that
were dropped was not 0. A text that lies exactly between two floats
never has more than 767 digits, so text of any length is read as the
nearest float, in a fixed 960 bytes of stack.

`float( )` no longer makes a copy of its text to cut the blanks off.

### 53.6 What it costs, and what it buys, measured

On an ARM Cortex-M3 (`arm-none-eabi-gcc` 13.2, `-Os`) the digits of a
float take 1,192 bytes of flash, `{x:.2f}` 908, `float( )` 1,428 and
184 of powers of ten, and the functions for long whole numbers under
them some 700: **4.4 KB where the C library took 28**.
A program that uses one of the three carries only that one.

Flash in bytes, the build that checks:

| program | `qemu-cortex-m3` before | now | `lm3s6965evb` before | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `primes.zeno` | 33,032 | 16,172 | 25,360 | 7,884 |
| `tour.zeno` | 44,504 | 22,000 | 36,840 | 14,032 |
| `instruments.zeno` | 52,816 | 31,296 | 45,136 | 23,336 |

A program with no float in it is the same size as before. On
`lm3s6965evb` a program now has of the C library `memcpy`, `memset`,
`strlen` and their like, and the functions of `math` it calls. The
soft floating point of a chip with none of its own comes with the
compiler, and is some 3 KB.

**The quick way of reading (53.5) costs flash on such a chip.** Its
one multiplication or division of floats brings the compiler's
functions for them, 2.2 KB, into a program that reads a float and
never multiplies or divides one itself: `sentence.zeno` is 19,932
bytes on `lm3s6965evb` and would be 17,696 without it. It stays,
because a program that reads a float nearly always does sums with it
and has those functions anyway, and without it reading is three and a
half times slower than it was, on a computer too. **Rejected:** the
quick way only where the processor has floating point of its own.
Each compiler says that with a macro of its own, and the C Zeno
writes would read text one way on one chip and another way on the
next.

While it works, a float's digits take 800 bytes of stack, `{x:.2f}`
640, and a long text read as a float 960. The C library asked `_sbrk`
for memory in their place, and kept 2 KB of its own: `primes` has
33,952 bytes of RAM in use on `lm3s6965evb`, where it had 36,028.

On a computer (a million of each, x86-64, `-O2`):

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `str(x)` of floats that need 17 digits | 5.8 s | 0.96 s |
| `str(x)` of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, ... | 1.85 s | 0.35 s |
| `f"{x:.2f}"` | 0.51 s | 0.06 s |
| `float(text)` of six short texts | 0.11 s | 0.11 s |

Writing is five to eight times faster, because the old way called
`snprintf` and `strtod` once for each length it tried. Reading is as
fast as `strtod` for the short text programs mostly read, and three
and a half times slower for text of 16 digits and more, which goes
the long way (0.38 s for a million of them).

### 53.7 How it is held to its word

- **`a_float_is_written_and_read_with_no_c_library`** types 14,118
  floats at a program that prints each as it is and with 0, 2 and 9
  decimals, 6,000 f32s, and some 11,400 texts to read: every kind of
  float (any bits, readings, every power of two, the smallest ones), text
  with too few digits and far too many, whole numbers exactly between
  two floats with a hair over and under, and halves of the smallest
  floats in 750 digits. What comes out has to be what Rust's own
  functions give, under `zeno run`, in a build and in a firmware
  build. It also reads the runtime for the five calls that are gone.
- **`floats_are_written_and_read_on_a_cortex_m3`** types some 400 of
  them at the serial port of both emulated boards: floats of every
  kind, f32s, text of 750 digits, text that is no float. Each board
  prints what `zeno run` prints, in the build that checks and in the
  minimal one. On `lm3s6965evb` there is no C library under the
  digits, and on both the processor is a 32-bit one with no floating
  point of its own. It has not run on a real chip.
- While it was written the C was compared with the C library of this
  computer (glibc, which is exact) on several million floats and
  texts, a part of them with the address and undefined-behaviour
  checkers on.
- **`tools/board.py`** (51.7): 228 of 228 programs on `qemu-cortex-m3`
  and 208 of 208 on `lm3s6965evb` in the build that checks, 212 of
  212 and 193 of 193 in the minimal one.

### 53.8 What stays with the C library

- **A minimal build for a computer** still writes `{x:.2f}` as
  `printf`'s own `%.2f` (30.6): `printf` is there anyway. So there a
  NaN with decimals is still `nan`. A minimal build for a board goes
  through the runtime (52.4) and prints `NaN`.
- `import c` shows a pointer with `snprintf("%p")` (chapter 44). Only
  a program that imports C has it.
- The simulated board prints a pin's change with `printf`
  (`qemu-cortex-m3`, and every computer).
- `math.sqrt`, `math.sin` and the rest are the C library's.

### 53.9 Left for later

- The checks without GCC's built-ins (the rest of item 8).
- `{x:.2f}` through the runtime in a minimal build for a computer
  too, if the NaN there ever matters.
- The rest of 52.9: `--memory` through the board, an analog pin, a
  PWM pin and an interrupt on `boards/lm3s6965evb`, a board that runs
  alone, and a trial on a real board.

## 54. The history: every commit, under its release

[`HISTORY.md`](../HISTORY.md), at the root of the repository, lists
every commit, oldest first, under the release it went into, with one
plain line on what it changed. zeno-lang.org shows the same file at
`/history/`. It is there so that somebody who reads it from the top
can follow how the language was built: this file says why Zeno is as
it is, and that one says in what order it came to be.

(This chapter was numbered 49 for a few hours. The ticker's chapter
had that number already, in commits that were waiting for the release
of 0.6.0 to be over, and the code and the docs name the ticker's
decisions by it in many places. This one was named in two.)

### 54.1 A script writes the file, from git and a file of notes

**[`tools/history.py`](../tools/history.py) writes `HISTORY.md`.** Git
gives the commits, their order, their dates and the tags.
[`tools/history-notes.txt`](../tools/history-notes.txt) gives the
words: a line for each commit, a heading for a run of commits, and a
paragraph for each release.

**Why a script?** A list of three hundred commits kept by hand is
behind at the next commit, and nobody can see that one is missing. The
script counts them, and `--check` fails when the file is behind.
**Why notes beside it?** The first line of a commit message is written
for somebody in the middle of the work ("Decisions 5.15: whoever
receives a value owns it"). The page is for somebody who is not.
**Turned down:**

- **`git log` alone.** It has every commit and none of the story: no
  release, no word on what a run of commits was for.
- **The plain line inside each commit message.** The commits that are
  there cannot be given one without writing the history again, which
  changes every hash and breaks every link to a commit.
- **`git notes`.** GitHub does not show them, and a clone does not
  fetch them unless it is told to.

### 54.2 A release is a tag

**A tag `vX.Y.Z` on a commit ends a release, and nothing else says
so.** The commits up to and with the tagged one are that release, and
what follows the last tag is under "Unreleased". So a new tag makes a
new heading by itself, and the notes cannot disagree with git about
what a release holds.

The paragraph of a release is in the notes, under its number. The
block named `Unreleased` goes with whichever release now holds its
first commit: a release that is tagged before anybody has touched the
notes still gets the paragraph that was written for its commits.

**The script stops in a clone that has no tags or only part of the
history**, and says which `git fetch` to run. A clone made for one
task is often shallow. Without this, every commit it has would be
written under "Unreleased" and the file would look whole.

### 54.3 A commit with no note is still listed

**A commit that has no line in the notes is listed with the first
line of its own message**, under the heading "Later commits" when it
comes after the noted ones. The page says it has every commit, and it
keeps saying so between the day a commit is pushed and the day
somebody writes its line. `--missing` prints the lines to fill in.

**Turned down: leaving such a commit out until it has a line.** Then
the page is whole only when somebody remembers.

### 54.4 Oldest first, and the name is not CHANGELOG

**The first commit is at the top.** The page is read as a story, and a
story starts at its beginning. A changelog is the other way round,
because it is for somebody who has one version and wants to know what
the next one changes. Zeno has that already, in
[`docs/releases/`](releases/), one page for each version, which is
also the text of the release on GitHub. Two files with one job would
drift apart, so this one has another job and another name.

### 54.5 The commit that brings the page up to date is not on it

**A commit that changes only `HISTORY.md` and the notes is not
listed.** A commit cannot hold its own name: the name is worked out
from what the commit holds. So a commit gets its line in a later
commit, and that later commit holds the two files and nothing else.

**Turned down: listing it, one step late.** Every time the page was
brought up to date it would gain a line that says only that it was
brought up to date, and would need bringing up to date again.

### 54.6 One file, shown in two places

**The site's `tools/build.py` turns `HISTORY.md` into `/history/`**, as
it turns this file into `/decisions/`. Nothing is written twice. A
short name of a commit is a link to the commit on GitHub, in the file
and on the site, so the page can stay one line to a commit and the
whole of each is one press away.

## 55. Checks in plain C, for a compiler that is neither GCC nor Clang

The C that `zeno build` writes is C as the standard of 1999 has it,
but for a handful of things it asked of GCC and Clang by their own
names for them:

- `__builtin_add_overflow`, `__builtin_sub_overflow` and
  `__builtin_mul_overflow`, which say whether a sum, a difference or a
  product was too big (5.5e);
- `__builtin_ctzll` and `__builtin_unwind_init` in the collector;
- `__attribute__((noreturn))` in front of a function that never comes
  back, and `__attribute__((noinline))` in front of three that are to
  stay functions of their own.

A compiler that has none of those names stopped at the first. tcc,
the Tiny C Compiler, is of that kind, and is the one that could be
tried here. IAR's compiler, Keil's older one and the compilers some
chip makers ship are too, as far as their manuals say: none of them
can be run where Zeno is made.

This chapter is the last part of item 8 of
[`missing.md`](missing.md). **Each of those things is now written a
second time in plain C, and one mark, `ZENO_PLAIN_C`, says which of
the two a compiler gets.** tcc builds every example, in every kind of
build, and each does what it does built by gcc.

Nothing in the language changes, and a build by GCC or Clang does what
it did.

### 55.1 One mark, decided in one place

**At the top of `runtime.c`:**

```c
#if !defined(ZENO_PLAIN_C) && !defined(__clang__) && !(defined(__GNUC__) && __GNUC__ >= 5)
#define ZENO_PLAIN_C
#endif
```

Every place that has two forms asks `#ifndef ZENO_PLAIN_C`, and no
place asks what the compiler is. GCC has had the three overflow
built-ins since version 5, so an older GCC, which some chip makers
still ship, gets the plain C as well.

**Building with `-DZENO_PLAIN_C` asks GCC and Clang for the plain C
too.** That is what makes it testable: the plain C can be held to the
built-ins on the same machine, by the same compiler, with no other
compiler at hand.

**Turned down: asking for each built-in by itself** (`__has_builtin`).
GCC only has that question since version 10, and five marks are
thirty-two files to test where one mark is two.

**Turned down: `#define __attribute__(x)`**, the one line that makes
every attribute vanish. The name belongs to the compiler, and a
compiler's own headers may use it.

### 55.2 The checks, written out

Four functions say whether a result fits and hand it over when it
does: `zeno_add_overflows`, `zeno_sub_overflows`,
`zeno_mul_overflows` and `zeno_mul_overflows_u64`. Each has the
built-in and the plain C in it, and `zeno_add`, `zeno_sub`, `zeno_mul`,
the u64 ones and `int("...")` call them.

**A sum and a difference** are worked out as numbers with no sign,
which C lets wrap round, and the signs are looked at: a sum overflowed
when `a` and `b` have one sign and the sum has the other. The result
itself is then C's own `a + b`, worked out only once it is known to
fit.

**The plain C never works out a number that does not fit**, since that
is the thing C leaves undefined, and it never turns a number with no
sign that is too big into one with a sign, which C leaves to the
compiler (C99, 6.3.1.3). So it is the same on every compiler, and a
compiler that builds on a mistake not happening has nothing to build
on.

**A product** is taken as halves of 32 bits, so that every product of
two halves fits in 64:

```
a * b = a1 * b1 * 2^64 + (a1 * b0 + a0 * b1) * 2^32 + a0 * b0
```

The first part fits only as 0, so one of the two top halves is 0.
What is left of the middle is moved up 32 bits, so it must fit in 32.
And adding the last part must not carry. For numbers with a sign the
two are multiplied with their signs taken off, and the product has to
fit with its sign put back: below zero there is room for one more.

**Turned down: finding out by dividing** (`a > INT64_MAX / b`, as
CERT's rule INT32-C writes it). A Cortex-M3 has no instruction that
divides 64 bits: it is a call into the compiler's library of some
hundreds of steps, for every product a program works out.

**Turned down: a number of 128 bits.** `__int128` is GCC's and Clang's
again, and on a 32-bit processor they do not have it either.

**A sum of two u64s needs no built-in in either form**: with no sign C
wraps round, to less than it began with. Both forms are now that one
line.

### 55.3 The word in front of a function

`ZENO_NORETURN` is `__attribute__((noreturn))` for GCC and Clang,
`_Noreturn` for a plain compiler that reads the C of 2011, and nothing
for one that does not. `ZENO_NOINLINE` is the attribute, or nothing.

**With nothing there the C is still right.** The first only lets the
compiler leave out the way back from a call that never comes back, and
the second is a hint about speed. A compiler may then warn that a
function "might return no value" where its last line is a call that
stops the program (tcc does). It never reaches the end, and C only
minds if the value of such an end is used (C99, 6.9.1).

### 55.4 The top of the program stays out of `main`, in the compiler's word or without one

The collector looks for the program's variables on the stack below
`main`'s. So the top-level code is a function of its own,
`zeno_program`, and it must stay one: put inside `main` by the
compiler, its variables could lie above the place the collector
starts from. That was `__attribute__((noinline))`, the one attribute
that something depended on.

**GCC and Clang keep the attribute, as `ZENO_NOINLINE`, and `main`
calls the function by its name.** A compiler that has no such word
calls it by its address, read from a variable it cannot see through:

```c
#ifndef ZENO_PLAIN_C
    zeno_program();
#else
    void (*volatile program)(void) = zeno_program; /* called so, it stays out of `main` */
    program();
#endif
```

No compiler can put a function inside `main` when it cannot know which
function is called. A build with no collector has nothing that looks
at the stack, and there `main` calls `zeno_program` by its name for
every compiler.

**Tried first, and turned down by the count before 0.7.0: one way for
every compiler.** The first form of this stage called through the
pointer in every build with a collector, GCC's too, and took the
attribute off everywhere, so that a build with no collector could have
the one function put inside the other (4 to 32 bytes less on a chip).
The comparison with 0.6.0 that a release is held to (docs/release.md)
found both in the instructions a program runs, with the C of the
program the same line for line:

| `bench/` program, instructions | 0.6.0 | pointer, no attribute | attribute, by name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fib 30`, `--release` | 24,062,434 | 24,356,168 (+1.2 %) | 24,060,625 |
| `trees 14`, `--fast --owned` | 288,528,748 | 291,298,958 (+1.0 %) | 288,531,936 |

GCC makes a copy of `fib` for the one place that calls it when it can
see that place, and cannot when the caller is reached through a
pointer; and with `zeno_program` inside `main` it lays the loop of
`trees` out differently. Neither is a mistake of the compiler's, and a
few bytes on a chip are not worth one instruction in a hundred of
every program on a computer. What a program asks for nothing of must
cost it nothing (24.29, 34.5), so GCC and Clang are given what they
were given in 0.6.0, and only a compiler that could not read that gets
the other form.

### 55.5 The collector in plain C

**The lowest bit of a word that is set** is found by halving the word
six times.

**The registers are read with `setjmp`.** A pointer may be nowhere in
memory when the collector runs, only in a register. GCC and Clang have
a name for putting the registers on the stack. Plain C has one thing
that reads them: `setjmp` copies them into what it is handed. The
collector looks through that like any other memory, and then calls the
function that looks through the stack by its address, as in 55.4, so
that it lies below everything on any compiler.

Two things about it are not as good as the rest of this chapter, and
both are written down here and not hidden:

- **A C library may keep registers back from `setjmp`.** The C library
  of Linux scrambles three of them on a 64-bit Intel processor (the
  stack pointer, the frame pointer and the place to go back to), so
  that what `setjmp` filled cannot be used to break into a program. A
  pointer that a compiler kept in the frame pointer and nowhere else
  would not be seen. With gcc 13 and Clang 18 told to take the plain
  C, the collector's own function puts that register on the stack as
  it begins, at `-O1`, `-O2` and `-Os`, so it is seen there. Nothing
  in C promises that. GCC and Clang never take this path unless they
  are asked to, and tcc keeps nothing in a register across a call.
- **A firmware build with a collector cannot be built in plain C, and
  says so.** A firmware build's promise is that its C has no `setjmp`
  in it at all ([`firmware.md`](firmware.md)), and that promise is
  worth more than this corner. So there the plain C is one line,
  `#error`, that says to build with GCC or Clang, or with
  `--no-collector` or `--owned`. A build for a board has no collector,
  and is not touched by this.

The collector is for a computer, where the compiler is nearly always
one of the two. It was written in plain C all the same so that tcc
could be used to try the whole of the runtime, and it found nothing.

### 55.6 Found on the way: floats on a compiler that is neither

`a * b + c` is two steps in Zeno, each rounded. A processor that has
one instruction for both gives another last digit now and then, and a
C compiler may use it unasked, so the runtime says not to. It said so
to gcc and to Clang, each in its own words, **and to no other
compiler at all.**

**The line C itself has for it, `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF`
(C99, 7.12.2), is now given to every compiler but gcc**, which does
not read it and keeps its own. A compiler for a Cortex-M4F or an M7
has such an instruction, so this is the kind of compiler it matters
to. It could not be tried here: tcc never joins the two steps.

### 55.7 What it costs, measured

On a computer (x86-64, `-O2`), a loop of a hundred million rounds,
each with two products, a sum, a difference and a count:

| | with the built-ins | in plain C |
|---|---|---|
| gcc 13 | 0.19 s | 0.23 s |
| Clang 18 | 0.19 s | 0.24 s |

Fifty million products that nearly fill an int take the same time
either way (0.22 s with gcc, 0.29 s with Clang). The same two loops
built by tcc take 4.7 s and 2.0 s, which is tcc's doing and not the
checks': it does not optimize.

On a Cortex-M3, the functions themselves, in bytes (`-O2`):

| | with the built-in | in plain C |
|---|---|---|
| a sum, a difference | 28 | 42 |
| a product | 190 | 142, and 66 for the u64 one it calls |
| a product of u64s | 76 | 66 |

And whole programs for `boards/lm3s6965evb`, in bytes of flash:

| program | with the built-ins | in plain C |
|---|---|---|
| `hello.zeno` | 936 | 932 |
| `scheduler.zeno` | 7,480 | 7,188 |
| `primes.zeno` | 7,884 | 7,780 |
| `modbus.zeno` | 9,720 | 9,596 |
| `tour.zeno` | 14,032 | 14,208 |
| `instruments.zeno` | 23,336 | 23,288 |

**So on the chip the plain C costs nothing to speak of.** A 32-bit
processor has no overflow flag for a number of 64 bits, and what GCC
writes for its own built-in there is about what the plain C says. How
long each takes on a real chip was not measured: QEMU does not keep
time the way a chip does.

### 55.8 How it is held to its word

- **`plain_c_asks_gcc_for_nothing`** reads the runtime with the mark
  decided: told to be plain, no `__builtin_` is left in it, and no
  `__attribute__` but the one only Windows reads (55.9). The program
  written after it never has either.
- **`plain_c_finds_an_overflow_where_the_built_ins_do`** takes the
  four functions as the runtime has them, writes each out in both
  forms in one C file, and holds the plain one to the built-in on
  every pair of 384 numbers at the edges (each power of two, one less,
  one more, and each of those below zero) and on twenty million pairs
  of every length, with the products that just fit and the ones that
  just do not. The file is read as the C of 1999 with nothing added.
  **`plain_c_finds_an_overflow_on_a_cortex_m3`** runs the same on the
  emulated chip, where a number of 64 bits is two words.
- **`a_program_overflows_in_plain_c_where_it_does_under_zeno_run`**
  types 3,000 pairs of ints and 3,000 of u64s at a program that
  prints each sum, difference and product, or that it was too big.
  What comes out has to be what Rust's own checked arithmetic gives:
  under `zeno run`, built, built as plain C, built as plain C with the
  collector run before every piece of memory is handed out, and built
  by tcc where there is one.
- **`a_program_overflows_in_plain_c_on_a_cortex_m3`**: on both
  emulated boards, built as plain C, 300 pairs that only just fit are
  printed as `zeno run` prints them, and each of ten pairs that do
  not fit stops the program with the error, the line and the column
  of the one sum that was too big.
- **`tools/plain.py`** builds every example, every sample of the book
  and the corner programs for the collector, `--owned` and
  `--no-collector`, and compiles the C three ways: as it is, as plain
  C read by the standard of 1999 (`-DZENO_PLAIN_C -std=c99
  -pedantic-errors`, `-O2`), and with tcc. 266, 238 and 238 programs
  do the same in all three. With Clang in place of gcc the examples and
  the corner programs do too. The `plain` workflow runs it on GitHub.
- While it was written the two forms were compared on 291 million
  pairs, and on 48 million with gcc's checker of undefined behaviour
  on.

**No program of Zeno's has been built by IAR's, Keil's or a chip
maker's compiler.** None of them can be run here. What was tried is
that the C asks for nothing outside the standard of 1999, and that a
compiler which is neither GCC nor Clang (tcc 0.9.27) builds all of it.

### 55.9 What is still GCC's, or the system's

- **On Windows** one function runs before `main` to keep line ends as
  they are, by `__attribute__((constructor))`. gcc and Clang are the
  compilers a build is tried with there. Microsoft's compiler wants
  more than this chapter gives it, and is a stage of its own.
- **`import c`** (chapter 44) writes a few lines with `_Generic`,
  which is the C of 2011, and `zeno run` builds the library it loads
  with an attribute of GCC's. Only a program that imports C has them.
- **A board's own files** are written for the board's compiler:
  `startup.c` and `link.ld` in the two folders that come with Zeno are
  for `arm-none-eabi-gcc`. A board for IAR or Keil is a folder with
  their start-up file and their linker's file in it.
- **The C of 1999** is asked of the compiler (Keil's older compiler
  reads it with `--c99`), and of the C library `memcpy`, `strlen` and
  their like, with the functions of `math` a program calls.
- **`zeno build --llvm`** is Clang by its nature.

### 55.10 Left for later

- A trial with a compiler of a chip maker, when one is at hand.
- Microsoft's C compiler.
- The registers read without `setjmp` where the C library has a
  better way, if a plain compiler on a computer ever needs it.

## 56. `raises` in a function type, and what a build still refuses

Item 9 of [`missing.md`](missing.md) has one aim: **a build should
take what `zeno run` takes.** Nine parts take it there (9.1 to 9.9 of
[`plan-9-14.md`](plan-9-14.md)). This chapter is written as they
land, one section or more for each.

The first part is a function type that says what it raises:

```zeno
function parse(text: str) -> int raises ValueError { ... }

function each(texts: list[str], convert: function(str) -> int raises ValueError) -> int raises ValueError {
    var total = 0
    for text in texts {
        total += convert(text)
    }
    return total
}
```

Until now a firmware build, and so a build with no collector, refused
`texts.map(parse)` and `each(texts, parse)` with "cannot compile a
function that can raise, used as a value, yet" (5.5l). Both build now,
and print what `zeno run` prints.

### 56.1 The type, and what a call through it does

A function type is written as the first line of a function is, with
no names: after what it returns it may say `raises` and one kind of
error. A call through a value of that type can raise that kind, and is
checked as a call of a function that says so: the caller catches it,
or says `raises` itself.

```
error: `each` can raise ValueError here but does not say so. Add `raises ValueError` to it, or catch the error
```

`var f = parse` gives `f` the whole type, `raises` and all, in a
firmware build (and with no collector). An ordinary build gives it the
type it gave before, for the reason in 56.4.

**Why this way of writing it.** It is the function's own first line,
so there is nothing new to learn, and the printer and every message
already wrote a function that way. Two others were weighed in the
plan: `raising function(str) -> int` is one more word in a place no
other word goes, and cannot say which kind; `function(str) -> int or
raises ValueError` reads as if the error were a value that comes back,
which it is nowhere but in the C of a firmware build.

**A fault on a type needs no rule of its own.** In a firmware build a
division by zero, a bad index and their like stop the program, so a
function that says `raises ZeroDivisionError` with nothing in it that
raises one by hand is refused (5.19m, 6.9). The plan asked whether a
type that says `raises ZeroDivisionError` should be refused the same
way. It is not: the only functions that can be put in such a type are
ones that raise nothing, and ones that say `raises ZeroDivisionError`,
which 5.19m has already held to raising it by hand. So the error that
comes through the type is always one that travels as a value, and
`except ZeroDivisionError` around the call catches it in every build.
Refusing the type would refuse a program that is right.

### 56.2 `raises` after a result belongs to the function it ends

This line built before, and means that `make` raises `Missing`:

```zeno
function make() -> function(int) -> int raises Missing { ... }
```

A type that read `raises` for itself would take the word from `make`,
and the line would come to mean something else without a word of
warning. The first rule of the plan forbids that. So **`raises`
belongs to the outermost function whose result it follows**, in a
first line and in a type alike. A function type that is itself the
result, and raises, stands in brackets:

```zeno
function make(n: int) -> (function(int) -> int raises ValueError) raises Missing { ... }
```

Brackets may stand around a function type and nothing else:

```
error: brackets in a type go only around a function type, as in `(function(int) -> int raises ValueError)`. One type is written without brackets
```

**Why not `(int)` too.** It would be a second way to write `int`
(question 1 of the audit).

**What the brackets also give.** `(function(int) -> int) or none` is a
function that may be missing, where `function(int) -> int or none`
is, as it always was, a function whose answer may be `none`. That
