  here are mended and tested (a third is in 57.5): an object received
  as a further value kept the type "owned" inside the list of values
  and could not be read, and the text room was not given back after a
  `Receive`, so a loop of them ran out of room. The review found a
  fourth: values written out, `return make(n), fail(n)` or `let xs, s
  = make(n), fail(n)`, where a later one raised after an earlier one
  had made a list, left the list behind, since the failure leaves at
  once and the list had not reached its place. Each value that has to
  be freed is now held until all are worked out, as an argument is
  held until its call, and `edge-several-2.zeno` counts the blocks of
  all three forms.
- **The targets**: `lower.rs` makes `return a, b` a call of
  `several(...)`, and a `Receive` a temporary and one call of
  `received(value, count, at, line)` for each place, which checks the
  count (57.3). Two functions and a wrapper type in each runtime.
- `printer.rs`, `modules.rs`, and the language server, whose hover
  shows `divide: function(a: int, b: int) -> (int, str)` and each
  name that received a value with its own type.

### 57.5 What it costs a program that does not use it

Nothing that could be found. `runtime.c` is unchanged, so the runtime
test of 56.19 holds. `tools/same.py` against the zeno built from the
tag v0.7.0: 6,795 builds, 6,492 the same and 303 different, which are
the 273 of item 9 and the two new programs about several values
(`edge-several` and `edge-several-2`, which 0.7.0 refused); no program
0.7.0 built is built differently. `tools/refused.py` has three more
operations (a value received first, received later, and swapped) on
every type, and found one more fault, mended: a function written among
the arguments of a call that gives several values took, with its own
`return`, the places the call was to give them to. The bytecode of the
84 programs in `examples/` and `tools/targets/` that are not about
several values: identical to 0.7.0's for every program 0.7.0 could
parse (five programs that use item 9's `take` differ, because 0.7.0
refused them). The sizes are in 57.4. Speed was not timed (section 6
of the plan's changes).

### 57.6 Left for later

- Swapping two items that have one owner: `xs[i], xs[j] = xs[j],
  xs[i]` reads each item as a look, and with no collector a list of
  objects or lists refuses it with the message any item that is only
  looked at gets. A `swap(i, j)` method on a list would be the way in.
- Several values in a `for`: `for q, r in pairs()`.
- A default for one of several results.

## 58. Generics, and what interfaces left out

Item 11 of [`missing.md`](missing.md), as [`plan-9-14.md`](plan-9-14.md)
plans it. 58.1 to 58.19 are generic enums, bounds, generic interfaces
and a method with a type parameter of its own (11.1, 11.2, 11.3 and
11.5). 58.20 onward are the three things 10.10 left out of
interfaces (11.4). Each is asked for by what a program writes: `enum
Name[T]`, `[T is Shape]`, `interface Name[T]`, the name `Ordered` where
the program has none of its own, a default in an interface, a class
whose function takes out, the word `owned` in front of `interface`. A
program that writes none of them is checked, run and built as before: `tools/same.py` finds every C file, IR file, joined program and
bytecode the same as before each part, for every program but the new
one of the part.

### 58.1 Generic enums

```zeno
enum Maybe[T] {
    Nothing
    Just(value: T)
}

function first_even(numbers: list[int]) -> Maybe[int] {
    for n in numbers {
        if n % 2 == 0 { return Just(n) }
    }
    return Nothing
}
```

**The rules** are those of a generic class (3.16 to 3.16c), and
nothing new: square brackets after the name, a capital for each
parameter, and the types worked out where the enum is used, never
written there. `Maybe[int]` written as a type is a copy of the enum
for `int`. A case is written by its name alone, as any case is.

- `Just(3)` is a `Maybe[int]` by what it carries. It is worked out as
  a call of a generic function is (3.16b): from the values, then from
  an argument that is a function, then from the place the result goes.
  `Ok(3)` of `Result[T, E]` says `T` and not `E`, so it needs a place
  that says the rest: `let r: Result[int, str] = Ok(3)`.
- `Nothing` carries nothing, so it takes its type from the place it
  goes: a variable, a parameter, a field and its default, an item of a
  list or a value of a dict whose type is said, what the function
  returns, the other side of `==` or `!=`, and an argument of a
  generic, once the other arguments have said what `T` is
  (`or_else(Nothing, 5)`, `Link(3, End)`).
- Where nothing says, it is an error that shows how to write the type:
  "`Nothing` is a case of the generic enum `Maybe`, and nothing here
  says which `Maybe` it is. Put it where its type is written, as in
  `let x: Maybe[int] = Nothing`". The same for `Ok(3)` with nothing to
  say `E`.
- A `match` on a `Maybe[int]` must handle each case, and the message
  names the case left out as for any enum: "this `match` does not
  handle Nothing". A case of `Maybe` against a value that is not a
  `Maybe` "can never match" it.
- A case name is one enum's alone in a file, generic or not: the rule
  of 13.9 that two enums cannot both have a `Nothing` stays as it was,
  with the same message, naming whichever is written first.
- A generic enum cannot give its cases numbers (`Ack = 6`): a case
  with a number carries nothing (35.1), and a generic enum is for
  carrying a `T`. The message says to take the number away.
- `Maybe(3)`, calling the enum, says that a value of an enum is one of
  its cases. `let f = Just` is refused as `let f = first` is (3.16e).
  `Maybe` with no types where a type goes says how many it takes.
- What a reader sees is `Maybe[int]` in every message, and what
  `print` shows is the case, `Just(3)` or `Nothing`, as for any enum,
  in every engine and every build.

**Why the place says the type of `Nothing`, and not a default.** Rust
and Swift work it out from every later use of the variable as well,
which is a second kind of inference that no other part of Zeno has:
a line would mean something that depends on a line below it. Java
makes `Optional.empty()` a value of any type, which needs erasure,
the road 5.14 turned down. The rule here is the one 3.16b already
gives a generic class built with no argument that says (`let s:
Stack[int] = Stack(items=[])`), and a `Nothing` with nothing to say
what it is was never meant to be written. `print(Nothing)` is refused
for that reason: it would print the same for every `T`, but the
compilers need one copy to print it from, and a rule with an
exception for `print` is two rules.

**Why not `T or none`.** It exists and is still the short way when
nothing needs to be said about the absence. A `Maybe[T]` is what a
program writes when the absence is a case of its own, or when `T` may
itself be `none`: `Maybe[int or none]` keeps "nothing found" and
"found a `none`" apart, which `int or none or none` cannot. `Result[T,
E]` carries a reason, which `none` does not.

**How it is built.** The parser reads `[T]` after the name of an enum
(`Enum::type_params`); its refusal is gone. In the checker a generic
enum is a `Generic` whose `Template` is the enum, and a copy is an
`EnumInfo` with its `origin`, made by `copy_enum` as `copy_class`
makes a class (5.14). The cases of the generic are declared as
`Ty::GenericCase`, the generic and the place of the case. A call of
one is a call of a generic whose parameters are the values that case
carries and whose result is `Maybe[T]` (`case_outline`), so the one
`infer` of 3.16b works out its types; it then is a call of the copy's
case, checked as any. A bare case reads the type of its place from
`expected_case`, which `expecting` notes for a name as it notes the
type of a call's place (`generic_bare_case`). In a call of a generic,
a bare case waits (`Later`) until the other arguments have given the
types, and then takes the type its parameter has in the copy
(`settle_later`). In a `match`, a case finds itself in the copy that
is matched (`copy_matched`). A generic enum that nothing uses is
checked once with `T` as "anything", as a generic class is, and a
`match` in it on a value of unknown type is not reported as missing a
case, since each copy is checked for that.

**Which copy each case means** is noted in `copy_called`, the table a
call of a generic already used (5.14): the call for `Just(3)`, the
name for `Nothing`. It is keyed by the node in the syntax tree, and a
copy of a generic function has a tree of its own (`Function::fresh`,
5.14c), so `return Just(x)` inside `wrap[T]` is noted once for each
copy of `wrap`, with the copy of `Maybe` that copy means. Item 9 once
had notes keyed by line and column, which the copies share; these are
not. The test calls `wrap` and `none_of` with an int and with text in
one program, built every way.

**The compilers** write one enum for each copy (`z_Maybe_int`, its
cases `zeno_new_Maybe_int_Just` and `zeno_case_Maybe_int_Nothing`),
and nothing for the generic. A copy's cases are left out of the table
that finds a case by its name alone, since every copy has a `Just`;
a case of a copy is found by the copy the checker noted, and a pattern
finds its case in the enum of the value matched (`case_in`). An enum
that is not generic goes the way it went, and `tools/same.py` shows
that no program without a generic enum is built differently. With no
collector a `Maybe[Frame]` owns its frame and a `Maybe[list[int]]` its
list, as an enum that carries them does (5.16); a name a `case` gives
to what it carries is a look, by the rules of `match`. The interpreter
and the VM run the generic as it is written. The targets do not look
at types.

**Tests.** `checker::tests::a_generic_enum_takes_its_types_from_where_it_is_used`,
`what_a_generic_enum_says_when_it_cannot`, and
`emit_c::tests::a_generic_enum_every_way` with
`tools/targets/edge-generic-enum.zeno`: `Maybe`, `Result` and a
`Chain[T]` that holds itself, over numbers, text, a list and an
object; `Nothing` in each place that says its type; copies made
inside generic functions and a generic class; `Maybe[Maybe[int]]` and
`Maybe[int] or none`; a thousand rounds; and every way out of a
`match` (its end, `return`, `break`, `continue`, an error raised
inside and caught outside); and several values from one function
(chapter 57), one of them a `Maybe[T]`, from a generic function and a
plain one. It prints what `zeno run` prints in the
six builds, and with no collector 0 blocks are left. `tools/refused.py`
has `Opt[int]`, `Opt[str]`, `Opt[list[int]]` and `Opt[P]` among its
types; every refusal it finds for them is one a plain enum or a list
gets in the same place.

### 58.2 A look at a copy, given to a parameter of a generic

```zeno
function size[T](s: Stack[T]) -> int { return len(s.items) }

let s = Stack([1, 2])
print(size(s))
```

With no collector, 0.7.0 refused this: "`s` of `size` should be
Stack[T], but this is a Stack[int] that is only looked at". The
argument is a look at a value that `s` owns, and the parameter, which
has no `take`, looks: it is the right thing to pass. Working out `T`
did not see through the look. It does now, for a `Stack[T]` and a
`Maybe[T]` alike. The same program with a generic enum was the first
to meet it (`count(chain)` of 58.1), and it is mended in the one place
both go through (`bind`). A program 0.7.0 built is not touched: the
change is only reached where the refusal was.

### 58.3 Bounds: `function largest[T is Ordered]`

```zeno
function largest[T is Ordered](items: list[T]) -> T {
    var best = items[0]
    for item in items {
        if item > best { best = item }
    }
    return best
}

function total[S is Shape](shapes: list[S]) -> float { ... }
```

**The rule.** A type parameter may say `is` and an interface, on a
function, a class or an enum. Each use is checked against it before a
copy is made or found: the type that `T` stands for must be a class
that says it is the interface, or the interface itself. If it is not,
the error is at the use, where the program can mend it, and names
both: "`Task` is not `Shape`, which `total` asks of `S`. It is one if
it says so: `class Task is Shape`, with what `Shape` lists". Before,
the same mistake was found inside the copy, with a note saying which
copy; now the generic's own line says what it needs, and the call is
told. A line that asks twice, as `let r: Range[Task] = Range(...)`
does with the type and the call, is told once.

**How it is written.**

| | Written | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | `[T is Ordered]` | **Chosen.** It is the sentence a class already says, `class Circle is Shape`, with a word that was reserved already |
| B | `[T: Ordered]` | A colon in Zeno says "this name has this type" (`port: int`). `T` does not have the type `Ordered` |
| C | `function largest[T](...) where T is Ordered` | A second place to look for what the first has room for |

**`Ordered` comes with Zeno.** A type is `Ordered` when `<` works on
two values of it: every kind of number (int, float, f32, u64 and the
sized whole numbers), a quantity, and text. It is what `largest`, a
`sort` of one's own or a `Range[T]` need. It is a question the checker
answers about a type, not an interface that a program can see, since
no class could list the functions it would have. A class cannot be
`Ordered` yet: what `<` means for objects of a class is "operators for
a class" in `missing.md`, which comes later by the same road, and
each message that meets it says so: `largest([Task(1)])`, `class
Task is Ordered`, and `Ordered` written as a plain type. A program
that declares its own `Ordered` has its own, as with every name that
comes with Zeno: the name is looked up in the program first, and the
one that comes with Zeno is only reached where the program has none.
So no program that built before changes meaning, and nothing is
reserved.

**After `is` comes an interface.** `[T is int]` says that after `is`
comes an interface, such as `Ordered` or one the program declares;
`[T is Task]`, a class, says to write `Task` itself where `T` is used,
or to declare an interface that `Task` is. A name that is not declared
is "there is no type called" it, as anywhere a type goes.

**The body is still checked for each copy** (3.16d). A bound is a
promise checked at the use. It is not all that the body may do: a
generic with no bound that uses `>` is accepted, and stays accepted,
and `smaller[T is Ordered]` may call a function that is no part of
`Ordered`. Making the bound the whole truth would refuse generics that
build now, and would need a bound for each operator before the first
could be used; C++ took this road with concepts for the same reason.
What a bound buys is what `missing.md` asked for: the error moves from
inside the generic to the call.

**Why a bound, and not a parameter of the interface's type.** `shapes:
list[Shape]` does not take a `list[Circle]` (10.7): a list of circles
cannot take a square. `[S is Shape](shapes: list[S])` takes a list of
circles as one, and gives back an `S` that is a `Circle`, with its
fields.

**How it is built.** `ast::TypeParam` is a name and the type after
`is`, if any; `Function`, `Class` and `Enum` keep a list of them, and
`param_names` gives the names where only they matter. The parser reads
`is` and a type after each name; the printer writes it back. In the
checker each `Generic` keeps its bounds as written, and `asks` works
them out once, in the generic's own scope, so a program's own
`Ordered` is found first. `meets_bounds` is asked by `copy_function`,
`copy_class` and `copy_enum` before a copy is made or looked up; a
copy that does not meet its bounds is not made. Nothing else changes:
inside a copy `T` is the real type, so a call of the interface's
functions is checked as on any object, and a bound makes no code. The
compilers, the interpreter, the VM and the targets need nothing; a test
holds that the C of a program with bounds is the C of the same program
without them.

**Tests.** `parser::tests` (the bound read back);
`checker::tests::a_type_parameter_may_ask_for_an_interface`,
`a_type_that_lacks_what_is_asked_is_refused_at_the_call` and
`what_a_bound_says_when_it_is_written_wrong`;
`emit_c::tests::a_bound_every_way` with
`tools/targets/edge-bounds.zeno`: `largest` over ints, floats, text,
volts, milliseconds, u8, i16, f32 and u64; `total` over a list of
circles, a list of squares and a list of shapes; a generic class
`Range[T is Ordered]` whose methods call two other bounded generics,
`Pair[K is Ordered, V]`, a generic enum `Span[T is Ordered]`, and a
thousand rounds. It prints what `zeno run` prints in the six builds,
with 0 blocks left with no collector, and its C with and without the
bounds is the same.

### 58.4 One interface for each type parameter

`[T is Ordered, U]` must read one way: a comma begins the next type
parameter. So `[T is Ordered, Shape]` does not ask two things of `T`;
it makes `Shape` a second type parameter, which would hide the
interface of that name inside the generic. Where a name after a comma
is an interface of the program and an earlier parameter has a bound,
that is refused: "`Shape` after a comma is a second type parameter,
which hides the interface `Shape`. A type parameter asks for one
interface: `[T is ...]`. If `Shape` is meant to be a type parameter,
give it another name". A program that needs two has not been written
yet, and how to write two is left for when one is; the message keeps
that room free.

### 58.5 A generic that nothing uses, checked as its bound

A generic that nothing uses has no copy to check, so it is checked
once on its own (5.14d), with each type parameter standing for
"anything". A type parameter with a bound of the program's own now
stands for that interface instead. So `function f[S is Shape](s: S)`
that calls `s.perimeter()`, which `Shape` does not list, is found
though nothing calls `f`, with the message any call through an
interface gets. A parameter that is `Ordered`, or has no bound, still
stands for "anything": `Ordered` has no functions to list, and a
generic with no bound promised nothing. Once a copy is made, the copy
is checked as before, with the real type.

### 58.6 Generic interfaces

```zeno
interface Source[T] {
    function next(self) -> T or none
}

class Countdown is Source[int] { ... }
class Repeat[T] is Source[T] { ... }

function drain(source: Source[int]) -> int { ... }
```

**The rule.** An interface may have type parameters, written as a
class writes them. An interface is a class to every stage after the
parser (10.9), and a generic class has copies (5.14), so `Source[int]`
is a copy of the interface: an interface of its own, whose `next`
gives an `int or none`. A class says which copy it is after `is`, with
the types: `class Countdown is Source[int]`. A generic class may say
`is Source[T]`, and each of its copies is the copy of `Source` for its
own `T`: `Repeat[int]` is a `Source[int]`, `Repeat[str]` a
`Source[str]`. Everything else is the rules of an interface, unchanged
(10.4 to 10.8, 58.20 to 58.22): the class has each function of the
copy, written the same way; an object of the class goes where the copy
is wanted; a list of them written out is a list of the copy; a bound
may be a copy, `[S is Source[str]]` (58.3).

**`Source[int]` and `Source[str]` are two interfaces.** A `Countdown`
does not go where a `Source[str]` is wanted, and a `Source[str]` does
not go where a `Source[int]` is: "`a` should be Source[int], but this
is Source[str]". A class may be two copies, `is Source[int],
Source[str]`, if it has the functions of both, which can only be when
they do not meet; a class that has the functions of `Source[int]` and
says `Source[str]` is told what `Source[str]` asks for.

**Each copy is an interface of its own for 58.21 and 58.22 too.** A
copy has its own place in the checker's tables, so when `Slot`, a
`Holder[list[int]]`, takes out what it holds and `Name`, a
`Holder[str]`, does not, a call through a `Holder[list[int]]` is for
its owner only and one through a `Holder[str]` is for anybody. An
`owned interface Holder[T]` makes every copy owned, and each takes
only an `owned class`.

**The messages.** `class Words is Source`, with no types, says that
`Source` has type parameters and shows the class with them. `is
Shape[int]` on an interface with none says to write it without `[ ]`.
The wrong number of types is said as for a class. `Source()` says that
an interface has nothing to build, as for one with no types, and
`Source` kept as a value says it is written where a type goes.

**Why copies, and not one interface over every `T`.** The road of
Java, where `Source<Integer>` and `Source<String>` are one interface
at run time, is erasure, which 5.14 turned down for classes: a
`next()` would give back "anything", and every caller would need a
cast that the checker cannot see. A copy is what a generic class
already is, so nothing new had to be decided for the C, the LLVM, an
object with one owner, or `--memory`.

**How it is built.** The parser's refusal is gone: an interface reads
`[T]` after its name into `Class::type_params`, and `Class::is` is a
list of types where it was a list of names, so that `Source[int]` can
be written there (`interface_named`). `modules.rs` renames the names
in it as in any type, inside the class's own type parameters. In the
checker a generic interface is a `Generic` whose template is a class
that is an interface, and `copy_class` makes its copies as it makes a
class's. In `fill_class`, a name after `is` is looked up as before,
and a name with types is resolved as a type, which makes or finds the
copy; a copy is the same `ClassInfo` each time, so `is_one`, `fits`
and `stands_for` compare it as they compare any interface. The
compilers read the name of each interface after `is` from the
checker, which notes what each written type stands for
(`Types::interface_name`): `Source[int]` for a copy, and the name as
written for an interface with no types, as before. Both compilers
register a copy of an interface as they register a copy of a class,
and write the `switch` of 10.9 for each copy the program uses, over
the classes that are that copy. A program with no generic interface
reads the same names as before, and `tools/same.py` shows its C, IR,
joined program and bytecode the same. The interpreter, the VM and the
targets do not look at interfaces' types.

**Tests.** `parser::tests::interfaces`;
`checker::tests::an_interface_may_have_types_of_its_own`,
`what_a_generic_interface_says_when_it_cannot` and
`each_copy_of_a_generic_interface_is_held_to_taking_out_by_itself`;
`emit_c::tests::a_generic_interface_every_way` with
`tools/targets/edge-generic-interface.zeno`: `Countdown is
Source[int]`, `Words is Source[str]` and `Repeat[T] is Source[T]`,
used through `Source[int]`, in a list, as a bound, in a generic
function over `list[Source[T]]`, and a thousand rounds; and an `owned
interface Holder[T]` whose classes take out what they hold and whose
functions have a default, `Slot is Holder[list[int]]` and `Cell[T] is
Holder[T]`, in an owned list. It prints what `zeno run` prints in the
six builds, with 0 blocks left with no collector, and in each target
whose tools are installed. A program in two files with `class Count is
sources.Source[int]` was tried by hand in three builds.

### 58.7 A method with a type parameter of its own stays refused

```zeno
class Box[T] {
    item: T
    function convert[U](self, change: function(T) -> U) -> Box[U] { ... }
}
```

The plan builds this only if 58.1 to 58.6 make it a small step. They
do not, and it stays refused. A copy of a generic is made where it is
called, and today what is called with a dot is one function: a method
read from an object is a `BoundMethod` that holds one `FunctionInfo`.
A method with its own `U` would need, each its own work and none
shared with what 58.1 to 58.6 built:

- a bound generic as the type of `box.convert`, and the call of a
  method going through `call_generic` with the object as a first
  argument that says nothing about `U`;
- its copies made inside each copy of the class, `Box[int]` having
  `convert[str]` and `convert[float]`, and checked with `self` of that
  copy;
- in both compilers, those copies registered as methods of the class
  copy and compiled with it, and each call reading which copy the
  checker chose, where a method call today finds its function by name;
- with no collector, the rules of `self` (a look, or `take` where the
  method takes out, 5.19k and 58.21) held for each copy, and a method
  value of one (56.9) refused.

That is about a dozen places in four files for the item that the plan
calls the least needed, and no program in the repository, the book or
a review has asked for it. **The same work is done today** by a
function of the file that takes the object first, which every build
takes:

```zeno
function convert[T, U](box: Box[T], change: function(T) -> U) -> Box[U] {
    return Box(change(box.item))
}
```

So the message says that, with the names filled in: "the method
`convert` cannot have type parameters of its own yet. Write it as a
function of the file that takes the object first: `function
convert[T, U](box: Box[T], ...)`". It was "The class can have them:
`class Box[T]`", which in a generic class named a class that already
has them. A method of an interface stays refused by the parser, as
the plan says: it would be a copy for each `U` in each class behind
each `switch`.

**Tests.** `checker::tests::what_a_generic_cannot_do_yet`, for a
plain class and a generic one.

### 58.8 A generic given a list whose items are not all one type

`first([200 ms, 1 s])` runs with `zeno run`, which keeps each item as
it is and prints `200 ms`, and every build refused it, in 0.7.0 too,
with "`first` cannot tell what `T` is from this call: no argument
says", which pointed at the wrong thing. The list does say something:
that its items are two types. A build gives a list one type (the row
of [`compiler.md`](compiler.md) on such lists), and making the list
one of ms would change what it prints, `1000 ms` where `zeno run`
prints `1 s`. So it stays refused, by that row, and the message now
says why and what to write: "`first` cannot tell what `T` is from
this list: its items are not all one type, but a quantity in ms and a
quantity in s, and a build gives a list one type. Write them all in
one unit, such as `ms`". For an int beside a float it says to write
each as a float; for anything else, to make them one type or an enum
with a case for each, as the row does.

The checker notes each list written out whose items it could not join
into one type, with the types they are (`mixed`), and the one place
where a generic cannot tell a type reads it. Nothing else changes: a
list that is one type is never noted, and `zeno run` takes what it
took. The row names the case, and `tools/refused.py` has two programs
beyond its matrix, `first` given a list of two units and of an int
and a float, so a later change to either message is seen.

**Tests.** `checker::tests::a_generic_given_a_list_of_two_types_says_why_in_a_build`.

### 58.20 A default on a parameter of an interface's function

```zeno
enum Mode {
    Slow
    Fast
}

interface Motor {
    function spin(self, speed: int = 1_000, wait: ms = 5 ms, mode: Mode = Fast)
}

class Fan is Motor {
    function spin(self, speed: int = 1000, wait: ms = 5 ms, mode: Mode = Mode.Fast) { ... }
}

function drive(motor: Motor) {
    motor.spin()             # 1000, 5 ms, Fast
    motor.spin(wait = 20 ms)
}
```

**The rule.** A parameter of a function of an interface may have a
default. It is a plain value: a number, with a minus in front of it
or not; text (not an f-string); `true`, `false`, `none`; a quantity
such as `5 ms`; or a case of an enum that carries nothing, bare or
with the enum's name. Anything else is refused where it is written,
with what is allowed. The class writes the same default, and "the
same" is the same value: `1_000` and `1000` are, `Fast` and
`Mode.Fast` are. A default that differs, or none where the interface
has one, is refused at the class, with both defaults and both lines.
Had `Fan` above written `speed: int = 2000`:

```
error: `spin` of `Fan` gives `speed` the default `2000`, on line 11,
and `Motor` gives it `1000`, on line 7. Write the same default in
both, so that a call through a `Motor` and a call on a `Fan` mean the
same
```

**Where the interface writes none, the class may have its own.** It
could in 0.7.0 (10.6 compared names and types, and said nothing of
defaults), and such a program must go on being taken. A call through
the interface then gives every argument, and one that leaves it out
is refused at the call ("`spin` needs a value for `speed`"), so the
two calls still cannot differ without the reader being told.

**Why the same, and not "the class's own wins".** `motor.spin()` is
one line that runs a different class each time. If each class could
fill in its own default, the line would mean a different speed for
each motor, and nothing on the line or in the interface would say
so. With one value written twice, the interface tells the whole
truth, and the class says nothing that contradicts it. It is 10.6
again: the same first line twice needs no working out.

**Why only a plain value.** "The same" then has one meaning, which
the checker and the reader both see at a glance. `2 * 3` and `6`, or
`len(names)` and a number, would need the checker to work values out
(and `len(names)` is not the same at every call), and a rule that
says "the same when worked out" is a rule nobody can check by eye.
A quantity is allowed because a timeout with a unit is the default
firmware writes most. A case of an enum that carries values is not
plain: it is a function that makes one.

**`5 ms` and `5000 us`.** The planner's rule counts them the same
value, and the comparison does. In practice it does not arise: the
unit is part of the parameter's type (`wait: ms`), so a default in
another unit is refused as the wrong type before the two are
compared.

**How a call fills it in.** Nothing new: every engine already fills
a left-out argument from the default of the function it calls, and
a call through an interface calls the interface's function. Since
the class's default is the same value, a call on the object gives
what a call through the interface gives. The checker checks the
interface's default as it checks any default (its type, and what a
quantity in it needs), so the compilers find it noted.

**Tests.** The checker: every kind of plain value, equal in another
spelling; a call through the interface that leaves it out; the
class's own default where the interface has none, and a call through
the interface that leaves that out; each kind unequal, and none
where there is one; a default in the interface that is a sum, a
call, a list, an f-string and a case that carries values; one of the
wrong type. Every build:
[`tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno)
prints what `zeno run` prints, through C and LLVM, with a collector,
in firmware, and with none (0 blocks left), and in each target
language.

### 58.21 A function that takes out what its object owns, standing for one of an interface

```zeno
interface Pile {
    function take_last(self) -> Task
    function size(self) -> int
}

class Stack is Pile {
    tasks: list[Task]

    function take_last(self) -> Task {
        return self.tasks.pop()
    }
    ...
}

function drain(pile: take Pile) {          # the owner: allowed
    while pile.size() > 0 {
        print(pile.take_last().name)
    }
}

function peek(pile: Pile) -> str {         # only looks: refused
    return pile.take_last().name
}
```

```
error: only the owner can call `take_last`, which takes out or
replaces something the object owns (`Stack` is a `Pile`, and its
`take_last` does): somebody else may have been lent it. Here `pile`
only looks at it
```

**The rule.** A function that takes out or replaces what its object
owns (5.19k) may stand for one of an interface. A call through the
interface is then held to the guards of 5.15e, as a call on the
object is: only the owner may make it, not inside a loop or a
`match` that is looking at what it would take, and not on a line
that has already looked at the object. The interface's function says
nothing about it, and nothing is written: it takes out if the
function of any class that is the interface does, and the whole
program is known (7.11).

**How the checker knows.** It keeps the set of functions of
interfaces that some class's function takes out for, with the name
of one such class for the message. A class adds to it where 0.7.0
refused it. A call through the interface whose function is in the
set is held to the guards. The checker already reads the program
several times over, until a reading learns nothing new (for the
types of parameters with none written); the set is carried from each
reading to the next in the same way, and **what is reported comes
from a reading in which the set did not grow**. So a call read
before the class that takes out (later in the file, in another file,
or in a copy of a generic class made later) is held to the same
guards as a call read after it. The set only grows, and it is never
larger than the number of functions of interfaces, so the readings
end.

**Why not work it out at the first call** (as the plan first said).
Two things break it. A class whose function calls through its own
interface (a tree whose `count` adds up the `count` of its children)
is still being checked at that call, and the checker answers "takes
out" for a method still being checked, since that can only refuse;
such programs were taken by 0.7.0 and would be refused. And a copy
of a generic class that is the interface may be made after the first
call. The set, carried over the readings, has neither fault.

**Why not a word on the function** (`function take_last(self) takes`).
5.19k turned it down for a method: a word that must be kept in step
with the body is a second place to be wrong. An interface's function
has no body, so the word would have something to say there; but
then a class whose function stopped taking out would be told to
keep a word that is no longer true of it, or every interface with
it would change. The program is all there, and the checker can read
it.

**What it costs.** A class that takes out makes every call of that
function through the interface owner-only, even for the classes that
do not take out. That is the price of a call that runs one of
several functions: the caller cannot know which. A program that
needs the looser call writes two functions.

**A program of 0.7.0** has an empty set (each class that took out
was refused), so every call through an interface is checked as it
was.

**Tests.** The checker: `drain` and `peek` above, with no collector;
`peek` written before `Stack`, with `Stack` in a second file, and
with a copy of a generic class `Box[T] is Pile` made after `peek`;
the loop's message (`for one in piles` around `piles[0].take_last()`)
and the line's (`print(pile.size(), pile.take_last().name)`); an
interface whose classes take nothing out, as before; a class that
calls through its own interface, where `count` (which takes nothing
out) is called on a loop's item, `strip` (which does) is called on
an item it popped, and `strip` called on a loop's item is refused.
Every build: [`tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno)
drains a `Stack` and a `Queue` through a `Pile`, takes out of a
`list[Pile]` by index, a thousand rounds, and the tree.

### 58.22 `owned interface`

```zeno
owned interface Shape {
    function area(self) -> float
}

owned class Circle is Shape { ... }
owned class Square is Shape { ... }

let shapes: owned list[Shape] = [Circle(1.0), Square(2.0)]
```

**The rule.** `owned` may stand in front of `interface`, as it stands
in front of `class` (5.8b). Each object that is an `owned interface`
has one owner, which frees it, with a collector as without one: it
moves when it is given away, a list of them is an `owned list`, a
parameter looks at one unless it says `take`, and a field holding
one is in an `owned class`. Only an `owned class` can be an `owned
interface`, and an `owned class` can only be an `owned interface`.
Each mismatch is refused at the class, and says which word to write:

```
error: `Dot` is an owned class, and `Shape` is not an `owned
interface`: an object with one owner cannot be where a shared one is
wanted. Write `owned interface Shape`, or take `owned` off `Dot`

error: `Dot` is not an owned class, and `Shape` is an `owned
interface`, whose objects each have one owner. Write `owned class
Dot`, or take `owned` off `Shape`
```

**Why taking out was not the whole question.** 10.10 said the two
refusals were one question, about a function that takes out called
through an interface. 58.21 answers that. But with a collector a
value of an interface is shared, and an object of an `owned class`
put where a `Shape` is wanted would be an owned thing inside a
shared one, which 5.8 forbids: the shared `Shape` could be copied
anywhere, and the owner would free the object under it.

| | How | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | `owned interface Shape`: its objects have one owner, only an `owned class` can be one, and an `owned class` can only be one | **Chosen.** It is the sentence `owned class` already is, with the word already reserved, on the first line of the interface where its reader looks |
| B | An object of an interface is owned when what was put into it is | The same type would be shared at one line and owned at the next, and nothing on the page would say which. 5.8b turned down the same thing for classes |
| C | An interface is owned when its classes are, worked out | Nothing written says it, against the rule that a feature is asked for by a word; and one more class could change every use of the interface |
| D | Leave the refusal | 10.10 left it open, and a `Resource` (12.1) needs it |

**With no collector, and in a file that says `memory owned`, nothing
changes.** Every object has one owner there already, the interface's
too: the word is allowed and says nothing new, and a class without
`owned` may be an interface with it, as it may hold anything owned.

**How it is built.** The parser reads `owned` before `interface`
(the word was reserved by 5.19c, so no program had it as a name) and
marks the interface owned, as it does a class. To the checker an
interface is a class (10.9), so an owned one is an owned class: its
objects are owned, the functions of it look at their object, and
every rule of 5.8 applies with nothing added. The rule above replaces
the old refusal. The compilers already free an object through its
interface (the `switch` of 10.9 has a case for each class), which a
build with no collector has done since 10.10; a build with a
collector now does it for an `owned interface`.

**Tests.** The checker: both mismatches; both words, and neither;
with no collector both mismatches are taken; a `memory owned` file
with a plain interface and class. With a collector: an `owned
interface` in an owned list, as a parameter that looks and one that
takes, as a field and one that may be `none`; given away and used
after; a list that is not owned; a function that replaces what its
object owns, called through the interface by a parameter that only
looks (refused, by 58.21). Every build:
[`tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno)
has `Shape` with a `Circle` that replaces its centre, a `Frame` that
holds one and may hold a spare, and a thousand rounds; with no
collector 0 blocks are left, and with a collector the C build runs
under valgrind with nothing wrong.

### 58.23 What interfaces still leave out

- **A default body** for a function of an interface. A class writes
  each function (10.5).
- **An interface that is another interface.** A class names both.
- **A way back** from an interface to the class (10.8).
- **A default that is not a plain value** (58.20), and a class whose
  default differs from the interface's.
- **A call through an interface that takes out, made by somebody who
  only looks**, even when the class behind it does not take out
  (58.21). It is the guard, and not a gap: the caller cannot know
  which class it is.

Generic interfaces and functions with type parameters of their own
are 58.1 to 58.19.

**Where 58.20 to 58.22 meet several values (57).** A function of an
interface may give two results and have a default, take out and give
two results, or be a function of an `owned interface` that does
both; the end of
[`tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno)
does each, in every build.


## 59. Cleaning up when a block ends, files in pieces, and folders

Item 12 of [`plan-9-14.md`](plan-9-14.md) has three parts: a value
that is cleaned up when its block ends (12.1), a file read and written
in pieces (12.2), and folders (12.3). The third is cut loose from the
other two and lands first. Its sections begin at 59.20, so that the
first two parts keep the numbers before it.

### 59.1 `is Resource`: something that is put back when its owner ends

```zeno
owned class Selected is Resource {
    line: Pin

    function release(self) {
        self.line.on()              # chip select is high again
    }
}

function read_id(bus: Bus, line: Pin) -> u8 {
    line.off()
    let chosen = Selected(line)
    return bus.transfer(0x9F)
}                                   # chosen.release() runs here, however the block is left
```

An open file, a chip-select line and a lock each have a second half
that must happen on every way out of a block. Until now it was
written before each `return`, and forgotten before one of them. Now
the class says it once: an `owned class` that is `Resource` has its
`release` called when the owner of the object ends. The choice of
this over `defer`, `finally` and a block of Python's `with` is 12.1
of the plan; here is what was built.

**`Resource` comes with Zeno**, as `owned interface Resource {
function release(self) }` (58.22). It is written into a program only
when the program names it and has no `Resource` of its own, so a
program that never says the word is the program it was: the same C,
IR and bytecode, which `tools/same.py` holds. A program with its own
`Resource` means its own, and nothing is released: it is an
interface like any other. It is not a reserved word.

**The rules.**

1. Only an `owned class` can be one: a shared object has no owner
   whose end could be the moment. ``class Plain is Resource`` is
   refused, and says ``Declare it `owned class Plain is Resource` ``.
2. `release` takes `self` alone and gives nothing, as the interface
   says. It may not say `raises`: it runs at the end of a block,
   where an error has nowhere to go, and the message says to catch
   the error inside it.
3. `release` cannot be called by hand. It runs once, and the message
   says how to end a resource sooner: give it to a function that
   takes it, `function done(held: take Held) { }`.
4. **It runs when the owner ends**: when the block of the `let` that
   holds it is left by reaching its end, by `return`, `break` or
   `continue`, or by an error passing through. Of two in one block,
   the one made last is released first. After `return x + y` the
   value is worked out first and the release runs second, so the
   value may use the resource. A loop's body is a block, so one made
   in each turn is released at the end of each turn.
5. A resource has one owner, like every owned value. `return` gives
   it to the caller, a parameter that says `take` takes it, `let b =
   a` moves it. Whoever has it at the end releases it; one that was
   given away is not released by the one who gave it, on any path:
   given away in one branch of an `if`, it is released at the end of
   the block only when the other branch ran.
6. **It does not run when the program is stopped**: by
   `program.exit`, or by a fault of a firmware build (5.5l). Stopping
   ends no block. A failed `assert` is not a stop: it stands only in
   a test, and leaves its test as an error would, so what the blocks
   of the test own is released, and the next test can open the same
   file (plan, Changes 18).
7. **Where a resource can be, in this version: in a `let`, or in a
   parameter.** The rest is 59.2.

**An error passes through as it was.** The release runs, and then the
error goes on with its kind, its message and its line unchanged, to
the `except` that catches it or out of the program. An error that
nothing catches releases on its way out, top of the file included,
and is reported after the lines each `release` printed, exactly as it
is reported in a program with no resource. (`raise e` names the line
of the `raise`, so the engines do not pass it on that way.)

### 59.2 Where a resource can be: a `let`, or a parameter

The compilers free an owned value on every road it can take, and for
them a `release` in front of the free would be all there is to do.
But the interpreter, the VM and the fifteen targets free nothing:
their values are shared, and collected by the language they are
written in. For them "the owner ends" has to be made into something
that runs, and for a `let` in a block that is one thing: code at each
way out of the block. For a field or an item of a list it would be
chapters 5.15 to 5.17 again, in every engine. A `let` covers the
guard of a block, which is what the needs above are. The rest is
refused, each with a message that says what to write, so letting it
in later changes no program (11.6). With a collector and with none
the checker says the same words.

| Where | What is said |
|---|---|
| `var h = Held("a")` | `h` holds a resource, which is released when its owner ends, so the variable cannot be given another value. Declare it with `let` |
| a list or a dict of them, `Held or none`, a field of any class, a case of an enum, a type parameter, what a function gives when it is one of those | *what* would hold a resource. A resource is released when its owner ends, and its owner is a `let` or a parameter, never a list, a dict, a field, a case of an enum, `or none` or a type parameter. Keep it in a `let` of its own |
| `print(Held("a").name)`, or a call standing alone | this call gives a resource, and nothing keeps it, so it would be released at once. Keep it in a `let`, which releases it when its block ends: `let held = ...` |
| one of several values (item 10): `return Held("a"), 1`, `let a, b = Held("a"), 1`, `let n, h = 1, Held("b")`, and `a, b = ...` | a resource cannot be one of several values: its owner, which releases it, is a `let` of its own. Give it back alone, and receive it alone: `let held = ...` |
| a default that makes one: `function f(h: Held = Held("d"))` | a default cannot make a resource: `h` would be made at each call that leaves it out, where no `let` owns it. Pass one at the call instead |
| a function that is kept, using a resource of the block around it | this function is kept, so it would take `h`, a resource, and nothing would release it when its block ends. Pass `h` to the function as a parameter instead |
| a parameter whose type is not written | the type of `x` of `show` is not written, so a resource cannot go to it. Write its type: `x: Held` |
| the top of a file that imports `web` | a page stays open after the program's last line, so the top of its file never ends, and `h` would never be released. Make it inside the function that uses it |

A call that gives a resource may be received by a `let`, by `return`,
or by a parameter that takes it, `done(Held("passed"))`: in each the
value has an owner the moment it is made. A resource may be held as
the interface, `let r: Resource = h`, and a parameter may look at one
as `Resource`; the release is then found through the interface, as
any function of it is (10.9).

**Where it meets chapter 58.** A type parameter never holds a
resource, so `function named[T is Resource](x: T)` may be written, and
a call that gives it a `Held` is refused with the message of the
second row, naming `` `T` of `named` ``; so is `Box[Held]` for a
generic class, `Just(Held("a"))` for a generic enum, and `class Maker
is Source[Held]` for a generic interface. A bound that
could be met by nothing is not refused where it is written: it is
refused the first time it is asked, at the call, as every bound is
checked (58.3).

The last row is the page's: a program that imports `web` goes on
after its last line, answering the page, so the top of its file never
ends. A function of the page may make one, as any function may.

### 59.3 The top of a file, its tests, and how a program stops

**The top of a file is a block.** A resource made there is released
after the last line, when the program ends as it should, last made
first, and before an error that nothing caught is reported.

**When a file is run for its tests, the top ends after its last
test** (plan, Changes 18). `zeno test` runs the file, then its tests,
and the tests see the file's variables, as `testing.md` has always
said. A resource of the top would be released before the tests if
the top ended at its last line, and a test that reached it through a
function would use something given back. So in `zeno test` and in
`zeno test --build` a resource of the top is released after the last
test, and in `zeno run` and `zeno build` after the last line. A list
that the top owns in a build with no collector already went this
way, given back after the tests; a resource goes the same road, its
`release` in front of that giving back.

Refusing a test that uses a resource of the top was weighed and not
taken: a test can reach it through a function it calls, or a function
held as a value, and no check could see every road.

**`program.exit` and a firmware fault release nothing**, at the top or
in any block (rule 6).

### 59.4 How it is built

The checker is the only part that knows which `let` holds a resource,
and the engines learn it from the program it gives back. After the
rules pass, `checked` rewrites the program, as it does for sized
numbers (10.27): the statements after a resource's `let`, to the end
of its block, go into a new statement, `StmtKind::Scoped { name, body
}`, the second inside the first; a body whose parameter takes a
resource is wrapped the same way; and each use that gives the
resource away (to a `take` parameter, by `return`, by `let b = a`)
becomes `ExprKind::Give(name)`. Both are made only by the checker,
and no program can write them. A `Scoped` opens no scope of its own:
the names made in its body belong to the block it stands in, so the
hoisting of functions and the free of other owned values see the block
whole (`ast::flat`). A program with no resource is not rewritten, and
the test `a_program_with_no_resource_is_not_rewritten` holds it.

**The meaning of `Scoped`, for every engine:** run the body; however
it is left, if the name still holds its object, call its `release`;
then go on leaving the same way. `Give(name)` reads the name and
leaves it empty.

- **The interpreter**: one arm, which runs the body, looks at how it
  ended, and calls `release` unless the name was emptied. `Give` reads
  the variable and leaves `none` in it. The top of a file under `zeno
  test` runs the file's tests at the end of its innermost `Scoped`.
- **The VM**: the body runs in a `try` of its own; at its end the `try`
  is closed and the resource released, and an error that comes to its
  handler releases and is raised again as it was (`Reraise`). `return`,
  `break` and `continue` release, last made first, the resources they
  leave, after the value of a `return` is worked out; each `try` begun
  inside is closed before the release, so an error in a `release`
  cannot be caught by a `try` already left. One new instruction,
  `Release`, calls `release` unless the variable holds `none`, and
  keeps the place of the error passing through. The variable is found
  where its `let` is, so an inner block that uses the name again does
  not hide it. `Op` is still 12 bytes.
- **C and LLVM**: every way out of a block already frees what the
  block owns (5.8h), and the release goes in front of that, block by
  block, innermost first. The release takes the object out of the
  variable first (`NULL` after), so that it runs once whatever happens
  inside it. In an ordinary build an error jumps over the blocks
  between a `raise` and its `except` (5.5i), so there the body is a
  frame of the kind a `try` has, which keeps the error aside,
  releases, and raises it again unchanged; it costs what a `try`
  costs, and only in a block that owns a resource. A firmware build
  passes errors as values, and needs no frame. Under `zeno test
  --build` the tests run before the last resource of the top is
  released. Nothing in `runtime.c` changed.
- **The fifteen targets** (`lower.rs`): `Scoped` becomes a lowered
  `try` that catches what the program raises, releases, and raises it
  again as it was, with the release also written at the end and at
  each `return`, `break` and `continue` that leaves it. A mistake of
  the program and `program.exit` go past every target's `try`. No new
  lowered statement and no runtime changed: the ones that were there
  are enough.

**Tests.** The checker: each refusal of 59.2, with a collector and
with none, and what is taken; a `Resource` of the program's own; a
program with none is not rewritten; the shape of the rewrite. Both
engines: an error that ends the program releases on its way out and
is reported unchanged; `program.exit` releases nothing; under `zeno
test` the top ends after its last test, and a failed `assert`
releases what its test held. The six builds, against the interpreter
and the VM, with no block left with no collector: `return` from inside
a `try`, `break` and `continue` from inner blocks and a `match`, a
resource held as `Resource`, a name used again in an inner block, an
inner function written after the `let` and called above it, a
`release` that catches its own error, an uncaught error reported
unchanged after the releases; and in `zeno test --build` a failed
`assert`, one inside a `try`, an error raised by a test, and the top
of the file released after the last test. Every engine and build:
[`tools/targets/edge-resource.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-resource.zeno)
prints a line from each `release` on every way out: the end, `return`
with a value that uses the resource, `break`, `continue`, a loop that
makes one each turn, an error through two blocks that each own one,
an error caught inside, two in one block, one given away, handed back,
taken by a parameter, moved by `let`, given away on one path of an
`if` and of a `match`, a name used again inside, and one at the top
of the file.

### 59.5 What a resource still leaves out

- **A resource in a field, a list, a dict, `or none`, a case of an
  enum, or as a type parameter** (59.2). An `owned class` that holds a
  resource would release it when the class is freed, which the
  compilers could do and the other engines could not.
- **Several values that hold one** (item 10).
- **A `var`.** Giving it a new value would release the old one, at a
  line where nothing is written.
- **A release that raises.**

### 59.6 A file read and written in pieces: `files.Reader` and `files.Writer`

```zeno
import files

let source = files.read_from("big.log")
let errors = files.write_to("errors.log")

for line in source {
    if line.find("error") is not none {
        errors.write(line + "\n")
    }
}
```

| Written | Gives |
|---|---|
| `files.read_from(path)` | a `files.Reader`, at the start of the file |
| `files.write_to(path)` | a `files.Writer` on a new, empty file, as `files.write` begins one |
| `files.append_to(path)` | a `files.Writer` at the end of the file, made if it is not there, as `files.append` |
| `reader.read_line()` | the next line without its line end, or `none` after the last (6.17, 6.18) |
| `reader.read_bytes(count)` | up to `count` bytes as a `list[u8]`: fewer at the end, none after it |
| `for line in reader` | each line in turn (59.7) |
| `writer.write(text)`, `writer.write_bytes(bytes)` | writes, and adds no line end (6.13) |

All of them but `for` raise `FileError`, with the messages of `files.read`
and `files.write`: ``there is no file `big.log` ``, ``cannot read
`big.log` ``, ``cannot write `errors.log` ``, and ``` `big.log` does not
hold text ``` for a line that is not UTF-8 or holds a zero byte, which is
what `files.read` says of such a file. A Reader and a Writer are
resources (59.1): the file is closed when the owner ends. There is no
`close`, which is what 6.12 wanted of an open file: nothing to forget.

**Why three functions and two types**, and not `open(path, "r")`: 12.2
of the plan. A wrong letter is found when the program runs, and reading
from a file opened for writing is a mistake the checker finds.

**Written in Zeno, over six small built-ins** (plan, Changes 20). The two
classes are in `library/files.zeno`, as `owned class Reader is Resource`
and `owned class Writer is Resource`, with `read_line`, `read_bytes`,
`write` and `write_bytes` as their functions and a `release` that closes
the file. Each holds the number of its open file and its path, both
`private`. So the release, its order, every way out of a block and every
engine and target come from 59.1 with nothing new. What asks the
machine is six built-ins beside `files.read`, one for each thing done
to an open file: `handle_open(path, how)` gives the number (0 to read,
1 to write from empty, 2 to add to the end), and `handle_line`,
`handle_bytes`, `handle_write`, `handle_write_bytes` and `handle_close`
take it, and the path for their messages. The library gives a program
only the functions it reaches (33), and the six are pieces of the
runtime (56.19), so a program that reads no file in pieces is built as
it was, to the byte.

| | How | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | Two classes in Zeno over six built-ins | **Chosen.** One place for the classes, and the built-ins are small enough to write sixteen times |
| B | Two types built into Zeno, as a `Serial` is | A new type, its methods and its release in the interpreter, the VM, C, LLVM and fifteen runtimes, twice; and a second road for a resource beside 59.1's |

**What a program cannot touch.** Only `read_from`, `write_to` and
`append_to` make one: `files.Reader(3, "x")` is refused, because the
class has private fields (10.2), and so is reading `reader.file`. In C
the number is the address of the open file, so a made-up one would be a
wild address. The six built-ins are callable only from
`library/files.zeno`: to any other file they are names the module does
not have, ``module `files` has no `handle_open` ``, the words a program
would have got before they were there. The checker knows the file a
call is written in (the line of a span says it), and asks it.

**A `write` hands its text to the system before it gives back.** Zeno
holds nothing back for the close: `release` raises nothing (59.1), so
what could not be written at the close would be lost without a word.
So the `write` that meets a full disk raises `FileError` on its own line,
and a program can catch it there (tested with `/dev/full` on Linux). A
writer that gathers its pieces before it writes them is left for later.

**Bytes on every system.** The file is opened as bytes, so a line end is
what 6.17 says, `\n` with a `\r` before it going too, and not what
Windows makes of it. A file written in pieces is the bytes that were
written.

**A count below 0** is a `ValueError`: ``` `read_bytes` was asked for -1
bytes, and a count of bytes is never below 0 ```. It is a value no count
can have, and it is said, rather than taken as 0 (which would hide the
mistake) or as "all of it" (Python's `read(-1)`, a second meaning for a
number). The check is written once, in Zeno, in `read_bytes`.

**On a board** these are the C library's, and a board with no file
system answers `FileError`, as `files.read` does there (6.20).

**The end is where the file ends at that moment** (plan, Changes 24). A
read that found the end looks again the next time: what was written to
the file since, by this program or another, is read. What is there
without a line end is given as a line, as the last line of any file is;
a `"\n"` written after it then ends an empty line. The reader does not
wait for more. Each engine had a rule of its own before: `zeno run`, the
VM and most targets read on, and the C library's `getc` remembers the
end, so every build gave `none` for ever. `clearerr` (C, C++), a seek to
where the stream is (PHP), and no "ended" mark kept beside a buffer (JS,
TS, Dart) make them one. C# opens both kinds shared both ways, so that a
file can be read while a Writer has it, as on every other system.

**With no collector** a line is built in the text room, as `input()`'s
is, so a line longer than the room stops the program with the room's own
message; the bytes of `read_bytes` are a list from the pool.

**An error that nothing catches names `library/files.zeno`**, the line
in the library that called the built-in, and not the program's line
(33.2: an error names where it was raised). It is in `missing.md`.

### 59.7 `for line in reader`

A loop over a dict is given its keys (6.38), and a loop over a reader is
given its lines: it is what everyone writes first, and it holds one line
at a time, where `files.read(path).lines()` holds the file.

It is not a new loop in each engine. The checker finds each `for` over a
`files.Reader`, and `checked` makes it the loop it means, as it makes
the rest of a resource's block a `Scoped` (59.4):

```text
while true {
    let line..next = source.read_line()
    if line..next is none { break }
    let line = line..next
    ...the body...
}
```

No name a program writes has two dots in a row (35.2), so `line..next`
is no one else's. `break` and `continue` mean what they mean in any
`for`. Every engine, build and target runs a `while`, a call and an
`if`, which they all could already.

**A reader that a call gives** has no owner to close it when the loop
ends: `for line in files.read_from(path)` is refused by rule 7 of 59.1,
in words of its own, ``a `for` cannot read from a reader that nothing
keeps: it would be closed at once. Give it a name first, `let source =
files.read_from(path)`, and then write `for line in source` ``. Two names,
`for i, line in source`, are refused: a reader has lines, not places. A
`Writer` cannot be looped over, as before.

**Tests.** Both engines: a file written by `write_to`, `write_bytes` and
`append_to`, read by `read_line`, by `for` with `continue`, and by
`read_bytes` across the end; a count below 0; a missing file; a write to
`/dev/full`, caught at the `write`; each refusal above. Every engine,
build and target:
[`tools/targets/edge-files.zeno`](../tools/targets/edge-files.zeno)
grows a file of a thousand lines with both line ends and none at the
end, read by `for` and by `read_line` and held to `lines()`; a file
opened three times in a row and then removed, which fails on Windows if
the first was not closed; files of every shape of line end; bytes read
in pieces across the end; a writer that adds and one that empties; a
file that is not there, a folder, a missing folder, a line that is not
text and a zero byte.

### 59.20 `files.list(folder)`: the names, sorted by their characters

`files.list("logs")` gives the names of everything in the folder, as a
`list[str]`: files and folders alike, with no `.` and no `..`, and each
name without the folder in front of it. It raises `FileError`, and
every kind of build can catch it, as `files.read` can.

**Sorted, by the numbers of the characters.** A system gives a
folder's names in an order of its own: Linux in the order of a hash on
some disks and of making on others, Windows by name in a way that
ignores case, a board's card in the order the names were written. A
program that prints a listing would print it differently from one
machine to the next, and a test of it could not be written once. So
the list is sorted, and by the one order every engine already has for
text: the order of `<`, which is the order of the numbers of the
characters, and for UTF-8 the order of the bytes. That makes `"10"`
come before `"9"`, `"B"` before `"a"`, and `"😀"` after `"ｚ"`.

**Turned down: the order a person would sort in**, `"9"` before `"10"`
and case put aside. It is not one order: what it does with `"é"`, `"ß"`
or Tamil depends on a language, and the program would print what the
machine's settings say. A program that wants it sorts the list itself.

**Turned down: the system's own order.** It is the reason for the rule.

**Where the languages differ.** Java, Kotlin, C#, Dart and JavaScript
compare text by UTF-16, which puts a character from beyond the first
65,536 (two halves in UTF-16, `0xD800` and up) before one from
`0xE000` to `0xFFFF`, such as `"ｚ"`. Each of those targets sorts with
a comparison of its own that walks characters or bytes, not halves; the others
(Rust, C, C++, Go, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lua) sort bytes or characters,
which is the same order. `tools/targets/edge-folders.zeno` has a name
on each side of that line.

**A name that is not UTF-8 is a `FileError`**: ``the folder `logs`
holds a name that is not text``. Linux lets a name be any bytes but
`/` and zero. Turning such bytes into `�`, as Rust's lossy conversion
does, would give a name that `files.read` cannot open; dropping it
would give a list that is not what is there. Every name in Zeno is
text, so a folder that holds one that is not cannot be listed. The JVM,
.NET and Dart turn the name into text of their own before a program
sees it, so on those four targets it arrives changed. That is said in
`folders.md`, and not mended: there is no way to see the bytes.

**The messages.** Nothing at the path is ``there is no folder `logs` ``;
anything else that stops it, a file at the path or a folder that may
not be read, is ``cannot list the folder `logs` ``. They follow
`files.read`'s two, with "folder" where it says "file".

**An empty path is no folder.** Java takes `""` for the folder the
program runs in, and C's `opendir`, Rust's `read_dir`, Python, Go and
Node do not. Zeno takes the second: ``there is no folder
`` ``, in every engine. `"."` is the folder the program runs in, on
every system.

**What the disk holds, and as `files.read` opens it** (plan, Changes 28).
Zeno lists the names the disk holds. On a disk that does not tell
capitals from small letters, as on Windows and macOS out of the box,
`b` and `B` are one file and one name; the tests use names that differ
by more than case. And a name that `files.list` gives opens its file
when it is handed to `files.read`, on every system. A C or LLVM build
on Windows reads and writes through `fopen`, which takes a name through
the machine's code page; 0.7.0's `files.read` and `files.write` do, and
by 56.19 they stay as they were. So the pieces of `files.list` and
`files.make_folder` take names the same way, with the C library's
`_findfirst64`, `_stat64` and `_mkdir`, and not its wide functions,
which turned a name `files.write` had made into a second, other name:
`é` came back as `Ã©`. A name the code page cannot hold, made by
another program, is listed with question marks; `folders.md` says so.

### 59.21 `files.make_folder(path)`: it worked if there is a folder at the end

`files.make_folder("logs/2026/november")` makes the folder and every
folder above it that is not there, as `mkdir -p`, Python's
`os.makedirs(exist_ok=True)` and Rust's `create_dir_all` do. It gives
nothing, and raises ``cannot make the folder `...` `` as its
`FileError`.

**What counts is the end.** It makes what it can, and then asks
whether there is a folder at the path. A folder that was there already
is no error, so a program can make its folders every time it starts
without asking first. A file in the way, at the path or above it, is
one; so is a folder that may not be written. Asking at the end, not
reading the error of each `mkdir`, gives one answer from every system,
including two programs that make the same folder at once.

**Turned down: an error for a folder that is there**, as plain `mkdir`
gives. Every program would have to ask `exists` first, or catch an
error that means nothing went wrong.

**An empty path fails.** No folder can be made at `""`.

**On a board** there are no folders, and both functions raise their
`FileError` (``cannot list the folder `...` `` and ``cannot make the
folder `...` ``), which a program catches as it catches one from
`files.read`.

### 59.22 `files.join(first, second)`, written in Zeno

`files.join("logs", "today.txt")` is `"logs/today.txt"`. One `/` goes
between the two parts, whatever their ends hold: `join("logs/",
"/today.txt")` is the same. A first part that is empty is no folder,
and the second comes back as it is. Nothing else is changed: `"a//"`
keeps its two, and `..` stays.

**`/` everywhere.** Every system Zeno runs on takes `/` between the
parts of a path, Windows too, so the same path is the same text on
every machine, and a program that prints one prints the same thing.
**Turned down: `\` on Windows**, as Python's `os.path.join` writes. The
output of a program would then depend on the machine it ran on.

**Written in Zeno**, in `library/files.zeno`, as chapter 33 put
`math.hypot` and `random.pick`. It is arithmetic on text, so it is
written once, and every engine, build and target gets it from there.
The file is the first part of a module whose other functions are
built in; it imports `files` to say so, and a program that does not
spell `join` gets none of it.

**Turned down: a `join` of any number of parts.** Zeno has no function
of a count of arguments that is not known; `join(join(a, b), c)` says
it in the words there are.

### 59.23 What is in the runtime, and what was left

**Two pieces of the runtime.** The C of `list` and of `make_folder` is
written into runtime.c as two pieces of decision 56.19,
`ZENO_FILES_LIST` and `ZENO_FILES_MAKE_FOLDER`, each found by its one
function. A program that calls neither is given the runtime it was
given before, to the byte, through C and LLVM alike. Each piece holds
both systems: `opendir` and `mkdir` where there is POSIX, and the wide
functions of Microsoft's C library on Windows, so that a name in Tamil
arrives as UTF-8, as the command line does. A list of
names made in a build with no collector is a list with an owner, as
`files.read_bytes` gives, and its text is freed with it: the test runs
it with 0 blocks left at the end.

`tools/same.py` against the `zeno` of 0.7.0: 6,492 of 6,780 builds the
same and 288 different, which are the 273 that `main` before this part
gave and the 15 builds of the new `edge-folders.zeno`. No program that
was built before is built differently.

**The targets.** Each runtime has both, in its own language's words:
`fs.readdirSync` in JavaScript, `os.listdir` in Python, `Dir.children`
in Ruby, `scandir` in PHP, `os.ReadDir` in Go, `Files.list` on the JVM,
`Directory.EnumerateFileSystemEntries` in C#, `Directory.listSync` in
Dart, `opendir` in C++, `std::fs::read_dir` in Rust and WebAssembly.
Lua itself cannot see into a folder: its runtime uses LuaFileSystem
where it is installed, and `find` and `mkdir -p` where there is a
POSIX shell, and on Windows without LuaFileSystem it raises the
`FileError`. A page has no folders, and leaves out a program that
makes one, as it leaves out one that writes a file.

**Left for later**, as the plan says: removing a folder, and saying
whether a name is a folder (`files.exists` is false for one, which is
enough to tell them apart for now). The Windows half of the C is
built by the trial workflow on Windows, not by the tests on Linux.

## 60. Tools: a message on `assert`, and tests of a compiled program

Item 13 of [`missing.md`](missing.md) is six small tools. Two are
built now: a message on `assert` (13.1 of
[`plan-9-14.md`](plan-9-14.md)) and the same tests run on the
compiled program (13.2). The other four are put off (section 5 of the
plan's changes). Neither changes what a program means: the first is
asked for by a second thing after `assert`, the second by
`zeno test --build`, and a program or a command that does not write
them does what it did.

### 60.1 A message on `assert`

```zeno
test "the board answers a reset" {
    let reply = reset()
    assert reply == Reply.Ack, f"the board answered {reply} to the reset"
}
```

```
FAILED: the board answers a reset
error: the board answered Nak to the reset
this is false. The left of `==` is Nak, and the right is Ack
 --> board.zeno:8:12
```

**The rule.** After the condition of an `assert`, a comma and one
text. When the `assert` fails, the text is printed on a line of its
own above "this is false...", which stays as it was. When it passes,
the text is not worked out.

**Why it is added now.** 10.17 turned it down because the test's name
and the two sides of the comparison already say most of what a
message says, and said it could be added later without changing
anything. What it cannot say is why the values matter: "the board
answered Nak to the reset" names the thing being tested in the
words of the board, which `== Ack` does not. And a condition that is
not a comparison, `assert ring.is_full()`, shows no values at all;
the text is the only way for it to say more than "this is false".

**Why a comma.** It is how Python writes it, so the reader has seen
it. `assert` is a statement and its condition is one expression, so
a comma after the condition can mean nothing else; it is not a list,
and not a call. The ways weighed:

| | Written | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | `assert c, "text"` | **Chosen.** One mark, read one way |
| B | `assert c else "text"` | `else` already begins a block after `if`; here it would begin a value |
| C | `assert(c, "text")` | Reads as a call of a function named `assert`, which the word was reserved to prevent (10.17) |
| D | `assert c` with a comment after it, which a failure prints | A comment that does something is a rule nobody can see |

**It must be text.** An `int` or a list after the comma is refused
with "what an `assert` prints when it fails must be text, but this is
int. Write `assert total == 6, f"the total was {total}"`". An
f-string makes anything text, so nothing is lost, and a message is
never a value shown in a form the reader has to guess.

**Worked out only when it fails.** A passing test does not pay for
building the text, and the text can use what is only there when
something has gone wrong: `f"the reply was {replies[9]}"` in a test
that passes never reads item 9. If working it out raises an error,
the test fails with that error, as any error that leaves a test
fails it (10.17); the line shown is the line of the `assert`.

**One text.** A second comma is refused with "an `assert` prints one
text when it fails. Join the parts into one: ...", and a comma with
nothing after it with "after the comma of an `assert` comes the text
that a failure prints: ...". `assert raises ValueError { }` takes no
text: the failure already says what was expected and what came.

**What is not changed.** The words "this is false..." and where a
failure points. `zeno run` goes past tests, as before. A build leaves
tests out (10.20), and so their messages with them.

**How it is built.** `ast.rs`: `StmtKind::Assert` holds the condition
and an optional text. `parser.rs` reads the comma, `checker.rs` checks
that the text is `str`, `printer.rs` writes it back, and
`Interpreter::assert` works it out after the condition is found false
and puts it above the line it always printed.

### 60.2 Tests of a compiled program: `zeno test --build`

```
$ zeno test --build --firmware board.zeno
board.zeno
  ok      three numbers add up
  FAILED  an empty list adds up to nothing

FAILED: an empty list adds up to nothing
error: an empty list should add up to 0
this is false. The left of `==` is 0, and the right is 1
  --> board.zeno:14:12
   |
14 |     assert total([]) == 1, "an empty list should add up to 0"
   |            ^


2 tests: 1 passed, 1 failed.
```

**The rule.** `zeno test --build` compiles each file with its tests in
it, as `zeno build` would compile it, runs the program, and prints
what `zeno test` prints, line for line. It takes what a build takes
that still makes a program that checks itself: `--firmware`,
`--no-collector`, `--llvm`, `--release`, `--pool`, `--text-room`,
`--memory` and `--board`. `--fast` and `--minimal` leave out checks a
test may be written to meet, and `--web` and `--target` make no program
that this computer runs, so each is refused with that reason. With no
`--build`, `zeno test` is what it was, and so is every build: a
program that is not built for its tests has not one line of C more.

**Why.** `zeno test` runs the tests in the interpreter. The program
that goes onto a board is the one C or LLVM makes of it, with no
collector, errors as values, numbers of a fixed width and the
runtime's own text and floats (chapter 53). 0.7.0 checks that the two
agree by running each example both ways (the rule of chapter 5), but a
test the user writes was never run in the build it is for. A test
that shares a list is now refused with no collector, as the program
would be, and a test that passes in the interpreter and fails in the
build says where the two part.

**Each test becomes a function at the end of its file.** Before the
checker, each test of the first file becomes a function with no
parameters that may raise any error, written after the file's last
statement (`with_tests` in `src/test_build.rs`). At the end it sees
every variable of the file, as a test does, and is checked by the
checker with the rules of the build, and compiled by each compiler as
any other function: nothing in the compilers learns what a test is
but `assert`. Its name, `test 1`, has a space in it, so no program can
write it or call it. The tests of an imported file are left out, as
`zeno test` leaves them out. `--only` takes its tests out before the
checker, so a test that is not run is not built.

**A failed `assert` leaves the test as `return` does.** It writes its
report, and then takes the road each build already has out of a
`try` and past what must be freed. There is no new road, no block is
left, and no `except` catches it, as none catches it in `zeno test`
(10.17). An error that leaves a test, raised or not caught, is caught
where `main` calls the test: in an ordinary build by the `try` of
setjmp that `try` uses, in a firmware build by the `false` the test
gives back (5.5).

**An `assert` in a function written inside a test is refused.** The
parser takes it, and `zeno test` runs it, as 0.7.0 did. But the
`return` of a failed `assert` would leave that function and not the
test, and a firmware build has no other way out of a function whose
type says it raises nothing; making one for this would be a second
kind of error. So `zeno test --build` refuses it with "under `zeno
test --build` an `assert` stands in the test itself, and not in a
function written inside it. Let the function give back what it found,
and `assert` that in the test". It is a refusal of this command, not
of `zeno build`, which leaves tests out (10.20); it is written in
`docs/testing.md` beside the table of what every build refuses.

**The reports wait in a room of 8 KB.** `zeno test` prints the line of
each test as it runs, and the reports of the failures under them. So
does the program: a failure writes its report into a static array of
8 KB, and the reports are printed after the last test. The room
exists only in a test build, and asks nothing of the pool, so it
works with no collector and on a board, where there is no `malloc`. A
