report that does not fit is left out whole, never cut, and counted;
one line says how many were left out and that `zeno test` shows them
all. 8 KB is some forty reports of the usual five lines; a board with
less RAM than that is not one a test program is run on.

**The command counts by marks, not by the number the program ends
with.** A program that an error or a fault stops already ends with 1,
and `program.exit` can end it with any number, so "ended with 1"
could mean one failed test, a fault, or neither. Instead the command
gives the program the name of a file in `ZENO_TEST_MARKS`, and the
program writes a mark there when its tests begin, one as each test
ends, passed or failed, and one when they are all over, each written
through at once. The command adds them up. With no mark of beginning
the program stopped before its tests, and the command says "board.zeno
stopped with this error before its tests. None of them was run.", as
`zeno test` does. With no mark of the end it stopped in a test, which
is counted as failed and named, and the command says how many after it
were not run. Nothing the program prints is read for its meaning, so
no line a program prints can be taken for a result. The program still
ends with 1 if a test failed and 0 if none did, for a script that
runs it.

**Run by itself, it says its own totals.** On a board, or run by hand,
nothing gives the program a file of marks, and it prints the line of
totals for its file itself. A program stopped before its last test,
by a fault or by `program.exit`, prints the reports it holds before
it ends, where the platform has a moment for that (`atexit` on a
computer), so a fault in the fifth test does not cost the reports of
the first four.

**A report shows the line, in whatever file.** An error that leaves a
test is shown at the line that raised it, which may be in an imported
file. A test build holds the text of every file of the program, as
strings of C, and looks the line up; the report is the one `zeno test`
prints, with the caret under the place and the note. On a board that
text costs flash, in a test build only: the fifteen lines of
`board.zeno` above are 286 bytes of it.

**A board.** `zeno test --build --board boards/qemu-cortex-m3
board.zeno` writes `board-tests.c` and builds `board-tests.elf` beside
it, as `zeno build --board` does (51.5), and says the command that
runs it. The tests run there, by whoever has the board, and the
program prints the same lines through the board's `zeno_board_print`
(chapter 52). Built and run so on QEMU's Cortex-M3, the program above
prints what `zeno test` prints and ends with 1.

**Where it differs from `zeno test`, on purpose.**

| | `zeno test` | `zeno test --build` |
|---|---|---|
| A fault of a firmware build: an index out of range, an overflow | the test fails, and the next runs | the program stops, as any firmware program does (5.5l); the command names the test it was in and how many were not run |
| `program.exit` in a test | the test fails | the program ends; the command says so as for a fault |
| An error before the tests | the snippet of the line | the compiled program's own message for an error nothing caught |
| A `try` that nothing in it can raise into, in a firmware build | runs | refused, as in any firmware program (5.5) |
| An `assert` in a function written in a test | runs | refused (above) |

**How it is built.** `src/test_build.rs` makes the tests functions,
refuses an `assert` in a function, and holds the part of the runtime
that only a test build has. It is text of the test build, and not a
piece of `src/runtime.c` (56.19), so nothing of it can reach another
program. `emit_c.rs` and `emit_llvm.rs` each compile `assert` and
`assert raises` in a test function (an `assert` that is not in one is
nothing, as before), call each test after the program's statements,
and end `main` with what `zeno_tests_end` gives back. `main.rs` reads
`--build`, builds the program in a folder of its own, runs it with
`ZENO_TEST_MARKS` set, and reads the marks.

**Left for later.** An `assert` in a function written in a test; a
fault that fails its test and goes on, which needs a way back from a
fault that a firmware build does not have; and reading the totals back
from a board, which needs the board's serial port read by the command.

## 61. Another language's code in a Zeno file: `inline` blocks

Partha asked whether Zeno should be a superset of the big languages,
so that their code could be pasted into a Zeno program. The answer
agreed on was no, and this chapter is what is built in its place: a
block that holds another language's code as it was written, which the
program calls. [`inline.md`](inline.md) is the walkthrough.

```zeno
import c

let bits = inline c {
    #include <stdint.h>

    int ones(uint32_t x) {
        int count = 0;
        for (; x != 0; x &= x - 1) {
            count++;
        }
        return count;
    }
}

print(bits.ones(0xA5))
```

Nothing here changes a program that has no block. A block is asked
for twice, by the word `inline` and by the `import` of its language,
and `tools/same.py` shows the rest (61.18).

### 61.1 A block, and not a superset

**The rule.** Zeno is not a superset of any language. Code of another
language goes in a block, is built or run by that language's own
compiler, and is called through the bridge Zeno already has to it.

**Why not a superset.** A superset has to take every program of the
other language for ever, with every mistake that language allows, so
the first thing given up would be the checks Zeno exists for: an
`int` that cannot overflow quietly, a name that cannot be `none`
unseen. A superset of two languages cannot exist at all where they
disagree: `a / b`, `{}`, `'x'` and `x = y` each mean something else
in C, Python and JavaScript. And a superset of one language makes
Zeno a dialect of it. TypeScript is JavaScript with types and can
never fix JavaScript's `==`; C++ carried C's every rule for forty
years.

**What a block gives in its place.** The same result for the person
who has code already written: the code is used as it is, today, and
not rewritten. It costs Zeno one new form and no new meaning: a block
is a value, and that value is one the language had (a library of C,
a module of Python or of Node).

| | The way | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | Zeno as a superset of C, or of several languages | Turned down, above |
| B | The other language's code only in its own files, used through `c.library("crc.c", ...)` and `python.module` | Works today, and stays. But ten lines of C want a file, a second list of declarations, and a reader who opens both |
| C | A block in the `.zeno` file | **Chosen.** The code sits beside the lines that call it |
| D | A converter that rewrites the code as Zeno | Built next, as `zeno convert`. It cannot take everything, and what it cannot take it leaves in a block, so it needs C first |

### 61.2 How a block is written

**The rule.** `let name = inline c {`, the code on the lines below,
further in, and a line that holds only `}`. The word after `inline`
is the language, and is the name of the module its `import` gives.

**Why these words.** `inline` says what is done: the code is in the
line of the program, and not in a file beside it. C, C++ and Rust
programmers know the word for assembly written in the middle of C,
which is the same idea. The language's word is the one the program
already wrote in its `import`, so there is one name for each language
and not two (`node`, and not `js` here and `node` there). The braces
are Zeno's own, as for every other block of the language.

| | Written | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | `let bits = inline c { ... }` | **Chosen** |
| B | `c { ... }` or `c.inline { ... }` | A name and a `{` begins nothing else in Zeno, and `c` may be a variable. The reader could not tell a block from a mistake |
| C | `c.code("""...""")`, a text given to a function | The text would be Zeno's: its `\n` and `{x}` would be read by Zeno first, and C's `"\n"` has to be written `"\\n"`. Pasted code would have to be edited, which is what a block is for avoiding |
| D | `extern "C" { ... }`, as C++ and Rust write it | There it declares what is elsewhere. Here the code is the thing itself |
| E | `@c` on the line above, or a comment that does something | A mark that changes what the next lines are is easy to miss, and a comment that runs is a rule nobody can see (60.1, D) |
| F | Text between three backticks, as in a page of Markdown | Nothing else in Zeno is written so, and a block has no name to be called through |

### 61.3 Where a block ends, and why Zeno does not read inside it

**The rule.** The first line ends with the `{`. Every line of the
block is further in than that first line. The block ends at a line
that holds only `}`, as far in as the first line. What is between is
not read as Zeno at all.

**Why indentation ends it.** To find the `}` that closes a block by
counting braces, Zeno would have to know what a brace inside a string
or a comment looks like in each language: `"}"`, `'}'`, `/* } */`,
`// }`, `# }`, a template of JavaScript between backticks with
`${...}` inside it, a regular expression `/}/`, a raw string of
Python. That is a small lexer for each language, each wrong somewhere,
and the mistake it makes is the worst kind: the block ends early and
the rest of the other language's code is read as Zeno, with messages
about lines that are fine.

A line that holds only `}` at the first line's own indentation can be
found with no knowledge of the other language. Code in a block is
indented anyway, so a `}` of the other language is always further in.
The rule can be said in one sentence and seen with the eye.

| | How the end is found | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | A line holding only `}`, as far in as the opening line | **Chosen** |
| B | Counting `{` and `}` | Wrong for a brace in a string or a comment, above |
| C | Counting them with a lexer for each language | Three lexers to keep right, and a fourth for each language added |
| D | A word the writer picks, as a shell's `<<END` | Never wrong, but a new form for the reader, and the writer has to pick a word |
| E | Indentation alone, with no `}` | Zeno's blocks end with `}`. One that did not would be the only one |

**A line that is not further in is a mistake**, and is not taken for
the end: "this line of the `inline c` block is not further in than
the line that opens the block. Everything in the block is indented,
and the block ends at a line that holds only `}`, as far in as the
line that opened it". An empty line is allowed anywhere. A block with
no such closing line is refused with "this `inline c` block has no
end...", at the line that opened it.

**This is the one place where indentation means something in Zeno.**
It was weighed against "the entire language must be unambiguous": the
rule has one reading, a mistake against it is refused and not
guessed at, and `zeno format` keeps to it. The other ways each have a
case that reads two ways.

### 61.4 `inline` is not a reserved word

**The rule.** `inline` begins a block only where it is followed by a
name, a `{`, and the end of the line. Everywhere else it is a name,
as before: `let inline = 3` means what it meant.

**Why.** A reserved word is taken from every program that used it as
a name, and 0.9.0 is not allowed to change what a program of 0.8.0
means. A name, another name and `{` at the end of a line is nothing
in Zeno today (two names side by side are always refused), so no
program that was accepted can be read otherwise now. That is the test
of 11.6.

The lexer looks ahead to the end of the line to decide. It is the one
place it looks further than two characters, and it has to be the
lexer: what follows is not made of Zeno's tokens.

### 61.5 A block is the whole value of a `let`

**The rule.** `let name = inline c {`. Not `var`, not `const`, not an
argument, not part of a larger expression. It may be at the top of a
file, in a function, or in a test.

**Why a `let`.** What a block gives never changes, so `var` would
promise something that cannot happen, and is refused with "an
`inline` block is the value of a `let`. What it gives never changes".
A `const` is a value known when the program is checked, which a
module of Python is not.

**Why the whole value.** `print(inline c {` ... `}.f(1))` would put
many lines of another language in the middle of a line of Zeno, with
the end of the Zeno line after the block's `}`, and rule 61.3 could
not hold. With a name, the block is in one place and its uses in
another, each readable alone.

**Why in a function too.** A helper used by one function reads best
there. The block is still made once: under `zeno run` the first time
the line is reached, and in a build it is part of the program's C
wherever it was written.

### 61.6 Which languages have a block

**The rule.** `inline c`, `inline python`, `inline node`. Any other
word is refused with a message that names the three and says what to
do in its place.

| Language | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| C | **A block** | The most code already written, and all of a board's. It is also what `zeno build` writes, so a block of C costs a built program nothing |
| Python | **A block** | The most used language, with a library for everything. Zeno is not for firmware only |
| JavaScript, through Node | **A block** | The same, and the code of every web page |
| Assembly | No block of its own: inside a block of C (61.15) | It has no types, and it is a different language on every processor |
| C++ | No block | A built program is one file of C given to one C compiler (44.12). A block of C++ would need a second compiler in every build, and a way across for classes, templates and exceptions, which C does not have. C++ with `extern "C"` goes to `c.library` |
| Rust, Go | No block | Neither can be built from ten lines: each wants a project, its own build tool and minutes. Their libraries are used through `import c` (44.6) |
| Java | No block | A class needs `javac` and a file named after it. `import java` uses a jar |
| TypeScript | No block | Node does not run it everywhere yet. Its JavaScript is what `inline node` takes |
| Ruby, PHP, Lua, C# | Later | Each has its `import` already (chapters 37 to 40), and a block is the same few lines for each. Left until someone asks, since each is a language to test on three systems |

**Why `inline node` and not `inline js`.** The block is a module of
Node, with `require` and `exports`, and runs in the Node that
`import node` starts. `js` would promise a browser's JavaScript too.
`inline js`, `inline javascript`, `inline py` and `inline asm` are
each answered by name.

### 61.7 A block needs the `import` of its language

**The rule.** A file with `inline c` and no `import c` is refused:
"an `inline c` block needs `import c` at the top of the file. The
import is what asks for the other language, and a file with no such
line uses none".

**Why.** The first lines of a file say everything it needs from
outside Zeno. A reader who sees no `import python` there knows the
file runs with no Python on the machine, and that has been true since
the first bridge (26.11). A block that brought the language in by
itself, from line 200, would end that. It is also the opt-in rule of
this project: a feature is asked for by a word the program writes,
and here by two.

### 61.8 What a block of C gives

**The rule.** A library of C, the type `c.library` gives. Its
functions are the ones written out in the block, with a body, that
are not `static`. Each is typed from its own first line. Everything
else in the block is the block's own: a `static` function, a
variable, a `#define`, a `typedef`, a `struct`.

**Why the same type.** Everything chapter 44 decided then holds with
nothing said twice: how a number is checked to fit, how a list is
lent for a pointer, what a `const` means, what is refused. There is
one table of how values go across, in [`c.md`](c.md), and a reader
who knows `c.library` knows a block.

**Why nothing is declared.** `c.library` is given declarations
because a library that is already built says nothing about its
functions. A block has the functions themselves, and their first
lines are the declarations. Asking for them again would be the same
words twice, and the second copy would one day disagree with the
first.

**Why `static` is the way to keep a function to the block.** It is
what C itself means by the word: a function no other file can see.
Nothing new is learned, and code pasted from a `.c` file that was
written well already says it.

| | Which functions Zeno sees | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | Every function with a body that is not `static` | **Chosen** |
| B | Only those listed after the block, or marked with a comment | A second list to keep right |
| C | Every function, `static` or not | A helper that takes a struct by value would refuse the whole block |

**A function Zeno cannot call that is not `static` is refused**, with
the reason `c.library` gives and one more sentence: "In an `inline c`
block, a function that only the block calls is marked `static`, and
Zeno leaves it alone". It is not passed over quietly: a function
that is there and cannot be called would be found only at the call,
with a worse message. A block with nothing to call is refused with
"this `inline c` block has no function that Zeno can call...".

**How the functions are found.** `bridge_c::block_declarations` goes
through the block once at the level of C's top: it steps over
comments, strings, lines that begin with `#`, and bodies between
braces, and keeps the first line of each function, the `typedef`s and
the `struct`s. What it keeps is given to the reader of declarations
that `c.library` has, so both are read by one piece of code. Unlike
61.3, this reads C, and has to: but a mistake here cannot move the
end of the block. The worst it can do is refuse a block or miss a
function, and both are said in a message.

### 61.9 What `zeno run` does with a block of C

**The rule.** The block is built once into a small library by the C
compiler of the machine, kept in the folder for what can be made
again, and called through the helper that `import c` uses. It is
built again when its text changes. `zeno run --vm` and `zeno test` do
the same.

**Why through the helper.** It is what `c.library("crc.c", ...)`
does, and it keeps the other language's mistakes out of `zeno`: a
block that writes through a bad pointer stops the helper, and Zeno
says "C stopped while Zeno was waiting for its answer" at the call
(44.4). Building the block into `zeno` itself would be faster for
each call and would let a block damage the interpreter.

### 61.10 What `zeno build` does with a block of C

**The rule.** Every build that writes C writes the block into the
program's C, as it was written, after the runtime and before the
program's own functions. A call of one of its functions is a call of
C in the same file. Before the block is `#line N "file.zeno"`, and
after it `#line K "program.c"`.

**Why in the same file.** It is the least there can be: no library
beside the program, no second step of building, nothing between the
call and the function, and the C compiler may put a small function in
line. For firmware that is the whole point: a few instructions that
must be C or assembly, on the board, with no cost.

**Why `#line`.** A mistake in the block is found by the C compiler
when the program is built. Without the mark it would name a line of
the program's C, five thousand lines down a file the writer never
opened. With it, the message names the line of the `.zeno` file, and
so does a debugger. The second `#line` gives the lines after the
block back to the C file.

**What a block can clash with.** The block is in one file with the
runtime and the program, so a name of the block could be one of
theirs. Zeno's own names begin with `zeno_` or `z_`, and the C
compiler refuses a clash with a message that names both lines. A
block can use the headers it includes, and those the runtime included
before it.

**All of them.** `zeno build`, `--firmware`, `--no-collector`,
`--owned`, `--minimal`, `--release`, `--fast`, `--board`, and
`zeno test --build`. `examples/bits.zeno` prints the same from each.

### 61.11 What refuses a block

**The rule.** Where a block cannot work, it is an error with the line
of the block. A block is never skipped.

| | `inline c` | `inline python`, `inline node` |
|---|---|---|
| `zeno build`, and every build that writes C | built in | refused: a built program is C, and has no Python or Node inside it |
| `zeno check --strict` | checked | refused: what the block gives is known only when the program runs |
| `zeno build --llvm` | refused | refused |
| `zeno build --target ...` | refused | refused |
| The playground | refused | refused |

**Why refused and not left out.** A program that built with its block
missing would fail at the first call, or worse, build to something
that does something else. Each of these already refuses the `import`
(44.8, 26.11), so a block there was refused before it was read; the
messages for the block itself are for the cases the import passes.

**`--llvm`.** The LLVM build writes IR, and C cannot be pasted into
IR. It could compile the block with clang and link the two; that is
left for later with the rest of `import c` under `--llvm` (44.10).

### 61.12 A block that cannot be started stops the program

**The rule.** A block of C that does not compile, or a block of
Python or JavaScript with a mistake that stops it from starting, ends
the program with what the other language said. No `try` catches it,
and a function with a block in it needs no `raises`.

**Why not an error to catch.** An error that can be caught is for
what may go differently next time: a file that is not there, a text
that is not a number. A block that does not compile will not compile
next time either. It is a mistake in the program, as a misspelt word
of Zeno is, and those are never caught. If it were an error, every
function with a block would need `raises`, to name something its
caller can do nothing about.

**When it is found.** In a build, when the program is built. Under
`zeno run`, when the line of the block is reached, and not before:
`zeno check` does not start a C compiler or Python, and stays as
quick as it was. What `zeno check` does find, for C, is everything
about the calls: a function that is not there, an argument of the
wrong type, too few arguments.

### 61.13 A block of Python is a module

**The rule.** The block gives a module of Python: what `python.module`
would give if the lines were a `.py` file. It runs once, top to
bottom, when the program reaches it. An error in it names the
`.zeno` file and the line there.

**How.** `inline.rs` makes an empty module with Python's own
`types.ModuleType`, compiles the text with `compile`, and runs it in
the module with `exec`. The text is given as many empty lines in
front as the `.zeno` file has above the block, and the file's own
path, so the line numbers Python counts are the file's. Nothing was
added to the helper of chapter 26: a block is made with the calls a
Zeno program could have written itself.

**Why the shared indentation is taken off.** Python reads
indentation, and a block is indented because it is in a block. The
indentation every line shares is the block's and not the program's
(61.16); each line keeps how far in it is from the others.

### 61.14 A block of JavaScript is a module of Node

**The rule.** The block gives what it puts in `exports`, or gives
`module.exports`. It is a module as a `.js` file is: it has
`require`, which finds packages from the folder of the `.zeno` file,
and `__filename`.

**Why a module of the older kind.** Node makes one from a text with
one call. A module with `import` and `export` can only be made from a
file or an address, and what it exports is given later, through a
promise. The older kind is what `require` gives, which is what
`node.module` uses (chapter 28). A block that writes `import` is told so by
Node.

### 61.15 Assembly

**The rule.** There is no `inline asm`. Assembly is written inside a
block of C, as the C compiler takes it, and a whole file of assembly
is given to `c.library` beside the `.c` files (`.s`, and `.S` for one
with `#include` lines).

**Why no block of its own.** A block gives functions, and a function
needs types for what it takes and gives. Assembly has none, so each
routine would need a declaration of C written beside it anyway; with
the assembly inside a C function, the function is the declaration.
Assembly is also not one language. Each processor has its own
instructions, and GCC, Clang, IAR and Keil each write them their own
way. The C compiler of the board already knows both, and Zeno would
have to learn them.

**What it costs.** One line more than a block of its own would: the
C function's first line. It gains the registers the compiler picks
for the arguments, and `static inline` if the writer wants it.

### 61.16 The indentation a block's lines share is not part of it

**The rule.** The spaces that every line of a block begins with are
taken off before the other language is given the text. A line the C
compiler names is the line of the `.zeno` file. A column it names is
counted from where the block's lines begin.

**Why.** For Python the rule has no choice (61.13). For C and
JavaScript the other way was weighed: giving C the lines as they are
in the file, spaces and all, so that columns are the file's too. But
then a text of C that runs over a line with `\`, or a template of
JavaScript over several lines, would have the block's indentation
inside it, and would change when `zeno format` moved the block. A
column that is four less is seen at once, since the compiler shows
the line; a text with four spaces more in it is not. One rule for
three languages is also easier to say than one and an exception.

### 61.17 The formatter

**The rule.** `zeno format` leaves every line of a block as it was,
and moves the block as one piece: its lines begin one step in from
the line that opens it, and its `}` is under that line.

**Why.** The formatter lays out Zeno, and the text of a block is not
Zeno. It can only move the block with its line, and it must, or a
block in a function that was itself moved in would break rule 61.3.

### 61.18 Nothing changes for a program with no block

`tools/same.py` built the 481 programs it had before this chapter
(every example, every program of `tools/targets/`, every sample of
the book that runs, the benchmarks) fifteen ways each with 0.8.0 and
with this compiler: 7215 builds, the same to the byte. The two new
examples are the only programs that differ, and 0.8.0 refuses both.

`inline` is still a name (61.4), no module was added, and nothing of
the runtime was touched.

### 61.19 Left for later

- **A library for a block of C**: a block that needs `-lz` has nowhere
  to say so, and goes in a `.c` file given to `c.library` until it
  has.
- **A constant of a block**: a `#define` or a variable is not seen by
  Zeno. `c.library` can declare a value (44.11).
- **Blocks of Ruby, PHP, Lua and C#** (61.6).
- **`zeno build --llvm`** with a block of C (61.11).
- **Colours inside a block in the editor**: the VS Code and Vim
  files colour a block as its language where the editor has that
  language; the playground does not.
- What `c.library` leaves for later is left here too: a function of
  Zeno given to C, a struct by value, small types given back as
  themselves.

**How it is built.** `token.rs`: `TokenKind::Inline` holds the
language and the text. `lexer.rs`, `inline_block`: decides (61.4),
reads the lines (61.3), takes off the shared indentation (61.16).
`parser.rs`: `ExprKind::Inline`, only as the value of a `let`.
`checker.rs`, `inline`: the import (61.7), and for C the library, by
`bridge_c::library_of_block`. `bridge_c.rs`: `block_declarations`
(61.8), and `Block`, which says where a block was written and writes
its `#line`s. `inline.rs`: what `zeno run` does (61.9, 61.12 to
61.14). `emit_c.rs`: `c_libraries` writes the block and
`with_blocks_placed` its line numbers (61.10). `emit_llvm.rs` and
`lower.rs` refuse (61.11). `format.rs`, `block` (61.17).

## 62. A file of Python written again as Zeno: `zeno convert`

Partha asked for converters that write another language's code as
Zeno, with Python first and then C, as the second half of what chapter
61 began: a block holds code as it was written, and a converter
rewrites it. [`convert.md`](convert.md) is the walkthrough.

```sh
zeno convert shop.py       # writes shop.zeno, and says what it did
```

Nothing here changes what any other command does. `convert` is a new
command, and a program of Zeno is compiled as it was (62.20).

### 62.1 One promise: never silently wrong

**The rule.** What the converter writes runs, and prints what the
Python printed, but for what a `# convert:` comment says. What it
cannot write so, it does not write: it keeps that piece as Python.

**Why.** A converter that writes most of a program well and a few lines
wrongly is worse than none. The person who reads its Zeno trusts it,
and a wrong line found a month later costs more than the whole
conversion saved. With the block of chapter 61, the converter never
has to guess: there is always a way to write what it cannot read,
which is to leave it as it was.

| | The way | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A | Write everything, as well as it can be guessed, and mark the guesses | Turned down: a mark that is not read is a wrong program |
| B | Refuse a file with anything it cannot read | Turned down: nearly every real file has one line it cannot read |
| C | Write what is sure, keep the rest in an `inline python` block that the Zeno calls | **Chosen** |

### 62.2 Inside `zeno`, written by hand

**The rule.** `zeno convert` is part of the `zeno` program. It reads
Python with a reader of its own (`convert_python.rs`), with no library
and no Python.

**Why.** Zeno has no dependencies (5.1, 5.2), and a converter that
needed Python's own `ast` module would need a Python of the right
version to convert, where the result needs one only for what is kept.
A reader of its own also knows exactly what it read: a construct it
does not know is a piece it keeps, with that as the reason, and not an
error deep in a tree it did not make.

**Not chosen.** A separate program, or a repository of its own: the
converter writes what Zeno's checker must take, and is checked by it
in the same process (62.9), so it belongs with the checker.

### 62.3 Pieces: the statements at the left margin

**The rule.** The file is cut into pieces, each a statement that begins
at the left margin with all that belongs to it. Each piece is written
as Zeno, or as Zeno with a note, or kept whole.

**Why.** A piece is what a reader of Python sees as one thing: a
function, a class, a loop, a line. Keeping one whole keeps its meaning,
since nothing inside it is changed. A finer cut (one statement of a
function in Zeno and the next in Python) would need the two sides to
share the function's local variables, which they cannot.

### 62.4 What is kept goes into one block, in the place it ran

**The rule.** One `inline python` block, named `py` (or `kept`, ...
if the file has that name). A kept `import`, `def` or `class` goes at
the top of it and the Zeno reaches it as `py.name`. A kept piece that
does something becomes `def convert_step_N():` with `global` for what
it gives a value, and the Zeno calls `py.convert_step_N()` where the
piece was. `if __name__ == "__main__":` in kept text is `if True:`.

**Why.** A program's lines run in order, and a kept loop must run
between the lines of Zeno above and below it. A function of the block,
called there, does exactly that. One block, and not one for each
piece, because the kept pieces share their names, as they did in the
file.

### 62.5 Types from the program itself

**The rule.** The converter learns each type from what the program
does: what a function is given at its calls, what it gives back, what
goes into a list, a dict, a field. It goes over the whole file in
rounds until a round learns nothing new, twelve at most. In the last
round a type still not known is a reason to keep the piece.

**Why.** Most Python has no types written. A function's parameters
are known from its calls, and those may be further down the file, and
a list's items from an `append` in another function, so one pass in
order cannot know them. A type written in the Python (`-> int`, `x:
float`) is used where there is one, and checked against what the
program does.

**What a variable of Zeno needs.** One type. A name that holds a whole
number and later a float is a float from its first value, with a note
(62.10); a name that holds a text and a number is kept.

### 62.6 What crosses between the two sides

**The rule.** A number, a text, a bool and `none` cross to the block
and back. A value of Python's own stays in Python, and Zeno holds it
as a handle. A list or a dict of Zeno goes to Python only if it is
written out in the call, held by nothing else.

**Why.** The bridge copies a list of Zeno into Python (`python.md`).
A copy of a list that the Zeno holds would not show what Python did to
it, and a later line of Zeno would read the old one. A list written in
the call has no other holder, so its copy is as good as it.

### 62.7 What a kept piece needs is kept with it

**The rule.** A piece that gives a value to a name a kept piece reads
is kept too, if the kept piece can run after it: it is further down
the file, or it is a function or a class, which run when called. A
piece that gives a value to a name that a kept function or class
defines is kept too, and so is one that gives a value to a name a kept
piece gives one, if a function of Zeno reads that name. An `import` of
a module Zeno has words for, and a name given one fixed value once in
the file, are written on both sides.

**Why.** Python can only call Python, and a variable lives on one
side. The order matters: a kept piece above a line of Zeno can never
read what that line gives, so it does not pull the line into Python.
Without that, one kept line near the end of a long file used to pull
in every piece above it that shared a name with it.

### 62.8 A name both sides give values

**The rule.** Where a kept piece and a piece of Zeno both give values
to a name, it is a variable on each side. The plan of the file checks
that every line of Zeno that reads the name after the kept piece reads
a value Zeno gave it after the kept piece, for certain: a line above
it in the same block or further out. A `try` whose every `except`
leaves (`continue`, `return`, `raise`, `break`) and reads nothing the
`try` gives counts as run whole. A line that may read the kept value
is kept, with "may still hold here the value that the piece at line N
gave it".

**The variable of a kept loop.** A kept `for` whose variable is read
only inside the loop, and by no function, has that variable for its
own, as a `for` of Zeno does. A loop of Zeno elsewhere with the same
name has nothing to do with it.

**Why.** Two loops with a variable `name`, one kept, are the usual
case in a real file, and are not one variable in any sense the program
uses. The check is what makes it safe to say so.

### 62.9 One piece kept at a time, and Zeno's checker has the last word

**The rule.** When some pieces cannot be written, one is kept: the
first whose reason is its own and not "the type is not known". Then
everything is done again. When every piece is written, the whole file
is read by Zeno's own lexer, parser and checker, in the same process;
a piece whose lines it refuses is kept, with the checker's message as
the reason. If a refused line belongs to no piece, the whole file is
kept as one block.

**Why one at a time.** What one piece cannot be written for is often
what another became: a name holds a function because the line that
gives it one is a `lambda`, and that line is kept; a type is not known
because a value came from the block. Keeping every failing piece at
once kept pieces for a reason that was gone a moment later. The rounds
are fast, and a file of 250 lines with a dozen kept pieces converts in
well under a second.

**Why the checker.** The converter writes text, and Zeno's checker is
the only thing that knows for certain what Zeno takes. Nothing it
refuses is given out.

### 62.10 Notes, once for each kind

**The rule.** Where Zeno runs the line and does what the Python did
but prints or raises a little otherwise, a `# convert:` comment says
so, above the first line of that kind. The report lists every line of
every kind. The kinds: a value shown Zeno's way; a very large or very
small float written otherwise; an error message in Zeno's words; an
`except` that also catches what only Zeno raises; `upper` and `lower`
on a to z only; `math.round` and a half; a variable that is a float
from its first value.

**Why once.** A comment on every `print` of a list would bury the
program. The report has every line for the person who wants them.

**Why these are notes and not kept.** Each is a difference a person
expects of a new language and can see at once, and none changes what
the program computes. Keeping every `print` of a list as Python would
keep most programs whole.

### 62.11 What Python has and Zeno has not, written once as Zeno

**The rule.** `sorted`, `list.remove`, `split` with a number and a
text times a number become calls of small functions of Zeno, written
once at the top of a file that uses them, each with a comment: `sorted`,
`remove_item`, `split_at_most`, `repeated`. A file that has a name the
same as one keeps the line that would need it.

**Why.** Each is short in Python and has no one word in Zeno, and each
is common. A function with its comment says plainly what is done, and
the person can replace it. `sorted` is generic over `Ordered`, so one
function serves lists of numbers and of texts.

**Not chosen.** Adding these to Zeno's library. That is a change to
the language, and decision 6.1 says Zeno gets a method only where it
cannot say the thing in one short expression already. It may come
later; the converter does not decide it.

### 62.12 Where each name is declared

**The rule.** A name is declared with `let` (given once) or `var` where
it gets its first value, if every use is in that block or further in.
Otherwise it is declared before the outermost statement that holds all
its uses, outside every loop, with the first value of its type (`0`,
`""`, `[]`, `none`).

**Why.** Python has one set of names for a whole function; Zeno has
one for each block. The first value is never read by a program Python
would run to the end, since Python would stop there with `NameError`
(62.18).

### 62.13 A parameter given a new value

**The rule.** `def f(n): n = n + 1` is `function f(n_given: int)` with
`var n = n_given` as its first line; a call that names it says
`n_given=`.

**Why.** A parameter of Zeno cannot change, and cannot be shadowed in
the function's first block. The other name is the smallest change that
keeps every line of the body as it was.

### 62.14 A loop's variable read after the loop

**The rule.** Where a `for` variable is read after the loop, given a
value inside it, or is a plain variable as well, the loop of Zeno
counts with `word_item` and its first line is `word = word_item`. The
name is then planned as the plain variable it is.

**Why.** A `for` of Zeno has its variable to itself, and it is gone
after the loop; in Python it stays. `for line in lines: ...` then
`print(line)` is common.

### 62.15 Parts of texts and lists cut as Python cuts them

**The rule.** `xs[a:b]` is `xs.slice(min(a, len(xs)), min(b,
len(xs)))`, a negative literal end counts from the end and stops at
0, and the list must be a plain name or field so that it is worked out
once.

**Why.** Python gives what there is of a part past the end; Zeno's
`slice` raises `IndexError`. Clamping is what Python does, written out.

### 62.16 A question asked out

**The rule.** `if x:` is written as the question Python asks of that
type: `x != 0`, `x != ""`, `len(x) > 0`, `x is not none`. `and` and
`or` are values only between bools.

**Why.** Zeno has no truth of a number or a list (2.4), and
Python's `a or b` gives one of the two values, where Zeno's gives a
bool.

### 62.17 A loop that changes what it goes over is kept

**The rule.** A `for` whose block may change the list or dict it goes
over is kept, and so is one whose block calls a function of the file
that may change it, by its name or a field of that name.

**Why.** A `for` of Zeno takes its items when it begins; Python takes
each as it comes to it. The two agree as long as nothing changes the
list.

### 62.18 What is not promised

A program Python stops with `NameError` or `UnboundLocalError`; whole
numbers past 64 bits (loud in Zeno, but `int()` of a huge float gives
Zeno's largest); what a kept function's annotation says it gives; one
list under two names while a loop goes over one; `strip` and `split`
on spaces outside ASCII; when a kept `import` runs; the last digit of
`sin`. Each is in `convert.md`. Each is rare, and each but the first
two would need the converter to run the program to know.

### 62.19 How it is checked

**The rule.** `tools/convert.py` converts each program in
`tools/convert`, runs it with `python3` and with `zeno run`, and
compares what they print, or what Zeno prints with `x.expect` where a
note says why it differs, and then the report must have that note. The
first line of each program, `# kept: N`, is how many pieces are to be
kept. `cargo test convert` has unit tests of the reader and the
writer. The workflow `convert.yml` runs both on every push that
changes the converter.

**Why the count.** A rule that stops working keeps a piece that was
Zeno, and the program still prints the same. Only the count shows it.

### 62.20 Nothing else changes

`convert` is a new command. No word, rule or library of the language
was changed for it, and `tools/same.py` builds every earlier program
as before. The command writes a new file and will not write over one
unless it is told `--replace` or given `--to`.

### 62.21 Left for later

- ~~**C** next: a file of C written as Zeno, what it cannot read left in
  an `inline c` block~~: **done**, chapter 63. Still left:
  `--declare header.h`, to write the declarations of `c.library` from a
  header.
- **A list or dict given to a function of the block** where the Zeno
  never uses it again after the call, which would be safe.
- **`lambda`, functions inside functions, tuples as values**, as Zeno
  gets them.
- **TypeScript and JavaScript**, then Java.

**How it is built.** `convert.rs`: the command, `Note`, `Report`.
`convert_python.rs`: `lex`, `pieces`, `Parser`. `convert_python_write.rs`:
`units_of`, `names_of`, `loop_names`, `spread`, `tables_of`, `round`,
`plan` with `outlasting` and `after_kept_loops`, `Helper`, `assemble`,
`convert`. `convert_python_values.rs`: `expr` and the rest of an
expression. `convert_python_lines.rs`: `statement`, `for_loop`,
`function`, `class`.

## 63. A file of C written again as Zeno: `zeno convert`

The second language of chapter 62, as Partha asked: C after Python.
[`convert-c.md`](convert-c.md) is the walkthrough.

```sh
zeno convert meter.c       # writes meter.zeno, and says what it did
```

Everything in chapter 62 that is not about Python holds for C as it
is: one promise, never silently wrong (62.1); inside `zeno`, read by
hand (62.2); one block; Zeno's checker has the last word (62.9); notes
once for each kind (62.10); a new command that changes nothing else
(62.20). This chapter is what C needs besides.

### 63.1 Pieces are declarations, and a function is Zeno or C

**The rule.** The file is cut at each `;` outside braces, at the `}`
that ends a function, and at each line of the preprocessor. A function
is written as Zeno whole, or kept as C whole.

**Why.** A C file is a list of declarations, and that is what a reader
of C sees as one thing. Half a function in each language would need
the two to share its local variables, which they cannot (62.3).

### 63.2 The numbers are C's, bit for bit

**The rule.** Each type is read as C reads it on a 64-bit machine
(LP64: `int` 32 bits, `long` 64), and every sum gives what C gives:

| C | Zeno |
|---|---|
| `uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `uint32_t` and the `unsigned` of the same size | `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, with `u8.wrap(...)` where C goes round |
| The signed whole numbers | `int`, and a store into a smaller one checked (`i32(...)`) |
| `uint64_t`, `unsigned long`, `unsigned long long` | `u64`, with `u64.wrap(...)` where C goes round |
| `size_t` | `int`, where the value can never be below zero; else kept |
| `float`, `double` | `f32`, `float` |
| `/`, `%` of numbers that may be below zero | `c_divide`, `c_remainder`, toward zero |

**Why.** A converter for a firmware engineer's C that gets a checksum
wrong by one bit is worse than none. Zeno has `u8`, `u16`, `u32` and
`f32` (2.8, chapter 41), so the sums that matter on a board can be written
exactly.

**Why `size_t` is an `int`, and `uint64_t` a `u64`.** Zeno's `u64`
(chapter 42) meets an `int` only through `u64( )`. A `size_t` counts
and indexes beside `int` on nearly every line and is never past 2\*\*63,
so as a `u64` the Zeno would be a cast on every line for nothing; as an
`int` it reads as Zeno, and the converter keeps what could differ (`-`
or `~` of one, or one beside a number that may be below zero). A
`uint64_t` is asked for where all 64 bits matter: a hash, a random
generator, a register. So it is a `u64`, and an `int` beside one is
made a `u64` as C makes it, `u64(n)` when it is never below zero and
`u64.wrap(n)` when it may be, which is C's conversion exactly.

**Where the wrap goes.** `u64.wrap` reaches through `+ - * <<` inside
it (42.6) but not through `& | ^ ~`, so the sides of those are cut
first: `h ^= u64.wrap(h << 13)`.

**A wrap where it is looked at.** `a + b + c` of `u32` is one
`u32.wrap(a + b + c)`, not three, since going round once at the end
gives the same bits as going round at each step, as long as the sum
fits in 64 bits. A product of two `u32` may not, so it goes through
`times_u32`, which cuts each half first.

**Not chosen.** Writing `int` for every whole number and leaving the
sizes to the reader: most of the C worth converting is about sizes.

### 63.3 Signed overflow is loud, not cut

**The rule.** A signed sum C would carry past the top, or store into a
smaller type, stops the Zeno with `OverflowError`. The report has a
note where a store is checked.

**Why.** C leaves a signed overflow undefined, so no answer is C's.
Stopping says so. Cutting the bits would pick one compiler's answer and
hide it.

### 63.4 `printf` as an f-string, and a line held until it ends

**The rule.** A `printf` with a format written out is an f-string; each
conversion that Zeno shows the same (`%d`, `%5d`, `%-5d`, `%05d`, `%x`,
`%X`, `%.2f`, `%s`, `%-10s`, `%c`) is written, and one it does not
(`%e`, `%g`, `%o`, `%p`, `%+d`) keeps the piece. When any line is
written in parts, every line goes through `write_text`, which holds a
line until its `\n` comes, and `finish_text()` ends the last.

**Why.** Zeno's `print` writes whole lines. A program that writes in
parts must be written so that the lines come out as they did, and one
helper for every line keeps them in order. A kept C function that
writes too would be out of order with the held line, so then the Zeno
that writes in parts is kept.

### 63.5 A struct is copied where C copies it

**The rule.** A struct is a class. Where C copies one (`b = a;`, a
struct put into an array, given to a function that changes it) the Zeno
calls `copy()`, a method written once in the class. Where nothing can
tell (a struct a function only reads, or gives back from where it was
made), it is not copied.

**Why.** A class is shared in Zeno where a struct is a value in C. A
copy everywhere would be right and hard to read; a copy nowhere would
be wrong. The converter knows which functions change which parameters,
so it can write exactly the copies C made.

### 63.6 Three kinds of pointer are written; the rest is kept

**The rule.**

| A pointer that | Is written as |
|---|---|
| is indexed (`values[i]`), or is an array parameter | a list |
| points to one number the function writes through (`*out = ...`) | a list of one; the caller writes `let x_box = [x]`, the call, `x = x_box[0]` |
| points to a struct (`p->x`) | the object |
| is `const char *` | a text |

A call that gives the same variable twice, or a list and a place in it,
is kept. Every other use of a pointer is kept: a pointer variable,
pointer sums, `NULL`, `malloc`, lists made of pointers, a pointer to a
function.

**Why.** These four are what most functions of C use pointers for: to
give an array, to give back more than one value, to change a struct.
Each has a Zeno form that means exactly the same. A pointer kept as a
value (a list made of `next` pointers) has no Zeno form that would read
as Zeno, and C does it well, so it stays C.

**Why two places are kept.** `swap(&x, &x)` changes one variable in C.
The boxes are two lists in Zeno; the second write would win, and the
result could differ. It is rare, so it is kept rather than worked out.

### 63.7 What C can call, and where a variable lives

**The rule.** C can call only C: a function that a kept function calls
is kept. A variable lives on one side: a global that a kept function
uses is kept, and a Zeno function that uses a kept global is kept in
turn. The Zeno calls a kept function through the block with numbers,
floats, bools and texts C does not change; a call that would give it a
struct, an array or a text it may change is kept.

**Why.** The block is a library of C (chapter 61), and a library cannot
call back into the program that loaded it. A global copied to both
sides would be two variables. What crosses into the block is what the
bridge of chapter 44 carries by value, so nothing can be changed behind
the Zeno's back.

### 63.8 What the preprocessor changes keeps the whole file

**The rule.** `#include`, a `#define` of a value and `#pragma once` are
read. Any other line of the preprocessor (`#if`, `#ifdef`, `#error`,
`#line`) keeps the whole file as one block, with `main` called.

**Why.** An `#ifdef` chooses between two programs. The converter would
have to choose one, and the person who wrote it meant both. A `#define`
with arguments is kept with what uses it, since Zeno has no macros.

### 63.9 `main` is called at the end, with the program's arguments

**The rule.** `main` is called at the end of the file. A `main` that
may give back other than 0 ends the program with it
(`program.exit(exit_status)`). A `main(int argc, char **argv)` is kept,
and the block is given a few lines of C, `convert_argument` and
`convert_main`, so the Zeno can pass it the file's name and then each
word of `program.arguments()`. A note says `argv[0]` is the file's
name, where C gives the path the program was started by. A `main` the
converter cannot read is not called, and the report says so.

**Why.** A C program is its `main`. Without the call the Zeno would
print nothing, silently. The words cannot go across as one array (the
bridge carries no array of texts), so they go one at a time, which it
does carry.

### 63.10 Kept pieces are copied with all they need

**The rule.** The block has every `#include`, `#define`, macro, struct,
enum and typedef of the file in front of the kept pieces, and the
prototypes of kept functions. `static` is taken off a kept function so
the Zeno can reach it.

**Why.** The kept C must be compiled as it was. Copying everything that
declares and nothing that runs is always right, and costs a few lines.

### 63.11 Names, and the words of Zeno

**The rule.** A name of C that is a word or a builtin of Zeno (`len`,
`print`, `str`, `sum`, `match`) is written with a `_` after it, in the
Zeno only; the block keeps C's names.

**Why.** It is the smallest change that keeps the name readable and
can never clash with another name of the file, which the converter
checks.

### 63.12 Notes

C has two kinds: a number stored in a smaller type that does not fit
stops the program (63.3), and the last line written in parts is ended
(63.4); and a third for `argv[0]` (63.9).

### 63.13 What is not promised

What C leaves undefined (a signed overflow, an index past the end, a
variable read before it has a value: Zeno stops on the first two, and
gives the third 0); a `size_t` past 2\*\*63, which stops the Zeno
(63.2); the order C works out the arguments of one call in; `long` as 32 bits, as on Windows; the last digit of `sin`. Each is
in `convert-c.md`.

### 63.14 How it is checked

As 62.19, with the C compiled by `cc -std=c11` and run: what it prints
and the status it ends with must be what `zeno run` gives. The first
line of each program, `// kept: N`, is how many pieces are to be kept.
The programs are in `tools/convert/*.c`: a ring buffer, frame parser
and state machine as they are written for a board, a hash of 64 bits
and two random generators, a sieve, unsigned sums at each size, structs, pointers, `switch`, `printf` in parts, a
`main` that reads its arguments, and a file the preprocessor changes.

### 63.15 Left for later

- `--declare header.h`, to write the declarations of `c.library` from a
  header (62.21).
- Pointer variables that only walk an array (`p++` over `values`), as
  an index.
- `%e` and `%g`, as Zeno gets a way to show them.
- `long` as 32 bits, with a flag, for C written for Windows.
- TypeScript and JavaScript, then Java.

**How it is built.** `convert_c.rs`: `lex`, `pieces`, `Parser` with
`item`, `Names`, `IntTy`, `CTy`, `signature`. `convert_c_lines.rs`:
`Helper`, `Kind`, `FnInfo`, `World`, `Val`, and `W` with `expr`,
`binary`, `arith`, `call`, `output`, `format`, `statement`, `for_loop`,
`switch`, `function`. `convert_c_write.rs`: `convert`, `spread`,
`write_unit`, `assemble`, `takes_arguments`, `whole`.
